concepts.body: A review is a separate run linked to a finished source; a requested fix is another attempt, not a change to that source run.
concepts.detail: Review-kind templates need a source run and cannot use the ordinary standalone template launch. Presets select a review template, prompt, optional tests and blocking action. Attachments request automatic reviews after successful source completion; each preset gets its own durable launch intent. Review verdicts and fix decisions remain on the review run, with links back to the source and onward to a fix run when one starts.
concepts.title: Source run ≠ review run ≠ fix attempt

concepts.body: A reusable named definition differs from one execution of a particular version.
concepts.detail: WorkflowTemplate owns activeVersion and inputSchema; WorkflowTemplateVersion owns spec JSON; WorkflowRun stores specSnapshot, timing, status and lineage.
concepts.title: Template ≠ run

concepts.body: A node is a graph instruction; an activity is a side-effect boundary.
concepts.detail: cond/set/terminate are interpreter control flow. step, agent, mcp, eval, containerStep and shell nodes are dispatched through one table that shares input resolution, retry, onFail/onError and recording; agent, mcp, eval and containerStep become named worker steps with their own executors, and shell goes to the workflow’s shell activity. Human and signal nodes wait durably.
concepts.title: Node ≠ activity

concepts.body: An agent is a versioned persona/config; a skill is prompt text; a tool executes code.
concepts.detail: AgentSkillRef orders skills. toolKeys select capabilities, and mcpConnectionId links a tool source. The implementer supports local workspace tools; a generic agent node gets them only when it asks for a checkout of the run’s repository (workspace: true), under the agent-run grant (no opinion means the read tools).
concepts.title: Agent ≠ skill ≠ tool

concepts.body: A connection identifies a team-owned external target; a workspace materializes its execution context.
concepts.detail: Connection.type/config/token describe integration targets. Providers are git_repo, document, issue_tracker, record and api_only. Registered types have uneven handler coverage. A run may use only the connections pinned on it at creation.
concepts.title: Connection ≠ workspace

concepts.body: A stored input can be reused across executions; the acting launcher can change.
concepts.detail: RunInput.requestedById is submission history. WorkflowRun.launchedById identifies this launch; temporalRunId prevents trusting a reused workflow ID across executions. An Idempotency-Key on a work request binds to that user’s first submission and replays the run it started. A ticket’s workflow id is allocated with every row of the same repository (same host, owner and name compared case-insensitively, active or not) counted as one repository, so a run in flight on any of them conflicts; when the conflicting run belongs to another row, the response says the ticket is running without naming its workflow id. A retry or agent re-run keeps the request identity and adds an execution, which the Requests view groups under it. A service principal’s run records requestedByServiceId, carries no launchedById and uses the platform credential. A run an event automation starts is nobody’s launch: it carries no launchedById and uses the platform credential, never a user’s saved token. Runs started by labelling an issue or a pull request, by pushing commits, or by a person’s pull-request feedback (a changes-requested review or a fix command, not a Qodo review) are the exception, and only in attribution: that person’s linked GitHub account must resolve to an active platform user who is a member of the repository and passes the same launch decision as any launch, and that user is recorded as requestedById; the run still acts as the platform.
concepts.title: Request ≠ launch identity

concepts.body: Spec and run-pinned settings are captured, but not every configuration read is frozen.
concepts.detail: GLOBAL agent version maps, skill revisions and run-pinned settings are captured at run start; more-specific agent rows resolve their current active versions. A run-pinned key missing from a run’s snapshot is pinned the first time an activity’s request context reads it, at the value that read resolves, and a value already pinned is never replaced; a channel turn’s run is pinned at its own start and backfilled at its Slack channel’s scope, and a failed backfill falls back to the live value until the next lookup. Each agent’s runtime is pinned on the run at start, or at first resolution for an agent the start snapshot lacks. Non-run-pinned settings and credentials can change. This is selective reproducibility, not a hermetically frozen run. A credential pinned by an agent is not frozen either: the worker checks it on each resolution (behind the config cache) and falls back, with a warning, to the provider cascade if the pin is missing, belongs to another provider, or is out of scope for the run. A lookup that fell through to a broader scope (the usual case for a team run) is cached for CONFIG_CACHE_FALLTHROUGH_TTL_MS (5 s by default, never above the full window, 0 disables) rather than the full window, so a narrower row inserted later is seen within seconds.
concepts.title: Snapshots ≠ total immutability

concepts.body: Temporal persists execution history; PostgreSQL persists application state and searchable evidence.
concepts.detail: WorkflowRun/Step/Trace are a projection used by API/dashboard; ActiveWorkflow tracks engineering status and spend. Those records are not a replacement for Temporal history.
concepts.title: Two persistence planes

concepts.body: A policy decision records permission to proceed; another activity writes the outcome.
concepts.detail: publishOutcome returns auto/require_approval and approverCount. The template must route that result, and the step that writes checks the run’s latest decision that required approval: writeOutcome, a mutating runTool and a non-read-only mcp node all go through the same guard in lib/externalWrite.ts.
concepts.title: Decision ≠ side effect

concepts.body: Signals measure specific axes; passing one does not guarantee the task is correct.
concepts.detail: Online EvalResult rows include gates, review, merge, judge, trajectory, policy and PII. The offline harness compares paired golden-test outcomes and treats infrastructure errors separately.
concepts.title: Score ≠ correctness proof

concepts.body: A trusted signature proves publisher/content integrity, not safe execution or correct prompts.
concepts.detail: Install validates hash/schema and trust policy; skills and agents still require local verification. References to deployment-local MCP IDs may need rewiring. A bundle may declare dependencies only on connection types a generic step can actually reach (git_repo, mcp, issue_tracker, notion, confluence, zendesk, slack_workspace); the server refuses an install naming another, and the SDK’s validator applies the same list so an author learns it before shipping. An agent may carry its runtime: a harness runtime with a non-Anthropic model of its own is refused, an install shows a warning for each agent it moves onto the harness, and a bundle that omits the runtime leaves an installed agent’s runtime as it was.
concepts.title: Trust ≠ verification of behavior

concepts.body: Every automation decision is a row that outlives the automation, the connection and often the run.
concepts.detail: AutomationFire records one decision about one occurrence. An event automation’s rows are keyed on its owner — a repository (host/owner/repo, lowercased) or @kind/id for a team’s endpoint — not on the automation or its row, and the guards read that owner’s whole ledger for the source: deleting and recreating an automation cannot forget what was done, and two automations matching two workflows that fail on one push cannot open two fixes. Four keys do the work: dedupeKey names the occurrence on its host (a redelivery is decided once), subjectKey is what one run is enough for (a commit, an issue), scopeKey is what cooldown and in-flight count over (a branch, an issue), and producedKey is what a run produced (a pushed fix commit), matched by itself so a renamed repository still recognises its own output. A schedule fire and a template webhook call write rows of their own into the same table, best-effort and under an @owner key, so the Automations page can say what came of each; no event guard reads them. The daily prune deletes rows that started no run once past retention and keeps STARTED rows and any row with a producedKey.
concepts.title: Decision ledger ≠ run history

concepts.body: Memory is recalled automatically; knowledge is reviewed, published and retrieved only where granted.
concepts.detail: MemoryItem holds repository lessons and channel memory that later runs recall without asking. KnowledgeItem is a versioned record with an owner team, a status and a visibility, which a person approves for a wider audience and an agent reaches only through tools its toolKeys name or the knowledge steps.
concepts.title: Knowledge ≠ memory

concepts.body: A service principal is a team’s machine identity, with scopes and limits instead of a role.
concepts.detail: Its token sets request.principal, never request.user, so a handler cannot mistake it for a person; it reaches only routes that declare service scopes, and its runs act with the platform credential.
concepts.title: Principal ≠ person

concepts.body: A draft can hold lint errors and unaudited code; a version that serves runs cannot.
concepts.detail: Promote, activation and an experiment arm refuse a version with lint errors or an unreviewed AI-generated version, and re-check its authored code against its audit rows. A version snapshots its spec and its input schema.
concepts.title: Saved version ≠ serving version

concepts.body: A share lets a team see a repository and, unless it is view only, start work on it; the owning team’s budget and key still pay for the run.
concepts.detail: ConnectionTeamShare.canLaunch is read for new work only: a member of a sharee team with every reaching share set to view only can see the repository and its work but the repository decision refuses start-new-work (the dashboard hides it, and the server decides). Owning-team members and platform ADMINs are not held back. Epics, PRD runs and campaigns need team LEAD or ADMIN on the team that owns each repository (team.launch.multi-repo, asked of every repository’s owner); membership through a share does not count, and only a platform ADMIN bypasses the check. Cost lands on the owning team’s attribution and cap, not the sharee team’s.
concepts.title: Seeing ≠ launching ≠ paying

concepts.body: What a role may do is the capability catalog’s answer; which repositories a person can reach and which runs they can see are decided separately.
concepts.detail: A capability answers “may this team, organization or platform role do this for the team”. Reach answers which repositories a person may launch on: membership of the owning team or a share with launch allowed, plus the GitHub gate where it enforces. Visibility answers which runs and steps a person can read. All three must allow an action. An organization ADMIN holds governance capabilities on its teams (members, settings, repositories, budget) without being a member, and management listings add those teams, but launching work, answering approvals and holding credentials need a team role, and the launch paths keep the membership-based reach rule. A platform ADMIN passes capabilities and most gates; the separation-of-duties constraints are the exception, and a deactivated team removes a team role’s non-read capabilities without removing its members’ repository reach.
concepts.title: Capability ≠ reach ≠ visibility

features.body: Repository setup can name encrypted credentials, fetch LFS objects in submodules and key dependency caches from tracked-file globs.
features.detail: Setup secret management uses the LEAD route gate and the owning-team shell-author check; values are encrypted on the repository (a name the repository does not set can instead be filled by a team secret granted to it) while responses expose names, last-four markers and timestamps. Audit entries identify the name, not the submitted value. Setup resolves only the definition's named secrets, fails on missing or undecryptable values, and passes them through secretEnv to setup commands. LFS pulls cover the main checkout and fetched submodules, each with its own pinned endpoint and credential. The platform-wide, admin-managed workspace.lfsStorageHosts setting supplies additional storage destinations for restricted/blocked locks when LFS is enabled. Cache key globs search the Git index, not untracked dependency trees, and include matched paths and hashes; an excessive match set disables caching rather than setup.
features.title: Setup credentials, LFS storage destinations and tracked cache inputs

features.body: Opening a setup-file pull request accepts a queued request rather than waiting for the worker to finish.
features.detail: The authorized repository route starts a bounded Temporal execution and returns 202 with a repository-prefixed request id. Status reads recheck management access and reject another repository's request id. RUNNING is reported as queued, whether waiting for a worker or already executing; completion reports the PR or refusal, and a timed-out request reports failure. A Temporal connection error propagates instead of being relabeled as a completed failure. The repository editor polls queued status and distinguishes opened, refused and status-read errors. The proposal remains add-only: it refuses a setup file already present on the default branch.
features.title: Setup-file proposals have asynchronous request status

features.body: An emailed magic link first opens a confirmation page; loading that page alone does not spend the sign-in token.
features.detail: The gateway wraps the verification URL as a dashboard link with token, email and callback in its fragment, keeping them out of the initial dashboard request URL. The page reads the fragment without automatically verifying; an explicit Sign in action navigates to the auth verification endpoint. A missing token shows an invalid-link state. Auth configures a ten-minute link lifetime, and an error callback skips session bridging on the login page. This avoids consumption by simple link fetches, not every scanner or client that can interact with a page; verification itself sends the token to the auth endpoint.
features.title: Magic-link sign-in requires a confirmation action

features.body: The run page filters loaded trace events and opens captured Playwright traces in a self-hosted viewer.
features.detail: Trace search matches names, errors and available payloads, with kind, error-only and node filters. The detailed stream initially draws the newest matching events and offers more; an empty match is distinct from no loaded events. Loading full payloads pauses run-detail polling; a failed full-payload request falls back to the trimmed view with a notice. Resume live updates restores trimmed polling. Evidence cards open a captured trace through an authorized short-lived link in the web app's bundled Playwright viewer, not through the static platform explorer.
features.title: Trace inspection distinguishes live, full-payload and captured evidence

features.body: Generate repository setup locally, manage its saved definition through the API, run connection probes and pass an explicit launch egress policy.
features.detail: repos setup init runs before token loading and writes a starter .auto-swe/setup.yml from tracked file names, with a bounded directory-walk fallback when Git listing fails. An unrecognized stack produces an editable placeholder, not a verified install recipe. An existing readable setup file requires --force to replace. The command neither runs its install steps nor uploads them; a saved repository definition still wins over the checked-in file. repos setup prints, replaces from a parsed file, or clears that saved definition through the gateway's repository route. connections test calls the stored-config batch probe; repos test-access resolves an accessible repository and asks its scoped probe. Both have JSON output and exit 1 for returned failed checks; gateway HTTP errors exit 2. An empty or all-skipped batch exits 0, so zero alone does not establish readiness. run, agent run and workflows run validate open/restricted/blocked for --egress-policy and pass it to the gateway; omitting the flag leaves default policy resolution to the platform. These clients do not enforce server authorization or network isolation locally.
features.title: CLI setup authoring, diagnostics and launch policy

features.body: Choose free-form template or conventional pull-request titles, with repository overrides and a bounded optional classifier.
features.detail: Repository title format and nonblank template override scoped workflow.prTitleFormat and workflow.prTitleTemplate settings; the workflow-default template is the last template fallback. Conventional format uses a fixed workflow.prTitleType without a model, or asks prTitler for a type and summary from bounded request text and changed-file names when the type is auto. Classification failure or malformed output falls back to a conventional type and the request's first nonempty line, with the ticket ID as a final summary source. The formatter tidies and bounds that title; this classification is not a review verdict. The workflow PR path renders its chosen template; an Agent Run retains its descriptive legacy title in template mode unless a repository or registry template is explicit. Agent Run title policy uses its team/organization, while its classifier agent resolves at organization scope rather than the owning team's agent override. Policy/settings reads themselves are outside the classification fallback. The conventional form is type: summary within 72 characters: an unknown type becomes chore, the summary is made one line with its first letter lower-cased unless it opens with an acronym, and no scope or breaking-change marker is produced. prTitler is a tool-less, cheap-model persona that sees the request and the changed files’ operations and paths, never the code, and is not launchable as an Agent Run.
features.title: Repository-aware pull-request title policy

features.body: A scheduled, bounded sweep removes labelled workspace containers or pods that satisfy backend-specific expiry rules.
features.detail: The gateway synchronizes an environment-controlled workspace-reaper schedule at startup, every fifteen minutes by default. Its activity uses the selected worker’s backend and judges each object from its own labels and age, never from the process’s memory, so a live workspace of another worker on the same daemon or namespace is left alone. Docker lists marked containers (workspaces, service sidecars, egress helpers and ephemeral step containers carry a marker label and a creation stamp) and removes those past the longest activity that can hold a workspace plus an hour of slack, about seven hours, oldest first; containers with missing, invalid or future creation labels are retained. Kubernetes lists workspace-marked pods in its configured namespace, rechecks both labels and ignores pods already deleting, then selects terminal pods or pods beyond their deadline plus a ten-minute grace. Each sweep removes at most 25 objects (on Docker a workspace and each sidecar count separately), and records listing and removal failures for later sweeps without throwing. This cleans execution resources, independently of the run reaper that finalizes and bills stranded run rows.
features.title: Orphaned workspace cleanup

features.body: Run stored connection checks together, or inspect a repository's platform credential and the caller's saved token separately.
features.detail: The platform connections/test route (gated on platform.integrations.manage, so platform ADMIN only) checks configured GitHub, Slack, tracker, external knowledge and Figma integrations, per-host GitHub credentials, the configured approver App, active package registries and model-provider keys across scopes. Unconfigured integrations are skipped; the tracker also needs a real ticket ID. Per-probe exceptions become failed entries. The dashboard starts these checks only when requested and groups failures, working connections and skips. Batch checks use stored configuration; individual integration forms can also test supported draft values. GitHub App testing validates identity, mints the configured installation token and asks which repositories it reaches. A repository's separate test-access route requires team.repos.manage on the repository’s owning team (a LEAD or ADMIN of that team, an ADMIN of its organization, or a platform ADMIN); a passing check stamps the repository’s accessVerifiedAt, and it checks platform credentials and, when present, the caller's own token against that repository and its saved default branch. The batch does not include MCP servers or per-repository access. Probes answer with fixed wording per status class and never echo a remote body; the GitHub requests of the App, per-host, approver and repository probes, and the registry probe, use the guarded fetch and refuse or do not follow redirects, while the installation-token mint inside an App or repository check uses a plain fetch. The CLI’s connections test prints one line per connection, failing first, and exits 1 when any fails, and repos test-access does the same for one repository. The in-app assistant may start the all-connections check only as a confirmed action, and is refused the tests of a stored provider credential, a host credential or the approver App.
features.title: On-demand connection diagnostics

features.body: A run can finish while its tracker update fails; terminal write-back failures have a separate, classified notice.
features.detail: After finalizing a run, the worker best-effort syncs a real tracker ticket when notifications are enabled: SUCCESS sends workflow_completed, while FAILED or TIMED_OUT sends workflow_failed. The terminal event carries no PR URL. A returned failure is merged into contextSnapshot.trackerWriteback as the event and a closed-set failure class, never provider response text. GitHub scope refusal distinguishes an out-of-scope repository from a ticket ID that resolves to no repository. Jira and Linear ids name no repository, so their writes are held to the tracker.allowedProjectKeys list instead (empty means unrestricted): a ticket whose project or team key is not listed makes no provider call and is recorded as out_of_scope, while a list or run scope that cannot be read writes nothing but is recorded as unknown, so a transient fault never reads as a policy decision. A Jira ticket with no transition to a status named like the target is recorded as no_transition. The record keeps the tracker provider that skipped the write (a record from before that falls back to the currently configured provider), and the run page words out_of_scope per provider: a repository the run does not target for GitHub, a project or team the operator does not allow for Jira or Linear. For out_of_scope, no_repository and no_transition the page does not say the status may be unmoved, because the platform knows nothing was written. Providers report their first refused write; the run page parses the marker and uses fixed wording to distinguish a failed completion update from a missing failure comment. The notice does not change the run's terminal status.
features.title: Tracker write-back is separate from run success

features.body: PR evaluation combines matching source-run and successful linked-review verdicts; a clean linked review can fill absent evidence, not erase an existing warning.
features.detail: The severity reader considers source-run network outputs for the exact current head and takes worst-of with successful linked runs in PR or branch mode. Linked outputs must name that head and must not explicitly say diffVerified: false; stored mode is excluded. Network rejections and a negative published summary contribute at least WARNING even if their findings list is empty. When no matching original result exists, eligible linked verdicts supply the signal. A matching original with missing, empty or malformed verdicts returns missing instead of being rescued by a clean linked review. Brief findings merge separately, deduplicate by file/line/category/description, and retain linked-run attribution. The signal does not by itself grant low risk or approval; all other evaluation rules still apply.
features.title: Linked review evidence fills gaps without lowering original severity

features.body: The PR comment provides a deterministic reading guide alongside the evaluation, not another verdict or a test run.
features.detail: The brief separates extracted ticket criteria and open questions, recorded test counts, captured browser-evidence counts, current CI and selected current-head review findings. Optional brief-only reads fail to unknown, rather than independently raising the risk class. Tests and UI are recorded evidence, not coverage verification or a fresh browser run. Reading order puts contracts/manifests before directory-grouped source with heuristically paired tests. Skim claims require a same-directory exact rename without content changes or a narrowly checked whitespace-only patch; paths excluded by skim policy or risk flags cannot qualify, and whitespace-significant formats cannot qualify on the whitespace proof. Model prose is bounded and escaped; claimed handling of open questions is explicitly the run's own account, not independent verification.
features.title: A reviewer brief separates intent, evidence and a reading path

features.body: Seeded graphs maintain repository documentation, remediate a reported vulnerability, or review a Confluence document before planning tickets.
features.detail: docs-refresh uses the implementation step with allowedPaths, stops without a PR on an empty change, otherwise opens a draft without an in-run human gate or CI loop. Its prompt asks for markdown-only edits, but the executable guard permits markdown anywhere and any file under docs/. vulnerability-remediation consumes an advisory supplied in the request: it does not discover advisories. A no-change result succeeds without a PR; otherwise the graph runs the vulnerability and test gates, opens a draft and enters the shared bounded CI-fix loop. Both gates are advisory (onFail: warn), so a failed test or scan alone does not block the draft, and a scan is not assurance that the advisory is resolved. confluence-review-to-tickets uses separate reviewer and planner agents and checked JSON replies; a blocker or major finding forces not-ready. It policy-gates page comments, stops after comments when not ready, and otherwise asks a person to approve the proposed ticket structure, allowing bounded revisions, before a separate policy gate for ticket creation. Invalid review output terminates before comments; invalid plan output terminates before tickets, but comments may already exist. Neither automatically opens a human correction step.
features.title: Documentation, vulnerability and document-review library packs

features.body: Review-loop templates stop when a rejected review repeats its coarse rejection fingerprint, even if the finding text or line numbers differ.
features.detail: The reviewLoop helper passes the previous rejection fingerprint into runReviewNetwork. The activity marks a non-approved result stalled when a non-empty fingerprint matches. The fingerprint counts rejecting findings by reviewer, category and file, excluding reviewer crashes; it ignores finding text and line numbers, so a match is not proof of identical findings. The graph stores the rejection, checks stalled before its retry limit, and routes to its configured exhausted path. Approval clears the fingerprint. The fix node can inherit a template's explicit fixConfig, including allowedPaths; constraints on an initial implementation are not automatically universal constraints on every future session. Built-in template sync appends changed specs and promotes a still-active built-in version only when it is not in a live experiment; admin versions and deactivations are preserved. Review-kind metadata is filled separately when absent, without rewriting existing specs.
features.title: Repeated rejection fingerprints stop the fix loop

features.body: Review a finished workflow or agent run manually or through attached presets, with separate results and optional guarded fix rounds.
features.detail: Review-kind library templates provide network, Qodo and human-review variants. Manual launch checks source-run control and repository access; launch preparation checks review.enabled and template/preset scope. Global presets are platform-admin managed (a preset route that names no team asks team.codereview.manage with no resource, which only a platform ADMIN satisfies); a team’s presets and attachments are managed by a LEAD or ADMIN of that team through the same capability, and listed to its members through team.codereview.read, with no platform role involved. Team presets cannot be attached or launched across teams. The source-run picker exposes globals plus that source's team. Successful non-review runs enqueue independent global and team attachment intents, dispatched with durable claims and a stale-intent sweep, with bounded attempts rather than indefinite retries. PR and branch reviews verify recorded heads; stored diffs are checked and applied at the recorded base into a local-only commit. Optional runTests runs the repository's test gate on a verified checkout. Large changes are reviewed in bounded chunks inside one network step, merging worst-of verdicts and deduplicated findings. The run page links reviews and shows verification, verdicts and fix status. PR-mode publication posts a marked comment and requests reevaluation; successful PR/branch linked reviews with a matching head and no explicit unverified flag can supply otherwise missing PR review evidence, but cannot lower original evidence. PR fixes use an opted-in review_findings feedback automation and its existing guards; stored fixes launch a same-agent deliver:none follow-up. Transient failures can be retried with distinct, deduplicated attempts and DB-backed findings.
features.title: Code review after a run

features.body: Prepare repository workspaces with submodules, LFS and ordered install commands, optionally restoring a matching dependency cache.
features.detail: A repository's saved setup definition takes precedence over .auto-swe/setup.yml read from the workspace's base or pinned commit; only when neither exists does workspace.repoSetupStackDefaults enable detected-stack installs. A present invalid definition fails instead of falling through, and an explicit empty definition suppresses the fallbacks. Workspace creation resolves setup before the egress lock and executes it after the lock, as the workspace user (UID 1000 by default); with workspace.setupEgressPolicy set to open or restricted it runs under that looser setup lock, which is replaced by the run lock before agent code starts; callers that first move to the work branch defer execution until that checkout is ready. Submodules are fetched only from the repository's own host, with separately minted credentials, then LFS objects, then cache restore and sequential shell steps. Steps still run on a cache hit. Cache identity includes team, repository, definition, key-file hashes, image and architecture; caching is disabled with PostgreSQL artifact storage, and cache read/write failures do not fail otherwise successful setup. Platform admins or the owning team's admin members can manage the saved definition. The repository editor can copy or download the YAML or request a PR adding it; the proposal refuses an existing file on the default branch. The CLI can also generate a starter file locally without a token.
features.title: Repository workspace setup and dependency caches

features.body: Choose open, restricted or blocked workspace egress; a launch may narrow the configured policy, never widen it.
features.detail: workspace.egressPolicy is run-pinned at the template/team/organization scope, with restricted as the default. Restricted enforces the platform dependency-host baseline union team allowlist; open merges the baseline only with a non-empty team list, preserving unrestricted open/empty behavior. Baseline and team lists are read live, not frozen per run; template-code audit snapshots include both at sign-off. Compose and Helm enable the proxy on port 8792. GLOBAL restricted without a proxy refuses worker boot; scoped overrides retain runtime enforcement checks. The gateway rejects a widening launch request, and the worker rechecks when pinning. Restricted and blocked repository workspaces are network-locked to git and model/registry proxies, plus the forwarding proxy only for restricted and setup LFS storage hosts when needed. Docker resolves destinations to verified IP rules; Kubernetes uses pod-owned allow policies and verifies loss of direct public access. Failed locks destroy the workspace. Restricted ephemeral steps receive proxy-only holder locks; worker-originated MCP and connector calls remain outside this policy.
features.title: Run-scoped workspace egress policy

features.body: Attach Git-backed reference material at team, repository, template and run scope, pin snapshots and expose bounded read-only files and cited search results.
features.detail: Knowledge bases are separate from governed KnowledgeItems: Git is the source of truth, with no approval lifecycle. Same-organization TEAM, SHARED and ORG visibility gates attachment. Additive resolution selects at most four references, preserving mandatory team status and the most specific overrides. A Temporal execution pins SHAs and snapshot IDs; later resolutions recheck attachability. Indexing scans text files for injection, excludes flagged or incompletely scanned files and fails closed on truncated trees. Workspace agents receive read-only files and an untrusted prompt block. The text-only decomposition planner receives a separate bounded block of summaries and cited excerpts from pinned READY snapshots unless knowledgeBases is false; it requests no checkout credentials and mounts no reference files. The trusted delivery workspace does not mount KB files. Pinned KB snapshots make searchKnowledge available in Mastra and through worker-backed Claude Code and Pi tool bridges; an explicit searchKnowledge grant separately enables governed KnowledgeItems. The retrieveKnowledge activity can also merge governed results with pinned KB chunks. KB search matches the configured embedding model or reports text fallback and screens returned chunks again at recall time. File checkout and indexed search have different content boundaries; a failed checkout does not necessarily remove a ready snapshot from search. The dashboard manages KBs, links, shares and launch overrides.
features.title: Repository-backed knowledge bases

features.body: Execute versioned JSON graphs on Temporal, including bounded loops, signals, parallel branches and human pauses.
features.detail: The shared interpreter owns graph semantics; RunnableWorkflow supplies activity dispatch, signal waits, persistence and cancellation. A graph is not necessarily acyclic. A graph failure ends the run once, as a non-retryable WORKFLOW_SPEC_FAILED. A cancellation of the whole run bypasses onError, onFail and onBranchFail and ends the run CANCELLED, even inside a fan-out branch. A node’s retries stop at a failure the activity marks non-retryable, after which its onFail mode decides. A dispatch node that fails before its first attempt records a FAILED step. Before each attempt of a dispatch node the interpreter also records the step as RUNNING, one row per attempt keyed by run, node and attempt, so a live run shows the step in progress instead of only after its activity ends; the later terminal write updates that row, and after the RUNNING write the interpreter rechecks whether a fan-out has already been decided and cancels the branch rather than start the activity. A failed recording is swallowed, never failing the run. Inside concurrent fan-out branches, a signal waiter woken by a delivery another branch consumed waits out the rest of its own timeout instead of taking onTimeout at once. These paths, and the RUNNING write (interpreter-records-dispatch-start), are patched, so older histories replay the earlier behaviour.
features.title: Durable workflow graphs

features.body: Create, version, activate, import, export, compare and run reusable workflow templates.
features.detail: A template declares an input contract and workspace provider. The dashboard offers an editor and an outline view; nodes may carry optional group and title labels for display. The API validates node edges and references, refuses wait and human-step timeouts that are not positive durations, and flags context write paths through reserved segments (__proto__, prototype, constructor); a draft with such errors can be saved but not promoted, activated or used as an experiment arm. Generated versions require review before activation. When a template’s workspace provider needs a target connection that its inputs do not declare, the launch form shows a connection picker and will not submit without a choice. In the library list a workflow that cannot run shows a disabled Run with the reason (activate a draft, or promote a version). In the editor, Check workflow asks the gateway (team lead or above) to run the checks a save runs, as data: the strict parse, lint, whether the referenced agents and MCP connections exist, and the shell-authoring role and image allowlist for the template’s team. It writes no template, version or audit row and never executes the workflow, and the editor merges those findings with its own live lint, saying so when the server check could not run. Given a base version it also warns when the template has versions newer than it (STALE_BASE_VERSION); the editor sends the newest version the page knew of when it loaded, plus any version it saved or refined itself, so only versions saved elsewhere since the load are reported, and a caller that sends a name is told of RESERVED_TEMPLATE_NAME (the reserved-name rule and message the save routes share) and a team-scope NAME_CONFLICT (a lookup that mirrors the (team_id, name) unique index the save routes rely on, and pinned against a real database); a name is looked up only in a scope the caller may save into, so it reveals nothing about other teams, and a repeated global name is not reported because the save accepts it. It is a preview, not a promise that a save succeeds: it does not predict a save’s VERSION_CONFLICT (lost races for the next version number) or a name taken after the check, the editor sends no name because saving a version never renames (a rename through the metadata edit onto a taken name answers 409 NAME_CONFLICT), and a result belongs to the spec at the click and is hidden once the spec is edited. Selecting a node shows collapsed help for its type (what it does, when to use it, a gotcha, a JSON example), the palette shows only the type’s what and when on hover or focus; a node whose type this build does not know is drawn as unknown instead of breaking the canvas. Node help links to the type’s own section of the node reference and says what the node writes to its output, and the starter gallery offers specs built only from node types. The save confirmation counts container-code nodes (shell, containerStep, or a step naming the shell-category step) and nodes carrying an authored command (a gate step’s command, a runQualityGates gate’s, an eval gate scorer’s), the set the gateway gates (see the authored-code card), and the template page refuses such a save before sending it when the caller is known not to be a platform admin or an admin of the template’s team. The lint also errors on a publishOutcome risk class bound from inputs (ACTION_CLASS_BOUND) and on a syntax error in an assert scorer or approverCount expression, and warns on fields the runtime never reads (IGNORED_FIELD), on a step spelling of a typed node (STEP_HAS_TYPED_NODE), on a signal waited on by concurrent fan-out branches and on a writeOutcome step or mcp node that no publishOutcome step reaches (WRITE_WITHOUT_POLICY), and a save also warns when a judge names a rubric that does not exist. The New workflow dialog generates a draft from a description or from answers to questions, or creates a blank one with one placeholder (noop) step and an end node, nothing generated. A template’s page has a read-only Triggers card that lists what starts the template: the event automations that name it, or that take the source’s built-in default when that default is this global active template (matched by name), the cron schedules that name it, and a pointer when it has a webhook URL. Its lists come from the endpoints the Automations page uses, so it shows only what the caller may see, and it does not itself say whether a listed automation’s source is switched on (a note beside the list says a listed automation fires only while its source is).
features.title: Workflow library & visual authoring

features.body: Generate draft workflow specs from a description and explain existing specs.
features.detail: Generation is an activity, not arbitrary runtime code execution. Slack can draft and refine team-owned versions; a person activates them. The asynchronous and Slack generation paths and channel refinement are never shell-authorized, so they refuse a draft holding container code or an authored command (Slack is told to use the canvas), and channel refinement refuses up front when the current draft already holds one.
features.title: Natural-language workflow authoring

features.body: Agent identity, model, runtime, prompt, skills, tool keys and optional MCP connection are data.
features.detail: Template → channel → team → organization → global resolution selects the most-specific active version. GLOBAL lineage pins are frozen at run start; scoped overrides remain live. Skill text is pinned separately, by revision. A team member can list only the keys, names and models an override may name, without prompts, tools or connections; the full team library stays team-admin or ADMIN. In the library table an admin sees a No credential badge on a platform-wide agent that is not pinned to its own credential and whose provider the setup readiness check marks as lacking a credential an agent can use (none reachable, or a custom provider’s credential without an apiBase; a mispinned embedding model does not make its provider count as lacking one; a sub-role persona takes its parent’s status); team, organization and template overrides are never badged. A version may set its runtime (the Mastra loop, the Claude Code harness or Pi); only a platform ADMIN can set or change it, and the library form shows the picker only on the platform-admin page. Saving the Claude Code runtime is refused when the version’s own model, or the model it inherits along the platform-wide chain, is not Anthropic; saving a model that harness agents inherit is allowed and lists them. A new scoped override that names no runtime starts on the platform-wide row’s, which a team admin may restate but not change, unless the harness cannot drive the override’s own model. Restoring a version restores its runtime, and a seeded default-model move keeps it. An ADMIN can open usage per version and model for an agent’s whole lineage (7, 30 or 90 days, or a custom range): calls, errors, tokens, cost, average duration and runs, with rows that recorded no version reported apart, capped and flagged when truncated; the dashboard calls it not a controlled comparison and it offers no success or outcome rate. An agent pinned to its own credential shows that credential’s provider and last four characters instead. Saving requires a <provider>/<model-id> spec and stores the provider lowercased; an empty string still clears the model. A credential pin is checked at save: it must exist, be for the provider the model routes to, and be reachable from the agent’s scope (a team agent may pin a GLOBAL credential, its team’s, or its team’s organization’s; an organization agent a GLOBAL one or its own organization’s), otherwise the save answers 400 INVALID_CREDENTIAL. The response carries advisory catalog and credential warnings that the dashboard shows after create and edit on the platform and team libraries and after a restore, which only the platform library offers; an inheriting agent’s pin is not provider-checked, and a platform-wide, channel or template agent’s pin is not scope-checked at save (the worker falls back to the cascade at run time); a model with no reachable credential, or a custom provider whose reachable credentials lack an apiBase, saves with a warning rather than a refusal. A version may also set a reasoning level (off, low, medium or high), inherited with the model; a version left with neither a model nor one to inherit is refused (400 MODEL_REQUIRED). An edit of a deactivated agent is refused (409 AGENT_INACTIVE), so only an explicit isActive: true reactivates one. An ADMIN can change many agents’ models in one action: a preview reports each agent’s outcome (changed, unchanged, unmatched, inheriting, blocked by a save rule) and narrower-scope rows that shadow it, and the apply cuts a version per agent through the single-edit path, audits each, and is not atomic: one agent’s failure leaves the others applied.
features.title: Versioned agent library

features.body: Run a launchable library agent in a throwaway repository workspace, optionally publishing a branch or draft PR.
features.detail: Separate from the engineering template. The agent runs on the loop its own runtime names (Mastra, or a registered harness: claude-code or pi); an agent with none runs on the run-pinned workspace.agentRunRuntime setting, which is Mastra unless an admin sets it per team, organization or workflow template. The setting is read with the repository’s owning team, while the agent itself is never resolved at team scope. Step and wall-clock caps and admission limits apply. On Mastra the run is debited per step. On the harness it is one turn capped at the step ceiling: the budget is checked before the turn, each model call is debited with the budget re-checked after every debit, the wall-clock deadline stops the turn rather than failing it, toolKeys grant only the named workspace tools (none set gives the read-only tools, an empty list gives none), and its MCP connection, if it binds one, is relayed from the worker. A runtime no harness serves, or a model the harness cannot drive, is refused before any container is created. Delivery uses a fresh trusted container. A draft pull request it opens is recorded as a PullRequest row on the run’s own ledger row; a failed write appears as a pr.record_failed event on the run. No-delivery diffs are explicitly unverified. A launch may name a base branch (the CLI’s --base, or baseBranch in the request): it must be a valid branch name and not one of the platform’s own work branches, and the checkout is cut from it and the draft pull request opens into it; unset, the repository’s default branch is used. A signed-in user may also launch one through the MCP server’s start_agent_run tool, under the extra limits the local-agent delegation card describes. A service principal may launch one with the runs:agent scope, and a launch may ask for a completion callback (see those cards).
features.title: One-off repository agent runs

features.body: Gather the tracker ticket, validate context, implement with test feedback, review, fix CI failures, wait for human merge and learn.
features.detail: The default spec gathers the run’s tracker ticket (non-blocking) before validating and hands its text to validate and implement, and repeats review after CI fixes. A validate step that fails lets the run go on, but one that reports the request not actionable (every criterion it extracted is marked AMBIGUOUS, or a successful extraction found none; a failed extraction is no verdict) ends the run FAILED before implementation, with the ambiguities and a request for acceptance criteria in its result; the Qodo variant shares this prologue. A launch or retry by a signed-in person of an identical request (description and inputs, ignoring whitespace and the ticket id’s case) that stopped this way within the last 24 hours on the same template version, with no later run of it (only runs the caller can see are compared, at most 8 pages of 25), is refused 409 UNCHANGED_AFTER_NOT_ACTIONABLE unless the caller sends acknowledgeUnchanged, which the dashboard offers as Run anyway; the stop is read from what the run recorded, a retry that adds instructions and a service principal are not checked, and a failed lookup lets the launch go ahead. The implementation step’s TDD loop stops after a test run whose command cannot run at all (exit 126 or 127, or npm’s missing test script or missing package.json), since another pass cannot fix that, and still commits and pushes the change with failing tests. Its CI wait can use webhook signals or active polling; human merge is an external signal, not an automatic merge. An agent’s own runtime, inherited along its model chain so the fixers follow the implementer, else the run-pinned workspace.implementerRuntime setting, chooses whether implementer, fixer and merge-conflict turns run the platform’s Mastra tool loop, the Claude Code harness inside the workspace, or Pi’s loop in the worker, and the run pins each agent’s choice when it starts; under either harness a worker-side policy decides every tool call, within the tools the agent’s toolKeys grant. A reviewer closing the run’s pull request unmerged makes a later push step fail non-retryably rather than open a replacement. The implementer’s prompt carries what validation extracted: the concrete criteria as what done means and the ambiguous ones as numbered open questions it must not resolve by guessing, answered in the closing lines of its last message, which fixed code parses strictly and carries on the code result; the domain-logic reviewer numbers only the concrete criteria as requirements and is told an open question is no ground for rejecting. A very short request (under three words and sixteen characters once the key is removed, with no list-like line), with no ticket gathered and a re-read showing the tracker refused the run’s credentials, skips the validator model call and ends not actionable; a ticket the re-read does find is validated instead.
features.title: Ticket-to-PR engineering

features.body: Lint, typecheck, tests, build, vulnerability scan and performance benchmark activities, singly or batched in one workspace.
features.detail: A gate’s command is the step’s config, else the repository’s gate commands, else the same key in the trusted .auto-swe/gates.yml read from the base commit, else the default for the repository’s detected target, else the built-in yarn command; whitespace counts as no command at every level. The target is the root when it has a stack signal (a polyglot root resolves by a fixed precedence in which Node wins), else the one directory with a signal when the stored listing was complete and found exactly one; several signalled directories and no root signal leave every stack-default gate unconfigured, and a truncated listing with no root signal keeps the built-in commands. The stack defaults are a fixed table in code, not a stored value: Python gets pytest for tests only, JVM Maven or Gradle (by the target’s build file) for build and tests, Go build, vet and tests. A Node root’s manager is its package.json packageManager pin, else its one lockfile: npm and pnpm get that manager’s commands, Yarn Classic the yarn commands with no vulnerability-scan default, and Yarn Berry or an unrecorded manager the built-in yarn commands; a Node component takes its manager from its own lockfile names alone: a lone package-lock.json or pnpm-lock.yaml gets npm’s or pnpm’s commands, a yarn.lock or several lockfiles the built-in Yarn commands, and no lockfile npm’s commands. A component’s defaults run as cd '<dir>' && …, its stored path re-validated first (plain segments, at most four); only stack defaults get the cd, and step commands and repository gate commands run as written. A gate left with none (runPerfBench, a gate the target’s stack has no command for such as lint on Python, a vulnerability scan on Yarn Classic, or any stack-default gate of an ambiguous layout) fails rather than passing; once a target is known, another ecosystem’s command is not substituted. An eval gate scorer with no command of its own resolves through the same chain except the repository's gates.yml, while the TDD loop's test command uses the full chain, except that a Node target keeps its guess from the target's own package.json, run in its directory., as does the TDD loop’s test command, except that a Node target keeps its guess from the target’s own package.json, run in its directory. runQualityGates runs several gates in one workspace by default (per-gate isolation is the single-gate steps in sequence; stopOnFailure skips the rest), each gate keeping its own artifact, summary, eval signal and evidence row, and its aggregate passed is what onFail reads. A command written into a spec, and a git repository’s gate commands (set at onboarding through POST /repositories or the connection form, or changed through PATCH /repositories/:id, the connection form, or the CLI’s repos gate-commands; 403 GATE_COMMANDS_FORBIDDEN; audited, after on create and before and after on a change; re-sending the stored set is not a change, and onboarding with none or only blank ones takes no role) take the shell authoring role, as does moving a repository that has gate commands to another team (on the destination team), because these commands run in the agent workspace with network access, not in the shell sandbox. Graph failure modes can block, warn or retry; having a registered gate does not mean every template runs it.
features.title: Configurable quality gates

features.body: A repository whose detected target is Python, JVM or Go runs its workspaces on the image the deployer configured for that stack, unless a platform ADMIN named an executor image for it.
features.detail: One helper resolves a repository’s workspace image in a fixed order: the connection’s executorImage, then WORKSPACE_IMAGE_PYTHON, WORKSPACE_IMAGE_JVM or WORKSPACE_IMAGE_GO for the stack of its detected target (the root, or its only signalled directory), then the worker’s WORKSPACE_IMAGE. The variables are environment-only and checked with the other workspace settings when the worker starts; an unset one, a Node target (there is no Node variable), an ambiguous layout or no detection take the default. The stored detection only selects among the images the deployer configured; it never names one. Implementation and fix sessions, decomposition, CI verification, quality gates, agent nodes, agent runs and eval gate scorers pass that result to createWorkspace; the eval harness keeps its own pinned images. The executor-image probe (POST /repositories/:id/executor-image/probe, platform ADMIN) tests the named image, else the repository’s executor image, else the image its detection resolves to on the worker, else the default.
features.title: Per-stack workspace images

features.body: Split work, execute bounded fan-out branches, aggregate outputs, merge branches and resolve conflicts.
features.detail: Branch contexts are isolated and results are structured; decomposer output that fails its schema falls back to one subtask. Cross-repo epics are separate Temporal child workflows: each repository starts once its own dependencies have succeeded, and a failed upstream skips its dependents. The planner chooses order, not scope: every requested repository is in the plan, and an epic with nothing to plan fails with EPIC_PLAN_EMPTY.
features.title: Decomposition & parallel implementation

features.body: Enrich agent prompts with past lessons, tracker/knowledge content, Figma summaries and repository dependency context.
features.detail: The dependency graph supports manifest detection plus inference; upstream checkout is optional. Context helpers generally degrade on enrichment failures rather than blocking core implementation. The tracker and knowledge-base fetches check their base URL and handle redirects as described in the connector guard card. In the default ticket-to-merge graph a gatherTicketContext step reads the run’s tracker ticket (for Jira also its parent issue and up to its 20 newest comments, within a shared length budget) and a tool-less ticketContextGatherer agent, on the planner’s model, digests it into a typed summary, requirements, acceptance criteria, constraints, open questions and references; a failed digest falls back to the plain ticket, and a run with no ticket (none named, a platform-generated id, no tracker configured, not found) returns without a model call; on the GitHub Issues tracker so does a ticket whose repository the run does not target (see the GitHub tracker scope card). The text is bounded, never carries the raw provider payload, sits inside a delimiter its own text cannot close and is framed as requirements, not instructions; it is not run through the injection scanners. Templates without the step get the ticket in validate and implement only when the workflow.ticketContextFallback setting is on (off by default, overridable at team and organization); a ticket fetched this way is stored on first use, so a later edit in the tracker is not seen by the run. When a gatherer supplies an explicitly empty ticket block and an unstructured request is narrowly classified as thin, validation attempts another ticket read even with fallback disabled. A readable ticket feeds validation; unauthorized or forbidden credentials make that thin request not actionable without a validator model call. Structured, substantive or uncertain cases continue through normal validation.
features.title: Repository & design context

features.body: Approval, decision, input form and review nodes pause a run until response or timeout.
features.detail: WorkflowHumanStep stores context, deadlines and response data. A review node’s response is a note; it does not edit the content it shows. Creating a step also queues a run.waiting_for_human callback when the launch asked for one. HumanApproval supports distinct-approver counting. Workflow status remains RUNNING while it waits. When a step was announced in Slack, fully resolving it through the REST route (the Approvals page and other API clients) or Slack edits that message to show the decision and any note and drops its buttons. The edit is best effort and never undoes the recorded answer: a Slack error is logged, while a missing bot token or an unreadable stored message skips the edit silently. In Slack, a button for a decision option resolves the step in one click, while Approve and Reject open a modal for a note first. Opening it looks the step up among the steps the clicker may act on, tells a user whose Slack id is not linked to an account to link it, and tells the clicker to use the inbox if Slack cannot open the form. The submission is what resolves the step, through the same resolve core as the REST route, which checks access again. The modal’s private metadata round-trips through the client, so it carries the step, action and Slack user under an HMAC made with the Slack signing secret, and a submission whose signature fails or whose Slack user differs is refused, with the error shown in the form. For an approval step a rejection needs a reason of at least five characters after trimming, enforced in that shared core for the Approvals page, the API and Slack alike: the REST route answers 400 REASON_REQUIRED and the Slack modal shows the error in the form. An approver’s comment is optional, recorded with the response and shown, but never sent to the workflow in the signal. The REST list of steps shows pending steps by default, so resolved answers need status=ALL; actionable narrows it to pending, unexpired steps the caller may answer and has not yet answered, and answeredByMe (with status=ALL, or it finds only pending steps the caller has approved) to steps the caller resolved or approved. limit and offset page the list, and a total is counted and returned in meta only when one of those three is asked for, or when count=true asks for the total alone (the sidebar badge sends it with limit=1). myResponse is the caller’s own answer: their approval row, else the stored action when they resolved the step, and null for a step resolved by a timeout or by someone else. The Approvals page loads one capped list from the gateway, which filters by tab, sort, deadline and, when set, team and answerable-by-you; its kind and text search are sent to the gateway too (q matches title, description, request ticket and description, and repository as org, repo or org/repo), so a match past the cap is still found, and the page says when the matches themselves reach the cap. An agent can also open an INPUT step: when a Claude Code agent asks a question, the workflow loop creates an INPUT step titled for the asking agent, and the answer resumes the same activity (see the ask-and-resume card).
features.title: Four human interaction types

features.body: Classify an action by risk and choose automatic publication or human approval.
features.detail: publishOutcome records a decision, taking the risk class from the node’s config only (a class bound from inputs is the ACTION_CLASS_BOUND lint error, so such a version cannot be promoted or activated); templates route it to approval. The three generic connector-writing steps — writeOutcome, a mutating runTool and an mcp node whose server does not declare the tool read-only — refuse to act while the run’s latest decision that required approval has no approval recorded after it, so a later decision its policy auto-approves does not clear an earlier requirement; a run that recorded no such decision is not gated. Each such effect is claimed in the outcome ledger, one row per run, node and connection, before the provider is called and completed with what it returned: a retry returns a completed result, and one that finds a bare claim refuses non-retryably with OUTCOME_AMBIGUOUS rather than act twice. An agent’s own MCP tool calls and sandbox steps stay outside that boundary.
features.title: Policy-gated outcome publication

features.body: Sensitive-file, shell-command, content, diff, skill/LLM-output, memory-content, CI-log and PII-related scanning paths.
features.detail: A skill’s description and text, an agent’s system prompt (on create and on a version that sets one) and an eval rubric’s text (on create) are scanned in full, advisorily, as are skills in a bundle install and a skill import. A pattern that overran or is quarantined, a scanner that fails, or a pattern set that cannot be read yields a scan-incomplete warning, never a clean result. Some checks block tool calls; others only annotate findings. The memory gate is blocking but INJECTION-only (a slow or quarantined EXFILTRATION pattern cannot stop a memory write): it refuses a memory write that matches or whose INJECTION scan did not complete, fails a lesson step when no pattern could be loaded, and drops a recalled item that matches. CI log text is a further consumer of the INJECTION patterns only, and only in the CI triage template (the default graph’s CI fix does not screen logs): there the log tail given to the triager is redacted for common token shapes and screened with the INJECTION patterns except template-injection (which ordinary build output matches), and a log that matches, or whose scan did not complete, is diagnosed but never fixed from. Administrator regexes execute in a budgeted worker thread. Scanning is defense-in-depth, not proof that generated code is safe. An administrator can try a candidate pattern against pasted samples before saving it: the test route validates it as a create does, then runs it through the same budgeted executor one sample at a time, writes no pattern or audit row, and neither skips a quarantined rule nor quarantines the one under test. It stops starting samples once about three budgets of wall-clock time have passed, which includes time queued behind the gateway’s other scans (the rest are reported not run), and it runs under the gateway process’s budget and reports only the first match in each sample. A sample is run as one piece of text, so the tester does not reproduce the code-security scanner’s per-line scan or the shell scanner’s segment windows and collapsed spelling; it shows whether a regex matches, not what a scanner would do with the result. A governed-knowledge learning passes the memory INJECTION gate before it is stored, and recalled knowledge that matches is dropped. The post-diff security gate is one helper on every implementation, fix, merge-resolution and agent-run path; a gate that cannot complete fails non-retryably (SECURITY_GATE_UNAVAILABLE) and a spend refusal keeps its own type.
features.title: Layered runtime scanning

features.body: Run allowlisted images as shell steps or structured stdout, NDJSON or HTTP-sidecar contracts.
features.detail: Ephemeral containers default to no network, read-only root, dropped capabilities and CPU/memory/PID limits. The workspace volume is writable; opt-in egress filtering is DNS-based, not an IP firewall. Container code in any spelling (a shell node, a containerStep node, or a step naming the shell-category step) needs the shell authoring role and an image the allowlist accepts when saved, and the image is checked again when the step runs. A containerStep with no command runs the image’s entrypoint; a sidecar request is bounded by the step’s wall-clock cap, heartbeated and aborted when the activity is cancelled; a shell step whose workspace could not be finalized (committed and pushed) reports passed: false. These steps need the Docker backend: on a Kubernetes worker they fail non-retryably with WORKSPACE_BACKEND_UNSUPPORTED.
features.title: Shell & container-contract extensions

features.body: Call a named remote tool from a workflow or attach an MCP server toolset to an enabled agent.
features.detail: Generic agent nodes acquire local workspace tools only in a checkout (workspace: true); they may receive MCP tools. Enabling a connection type in the generic registry does not imply readSource/writeOutcome implements it. A connection may carry one bearer token, stored in the connection’s encrypted envelope columns and write-only: responses say only whether one is set, and audit rows record a boolean. With a token, the Authorization: Bearer header is attached only to requests for the server’s own origin and stripped from any other, the client is also pinned to the connection’s host, a redirect is refused, and the token is removed from connect error text. A connection may also carry up to five custom request headers (an API-gateway key, a tenant id): sealed together as one encrypted envelope that key rotation also covers, and write-only like the token, since responses list the header names and whether the set is unreadable and audit rows record names only. Names must be HTTP tokens and unique ignoring case, values visible ASCII (inner spaces allowed) with no line breaks and at most 2,048 characters. Authorization (the bearer token is where that credential lives), hop-by-hop headers, Host, Content-Length, Content-Type, Accept, Cookie, Set-Cookie, proxy-* headers and the MCP protocol headers are refused. Headers follow the token’s origin-only path on both transports, never overwrite a header the transport sets, and are removed from a request aimed at another origin. The connection test sends them too, with protocol and token headers taking precedence, and when headers are set its 401/403 message names the credentials in general rather than only the token. A stored set is re-validated when it is opened, so a row written by anything but the gateway route cannot put a forbidden header on the wire. A token or header set that cannot be decrypted yields no agent tools and makes an mcp workflow node fail, rather than connecting without what the server expects. Pointing a connection at another origin while keeping its stored token is refused with 409 TOKEN_ORIGIN_CHANGE, and keeping stored header values while changing the origin is refused with 409 HEADERS_ORIGIN_CHANGE. An unreadable header set can only be replaced or removed (409 HEADERS_UNREADABLE otherwise). The token and headers belong to the connection, so every run that uses it presents the same credentials, not the launching user’s. An ADMIN can also limit which of a server’s tools bind (allowedTools: exact names, and an empty list binds none; a tool outside it is never wrapped, so neither an agent nor an mcp node can call it) and set scanResults, which screens and fences every result as the Qodo connection card describes; without it a result reaches the agent as the server sent it. Each in-process MCP tool call is traced as mcp:<name> with the result the agent received, so text the screen withheld is never stored. An ADMIN may also turn on allowPrivateNetwork for a connection. It uses the same guard as the tracker and knowledge-base connectors: with it on, a server on a private address is accepted when the connection is saved, when it is tested, and each time the worker loads its tools. Loopback, link-local, cloud-metadata addresses and names, unspecified and malformed addresses and non-http(s) schemes are refused whatever the flag says. The flag is part of the connection’s saved configuration and every save re-checks the URL against the flag sent with it, so an update to a private-address server that does not send the flag is refused with 400 UNSAFE_URL. Every request the worker makes to an MCP server, with or without credentials, is resolved and pinned, and the opt-in covers only the connection’s own origin, so an SSE endpoint or redirect on another origin is strict. With a token or headers a redirect is refused; without them redirects are followed by hand, at most three hops, each hop text-checked and pinned, with MCP session headers kept for the server’s own origin and only a benign allowlist crossing to another. The admin connection test resolves and pins with the connection’s opt-in, never follows a redirect, and reports a refused resolution as an address on a network the connection may not reach. The admin connection test lists tools with the stored token, using streamable HTTP and falling back to the legacy SSE transport after a failure that another transport might fix; a URL ending /sse goes straight to SSE. An mcp node’s connection is a literal id in the spec, so it is checked when the node runs: the run’s template team must own it or have it shared (a global template may use any). Under the Claude Code harness, and under Pi, the agent’s connection is relayed from the worker: the worker connects with the connection’s credentials and guard and serves its tools to the harness through an in-process MCP server over the SDK’s pipe, so the credentials never enter the container. The policy allows exactly those tools, and the harness loads no other MCP server (a repository’s .mcp.json included).
features.title: MCP as nodes and agent tools

features.body: Let MCP clients list repositories, launchable agents, work requests, runs and pending human steps, read run evidence, library and report data, wait on a run, and optionally submit work, start an agent run, start and message an orchestration or cancel runs as the signed-in user.
features.detail: A stateless Streamable HTTP endpoint is an OAuth 2.1 resource server; better-auth issues tokens after a consent screen, and users can revoke connected apps. Off by default, and write scope needs a second switch; the tool set is built per request from the verified token, so the write tools exist only for a token holding mcp:write. Tools reach data only through the REST routes, so route authorization applies; writes add a per-user rate limit, and launches also a fixed check that the budget tier is STANDARD (no setting changes it), a required idempotency key and a concurrent-run cap, enforced by the routes themselves for a bridged call. A headless client that cannot open a browser can authorize through a device flow instead, off until its own ADMIN setting (mcp.deviceFlowEnabled) is on: a signed-in active user approves the exact scopes in a browser, and the CLI’s mcp login, token, header and logout commands run it, keeping the refresh credential in a file only that user can read. Beyond those, the server registers read tools grouped into domains (teams and pull requests with the run limits, epics and schedules, run evaluation results, effects, autonomy decisions and evidence, the agent and skill library, delivery, quality, human-step, automation and budget reports, and orchestrations), each declared with a tier and the one REST route behind it so the tool list, the route table’s opt-in and the declarations can be checked against each other. The tools marked admin tier exist only for a token that holds mcp:admin, a third scope that implies read but not write, is consented to separately in the browser or device flow, has no operator switch and is not tied to a platform role: the route behind each tool still applies its own role gate, so holding the scope does not make a non-admin an admin. The agent-delegation tools are described in the local-agent delegation card, and the orchestration write tools in the orchestration MCP card.
features.title: MCP server for external agents

features.body: A local coding agent connected to the MCP server can pick a repository and agent, start an agent run as the signed-in user, wait on it, and read back its branch, pull request, diff size and failure type.
features.detail: Four tools make the loop. list_agents (read) calls GET /agent-runs/agents and returns each launchable agent’s key, version, name and a short description, optionally resolved for a repository. start_agent_run (write) calls POST /agent-runs with an agent ref, repository, prompt, delivery mode (none, draft_pr or branch), optional base branch and a required idempotency key; it cannot set step or wall-clock caps, a budget tier or a callback, so the run takes the platform ceilings and the STANDARD tier, and the reply carries the workRequestId and the effective delivery and caps. wait_for_run (read) takes a run id or a work request id and waits up to 50 seconds (default 25): it polls the run-list, run and human-step routes every three seconds and returns on a status change, a terminal status, a pending human step on that run (with a link to the dashboard’s approvals page) or the timeout; given a work request id it waits for a run row to appear and follows the newest one. get_run also returns the recorded branch (only when it is a safe git branch name), a diff stat summed from the recorded filesChanged, and, for a failed or timed-out run, a failure type: the TYPE: prefix of the latest failed step (the last listed step whose node’s latest attempt failed), else the run’s own status, so a timed-out run with no prefixed step error reports TIMED_OUT; a value outside a fixed list, which includes a failed run with no prefix, reports UNKNOWN, so no error text reaches the client. When a call comes through the MCP bridge, POST /agent-runs itself checks, in order: writes enabled (mcp.writeToolsEnabled), the per-user burst limit, the STANDARD tier, a present Idempotency-Key, and the delivery mode against mcp.agentRunAllowedDeliverModes (GLOBAL only, ADMIN to change, default none and draft_pr, so branch delivery is refused with MCP_DELIVER_MODE_NOT_ALLOWED until an admin adds it); then the agent-run route’s usual repository, agent and ceiling checks, the idempotent replay, the agent-run admission limits, and last the per-user MCP run cap inside the launch transaction. The run’s launchedById is the token’s user, so it acts as that user and, where per-user GitHub credentials are on, uses their saved token. Its workflow id derives from the repository, the caller and the key: a bridged retry by the same user with the same key and inputs is answered with the original work request (already_submitted), also when it loses a concurrent insert to that first launch, and other inputs under the same key are refused with IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_MISMATCH. Each bridged attempt that reaches the route writes a McpToolCall audit row holding a digest of the input, not its text. Dashboard, CLI and service-principal launches skip these checks, and the agent-run re-run route is not reachable from MCP. The repository also ships client packaging that is not platform code: a Claude Code plugin (a marketplace entry, an HTTP MCP configuration that reads the deployment URL from AUTO_SWE_MCP_URL and asks for mcp:read, mcp:write and offline_access, and a delegate skill) and a Codex configuration snippet with an AGENTS.md section. Both describe the same loop, and a root test fails when either names a tool the gateway does not register.
features.title: Local coding agents delegate agent runs over MCP

features.body: Reply in threads, launch durable tasks, draft workflows and maintain channel memory.
features.detail: Opt-in capabilities include follow-up sessions, reactive interjections, ambient digests, passive ingestion, open-item nudges and organization signal flagging. Proactivity has cooldowns and budgets. When a task cannot start, or its thread already has one running, the thread is told so instead of receiving the agent’s acknowledgement. Linking a Slack account and installing the bot are each bound to the browser that started them by a nonce in a cookie. A scheduled sync (off by default) re-asks Slack whether each channel is private and turns the flag on for one that became private, never off, and replaces each private channel’s member list whole; a list it cannot read whole is kept and ages out. A private channel’s memory, open items, audit feed and turn runs are shown to platform admins and to members of the owning team whose linked Slack account is in a list synced within the staleness window; everyone else, or a channel with no fresh list, gets nothing. A code task launched from a private channel is an ordinary run on its repository, and its acknowledgement says so. Members of a channel’s team read its memory, open items and activity in the dashboard without the settings or the edit, delete, resolve and dismiss controls. Replies and several notices can be validated cards, described in the Slack cards card.
features.title: Channel-resident Slack assistants

features.body: Store lessons and channel memory with run/agent lineage and evidence; recall them for every agent that works on a repository; supersede, consolidate and forget them through their provenance.
features.detail: MemoryItem supports generic scopes and entities plus repo/channel/team/org links. Storage uses vector(1536); a row is compared only with rows embedded by the same model, and after a model change an admin starts a re-embed of the stale rows.
