Scoped searches set pgvector's iterative index scan (strict order), so a small repository beside a crowded one still gets its nearest rows; on pgvector before 0.8 the worker logs once and searches without it. A built-in engineering template that wires its review or CI loop’s exhausted path to a lesson step writes a lesson when that loop runs out of attempts, while scope-clarification, external-approval-gate, staged-deploy-signals, ci-triage-and-fix and model-catalog-refresh end FAILED without one (a review loop also ends this way when a rejection repeats the previous round’s findings), and ticket-to-merge also after a merge and after a merge-wait timeout that followed a rejection; the release templates and the four-eyes sign-off loop write none, and a step that throws writes none. commitToMemory is given bounded evidence chosen by outcome (a CI failure lesson gets the CI log, a review failure lesson the rejection), records the outcome by code, cites the pull requests, head commit and a short quote of that evidence, and grades its confidence; a low-confidence lesson is labelled on recall, not filtered. It also rebuilds the run's earlier review rejections and CI failures from its traces — grouped by Temporal activity id so a retry counts once, capped at five entries and 4,000 characters per kind — and fences them with the evidence. A new item at or above memory.supersedeThreshold similarity to older active items in the same repository or channel marks them superseded; they are kept but not recalled. Supersession only targets earlier (created_at, id) tuples; concurrent similar writes cannot retire each other, but can leave duplicate active rows until a later write. Consolidation soft-deletes merged items and keeps the sources' ids. An optional memory.lessonMaxAgeDays setting (off by default) keeps older lessons out of recall, searchLessons and consolidation through a SQL filter before the limit; nothing is deleted. The implementer, the three fixers and the review personas recall their repository's lessons by the text of what they are working on, and the Mastra loop also gets read-only searchLessons and explainLesson tools bound to that repository. Deleting a lesson or channel item forgets every merged copy of it and a merged item's own sources, restores the rows only the deleted merge or supersession hid, and audits both id lists in the same transaction; an admin route erases one Slack user's attributed channel memory the same way, and the Slack channels page has a card for it that asks for the member id to be typed again to confirm and reports how many items were forgotten and restored. Recalled memory is text a later run reads, so the worker gates it on injection patterns: a write through insertMemoryItem is refused before it is embedded when its lesson or rationale matches an INJECTION scanner pattern, and the two consolidation passes apply the same check to their merged notes before inserting, leaving the cluster as it was. Lesson and channel-memory retrieval drop any recalled item that matches, which also covers rows written before the gate and an admin’s edit: PATCH /slack-channels/:id/memory/:memoryId saves edited text without the check. A write is refused when its INJECTION scan is incomplete (a pattern overran its budget or is quarantined), and the two consolidation passes treat an incomplete, failed or unloadable scan the same way and leave the cluster as it was. A pattern set that cannot be read is different, because no rule ran: the lesson step fails and is retried (bounded; a lesson is lost if the outage outlasts the retries), while a direct lesson write is logged and dropped and a channel turn’s summary or passively ingested fact is not stored. Recall gates only on the patterns that ran, so an incomplete scan alone drops nothing; a scan that throws, or a pattern set that cannot be loaded, recalls nothing, and a lesson’s explanation is then withheld as could-not-be-scanned rather than as an injection match. Every prompt that carries memory — recalled lessons, and channel memory in a mention turn, a reactive interjection, an ambient digest and both lists of an org-flagging check — wraps it in a block that labels the notes reference data, not instructions. The gate does not use the EXFILTRATION patterns, and passing the gate is not proof that recalled text is benign. A shell step’s command text is masked for credential-shaped values before it becomes an auto-commit message or a stored lesson. The lessons routes list and delete only repository lessons (scope swe-lessons), not channel memory, and a lesson delete writes an audit row carrying the deleted content. Every role reads the lessons of the repositories it can reach; deleting one and consolidating a repository take team.lessons.manage on the owning team (a platform ADMIN, a LEAD or ADMIN of the repository’s active owning team, or an ADMIN of its organization who can reach the repository), and other members of a shared team only read. Anyone who reads a lesson can flag it as wrong with a reason; its managers see the reasons and delete the lesson, clear the flags or quarantine it, each audited with the reasons; a flag changes recall only when distinct flags reach the quarantine threshold, as described in the quarantine card. Repository lesson recall can also run in shadow or off mode per run, as described in the recall-modes card. A run’s page lists the lessons its agents recalled, read from its own lessons.retrieved trace events and shown to whoever can see the run, and the lessons it wrote.
features.title: Scoped semantic memory

features.body: Capture online signals, score workflow values, compare candidates to baselines and revalidate datasets.
features.detail: Hard floors are gate/assert/policy/PII. Trajectory and judge scores are soft by default; a judge call records its model and cost on the result row. A dataset run shares a runless token cap scaled by its case count and ends with a partial verdict when that cap, or its organization’s monthly USD cap, stops it after a case completed; the verdict records which, and run lists label it partial. Frozen fixture SHAs, golden tests, rubric versions and quarantined cases support reproducible comparisons. Each case names the toolchain its reference and candidate run on (node, python, jvm or go; none is node), which the worker maps to a pinned upstream base image rather than the repository’s executor image; a case cannot name an image, and a stored value outside the set is an error for that case, never node. Admins can follow per-scorer trends over a 7, 30 or 90 day window or a custom range of whole UTC days (at most 366, bucketed by week above 90 days), split by judge model, agent or implementer runtime and filtered to the results of one template’s runs, and see each dataset’s quarantined share of golden cases against its ceiling. Each case resolves its settings and Agent rows in the dataset’s team and organization scope. An eval run started through the API or CLI can name a runtime (Mastra loop or Claude Code harness) for either side; it applies as that case’s per-agent runtime pin and workspace.implementerRuntime pin, so it wins over the Agent’s own runtime, and a case whose runner is built on a different runtime fails with EVAL_RUNTIME_MISMATCH instead of being graded. A side without an override resolves its runtime per case, since an eval has no run to pin it on. Each harness result row records the candidate’s runtime, with the baseline’s in its metadata, and the run summary lists the runtimes each side ran on; the run pages, results table and CLI show them, and the dashboard does not start runs. The regression harness scores only flake-screened cases: a per-dataset screen runs each case’s reference evals.flakeScreenRuns times (3 by default) and marks it screened only when every run passes, a run over cases none of which is screened ends INCONCLUSIVE (the CLI exits 2), and an admin can reset a dataset or case to unscreened, which starts a screen. In a workflow, an eval node that blocks returns passed: false, so its onFail applies (under the default block the run fails); a blocking judge (judgeAdvisory: false) that cannot score fails closed while an advisory one does not, an errored scorer is left out of score and perAxis and reported in errors and on its result row, and a pii scorer that skipped a quarantined pattern fails. An eval run can also compare lesson-memory modes over an isolated per-dataset corpus, described in the eval memory card.
features.title: Evaluation & regression system

features.body: Route runs between template versions and track agent canary/control outcomes.
features.detail: This is evaluation/routing metadata. It differs from the staged-deploy-signals template, which waits for external staging and monitoring signals.
features.title: Experiments and canaries

features.body: Track tokens and catalog-priced USD across runs, runless workflows, teams, organizations and Slack channels, and stop a capped organization’s or team’s spend at launch and before each model call.
features.detail: Token tiers bind runs; a workflow with no run has a per-execution token cap. A run’s input cap counts each call’s input in dollar-equivalent tokens: uncached input at one, prompt-cache reads and writes at the model’s cache multipliers, fixed when the call is recorded, and the raw count when the model is unpriced or reports no cache breakdown; run pages and the per-execution cap still show and use raw tokens. The organization USD cap is checked at launch and again before every budgeted model call, which refuses with a non-retryable BUDGET_EXCEEDED whose message gives the spend and the cap (the organization id is only in the failure details); when that check cannot read the run’s organization or its budget it logs a warning and lets the call proceed uncapped. Both read finalized, in-flight and runless spend; the mid-run read goes through a per-organization cache of one config window. One rule, billedOrgId, places a run for the in-flight count, the mid-run guard, finalization billing and trace attribution: the work request’s connection, else the run’s own connection, else the repository of its own ledger row, else the organization a launch that named no connection was gated against (RunInput.billingOrgId, recorded by a template run on a team template, a service principal’s run, a template webhook call, and a team automation or inbound event), and the first source that exists decides. A connection-free run of a global template launched by a person or through its webhook has no organization and is billed to none. A scheduled fire gets its own ledger row and run connection from its schedule’s repository, and epic planning declares the first repository’s team as its spend owner, so neither sits outside the cap. A scheduled run reaper finalizes and bills runs whose workflow ended without finalizing them. Prompt-cache reads and writes are priced at cache rates: a model’s catalog row may set read, 5-minute-write and 1-hour-write multipliers, each falling back to the code table, where Anthropic 1-hour writes cost twice input. Each trace row records its owning team and organization, which drives per-team and per-org usage reports: platform ADMINs see everything, a team LEAD their team, an organization ADMIN their organization, and the usage page opens for anyone who holds at least one of those scopes rather than by platform role. A daily sweep (on unless an environment switch turns it off) rolls model-call traces up per UTC day, rewriting the most recent completed days each time; the report reads a day from that rollup only once it is older than those days and has rollup rows, and reads every other day from the trace rows, so a missing sweep changes speed, not numbers. The report also ranks spend by the person who launched the run: platform ADMINs see names and emails, a team LEAD or organization ADMIN sees names only for launchers in the team or organization the report covers, and everyone else is folded into one unnamed row outside the scope. The usage page exports the report’s model, agent and node breakdowns as a file through the same scope check. A model with no catalog price is refused when the organization its run bills to has a monthly USD cap (resolved by the same billedOrgId rule as the cap, so a PRD run or a code-route channel task counts through its connection), when a runless workflow’s spend owner is a capped organization, when the run’s attributed team has its own cap, and when the call belongs to a channel with a monthly cap; a repo-less channel task bills its channel, so only the channel cap refuses it. Anywhere else it is recorded at zero USD with token usage retained. The usage report and the workflow-template analytics accept a custom since/until range of whole UTC days (at most 366, not in the future) in place of the preset window; the usage series is bucketed by week above 90 days. The 7, 30 and 90 day presets on the usage report and the workflow-template analytics likewise cover whole UTC days ending with today, so a preset spans the days a custom range of that length would and its previous period is the equal-length span directly before it. A team may also hold its own monthly USD cap, charged to the repository’s owning team and enforced at launch and before each call beside the organization’s (see per-team budgets). Members see budgets as a state and percentage and only an organization ADMIN or platform ADMIN (or the team’s ADMIN for its own cap) reads the cap and the budget figures in dollars; Organization report digests carry the organization budget in dollars only when no Slack channel is a target and the creator and every email recipient are organization ADMINs or platform ADMINs; otherwise they carry a percentage, and a team digest carries only a percentage line: the tighter of the team’s and the organization’s cap, left out when neither is set or the spend cannot be read.
features.title: Cost, budgets & usage

features.body: Inspect node attempts, tool calls, LLM responses, artifacts, policy decisions and telemetry.
features.detail: PostgreSQL is the queryable application ledger; Temporal owns durable execution history. OpenTelemetry loads as a preload so HTTP is instrumented, and trace context travels in Temporal headers, so a gateway request and every activity of the run it starts share a trace without OpenTelemetry code in the workflow isolate. A run started by a schedule has no starting context, so the workflow interceptor derives one from the workflow id and first run id and its activities share that trace. The gateway stamps its signals and updates with the caller’s context, and activities scheduled after one carry a span link to it. Trace rows link to their spec node and span; an agent’s tool calls are recorded as they execute, with real durations, and survive a generate call that later throws. Model-calling activities (implementation, review, agent runs and nodes, merge-conflict resolution) write their rows about once a second while they run, workspace-preparation events included (best-effort: a failed write keeps them for the next one, and a re-sent batch inserts nothing twice); other activities write theirs when they end. Each model-call row names the agent row and version that actually ran, so a scoped override or an explicit version is recorded rather than the platform-wide pin; rows from before that, embeddings and some early failures have none. Worker logs, gateway logs and the bash, MCP and harness audit lines written inside an activity export over OTLP with trace context. The run page tails new rows, reconciles by count and asks for the spec snapshot only once; while it polls, each trace text field is trimmed (4,000 characters), and a full-payload toggle fetches untrimmed rows once and stops live updates. A run with no readable spec snapshot is shown as a transcript of its steps and trace events instead of a graph. Its Traces tab narrows the rows already loaded by text, kind or errors only, in the browser, and draws the newest 400 at a time, with older ones behind a Show more step. Large outputs can be offloaded to PostgreSQL, S3-compatible storage or a mounted filesystem (the artifact store); a context value spilled that way shows as a marker in the run page, which fetches its full text on request from the run’s own ready context-overflow artifacts (another run’s artifact is the same 404, an oversized one is refused) and renders it as text. One read of a run’s trace rows loads at most the newest 5,000, and the run page slides that window forward on a longer run. An in-app assistant turn tags its trace rows with the reply they belong to.
features.title: Run and agent observability

features.body: Record each activity attempt’s model traffic in full, secret values redacted, and log every read, export and identified refusal of it.
features.detail: While capture is on (an ADMIN registry setting, on by default, GLOBAL only and read as each attempt starts, so no restart is needed) the worker opens one transcript per activity attempt and records every in-process model and embedding exchange (vectors omitted) and, for a Claude Code turn, its exchanges through the model proxy or its SDK messages and session-file delta. Records are NDJSON with secret values redacted, flushed as gzipped parts to the artifact store with a hash per part and one over the parts; a single exchange over a size limit keeps only its head, and a transcript that passes its compressed-size cap (64 MiB by default) stops recording and closes as truncated. A transcript outlives its run, since deleting the run only clears the link, and a daily sweep deletes it after a retention (365 days by default) unless an ADMIN placed a legal hold on the run or on the transcript; the same sweep marks transcripts a dead worker left open as abandoned. Any signed-in person (never a service principal) lists a run’s transcripts and their metadata through the run’s visibility filter; reading content needs the run’s control filter (a runless transcript is ADMIN-only), directly or through a signed download link bound to one format and PII-scrub choice, and a caller short of the bar gets the same 404 as a missing transcript. Verification and legal holds need platform.transcripts.retention.manage, and the cross-run export (a bounded date range, PII scrubbing optional) and the access log need platform.audit.read, both held only by a platform ADMIN; service principals are refused, and the in-app assistant may call none of these routes. Each content read, download link, verification, export and hold change writes an access-log row with actor, role, address and user agent, and a streamed read records how it ended (complete, integrity error, stream error or aborted); a 401 or 404 on a content read or a download-link request is recorded as denied when the caller is identified, by session or by a verified link. Access rows have no foreign keys, so they outlive the person, run and transcript they name, and are kept for their own retention (2555 days by default, at least 365).
features.title: Agent transcripts and their access log

features.body: Scope resources by organization/team, share repositories with teams and apply role-based permissions.
features.detail: Repository reachability combines ownership/sharing with optional host-permission checks. Per-user credentials are bound to their verified origins and the current run launcher. Query guards supplement route-specific authorization; they detect missing tenant predicates on selected multi-row ORM calls, not whether a predicate names a team the caller may access. ReviewPreset and knowledge-base models participate in that guard. A repository on another approved GitHub host is reached only with that host’s own credentials or the launcher’s own token, never the instance’s; with neither, the run is refused (see per-host GitHub credentials). A team’s own page also lists the repositories shared with it (sharedRepositories on GET /teams/:id), read-only, active rows only, and under an enforcing repo-access gate only those the caller’s own GitHub permission reaches; a platform ADMIN is not gated. A non-admin onboarding a repository, or moving it to another host, must hold at least read access on GitHub through their own verified login, asked live and failing closed (no access and no such repository answer alike). Only a platform ADMIN may name a repository’s executor image, because it holds the run’s GitHub credential; and a connection whose destination (base URL, tracker provider, Zendesk subdomain) changes while its stored token is kept is refused with 409 TOKEN_ORIGIN_CHANGE. The invitee of an organization admin or a team lead waits for platform approval unless a platform ADMIN has marked the organization’s invites trusted. A share may be view only (ConnectionTeamShare.canLaunch off): its members can see the repository but the launch decision refuses new work through that share. Epics, PRD runs and campaigns require team LEAD or ADMIN on the team that owns each repository, a share does not count, and the refusal names repositories and never the owning team. A teamId filter on human steps, runs, repositories and pull-request views is checked against the caller’s membership (404 for a non-member) and only narrows.
features.title: Organizations, teams & repository access

features.body: Filter and page the configuration audit log and runtime security events.
features.detail: Audit rows name actors by email, and a deleted actor keeps its id. Security events page on the server. A separate summary route returns per-type counts: all time when no window is given, otherwise for the window plus the equal-length window before it. The dashboard always sends its selected date range (30 days by default), shows each count against the previous window, and filters the list when a type is selected. Both views are ADMIN-only. The audit search box matches the actor’s email or name and the entity type as substrings; an entity id (or actor id) matches only when the whole uuid is typed, because a partial id is not matched at all, and a search that matches more than 200 people considers only 200 of them. The CSV export applies the same filter as the list, writes newest first in batches, and holds at most a fixed number of rows: when more match, the response says so in a header and the dashboard tells the admin the file holds only the newest rows and states the limit, so a larger history needs narrower filters or a shorter date range. On the audit route, a WorkflowRun row also carries the id of the request it belongs to. Template, team and organization administration is recorded in the same log: template create (including a generated draft), edit, new version, promote and webhook enable or revoke; team create, update, deactivation, memberships and the shell-image and egress allowlists; organization rename and membership changes. Agent library create, version update and deletion are recorded at platform and team scope; an update entry holds the model, runtime and version before and after (the team entry also its key, scope and team), not the prompt. Refining a template into a new version, a draft saved by an asynchronous generation job, and the review mark that gates promoting an AI-generated version write no audit row. A template entry holds identity, status, version and routing fields, never the spec text, and a webhook entry records only whether one exists, never the token. Template, team, organization and agent entries are written after the change as a separate statement, not in its transaction, so a failed audit insert errors after the change has applied. A repository’s gate commands (on onboarding and on change), service principals and their tokens, and callback and event endpoints are recorded too, never with a token or secret; governed-knowledge actions have their own event table instead. Each row can also carry a context saying how the action arrived (credential path, a truncated address, the request id); the dashboard shows those three when a row is opened and the CSV export appends them as ip, via and request_id. An eval run started through the platform route writes one launch row after its workflow has started, and the MCP consent audit builds its context from the request itself. Audit rows are kept forever unless an operator sets a retention of at least a year (a stored value below that is ignored and nothing is deleted). When set, a scheduled sweep that an environment switch can turn off deletes older rows in batches, at most a fixed number per run so a large backlog takes several runs, never selects registry setting changes or its own summary rows (other entity types are pruned), and writes one summary row when it deleted something (if that write fails it is logged and the deletion stands). Runs the worker starts, where no request exists to write the row, get one launch row too: an epic child or a channel task when its run row is created, naming its launchedById or, when it has none, the requester on its work request (no actor when there is no request or that read fails), and a PRD child’s request wherever the child is known to have started, including when a retry adopts a launch an earlier attempt made. That write happens at most once per entity and source under an advisory lock, carries no request context, and on failure is only logged, never failing the run. A run started by a schedule writes no launch row; its automation decision row records it instead.
features.title: Audit and security-event review

features.body: Record who was refused and who read something sensitive, first-party, with an opt-in page-view stream.
features.detail: A response hook builds a row from the request object, not from request-scoped storage, and stores the route template that matched, never the URL, a query string or a body. A signed-in person answered 403 produces a denied row. A successful GET of a route that carries an activity tag (the audit log list and export, a run’s detail, the pull-request outcomes export and the people-analytics export, which answers CSV and is recorded as an export row) produces a read or export row on every mount of that route, deprecated aliases included; the activity views themselves, a run’s traces and transcript reads (which write their own access-log row) are not tagged. A 401, or a 403 with no identified person, writes no row and is only counted, by route template and status, in an OpenTelemetry counter. Authenticated callers are bounded, not unlimited: a read is written at most once per person and route every ten minutes (an export is never collapsed: each one writes a row within its budget), a denial once per person, route and status every minute, a page view once per person and page every five seconds, and each person has a separate per-minute budget for each kind (120 denials, 60 each of exports, reads and page views), so a flood of one kind cannot use up the budget that records an export; the excess is dropped and counted, and a dropped event does not mark its dedupe key. Rows pass through a bounded in-memory queue flushed in batches; when it is full a denial or export evicts the oldest page view, then read, before it would be dropped (it can still be dropped if the queue holds only denials and exports), and a failed write drops the batch, so events can be lost and the count is per gateway process. Recording never delays or fails a request, and shutdown waits only a few seconds for a flush. Page views are off unless an ADMIN switches on a registry setting; the dashboard then sends only the pathname, in batches of at most 20, never when the browser sends Do Not Track or Global Privacy Control, and the gateway reduces it to one of a fixed list of page route templates (a test keeps the list equal to the page tree) or drops it. A password sign-in that fails for a known address writes a sign-in failure row; the ADMIN failed-sign-in alert list counts those rows per account over a configurable window and marks accounts at or above a configurable threshold. A per-process counter records each threshold crossing. Alerts are shown on the dashboard and as a metric only, with no notification channel, and the list is built from those rows, so OAuth, magic-link and unknown-address failures do not appear in it. Events are kept for a configurable number of days (90 by default, at least 7); a scheduled sweep that an environment switch can turn off deletes older ones in batches, at most a fixed number per run, so a backlog clears over several runs. The ADMIN-only activity page and routes show exact per-day counts by kind (queried at most three days at a time), the most-denied routes, recent events and this process’s drop count; the in-app assistant may not call them.
features.title: First-party user-activity events

features.body: Launch scheduled repository work, template webhook calls and GitHub-event automations, and run maintenance sweeps.
features.detail: Temporal schedules also drive eval regression/revalidation, lesson consolidation, repository dependency scans and permission sync. Some jobs are off by default and need explicit operator configuration (repository access sync, Slack channel privacy and membership sync, eval regression and revalidation); lesson consolidation, repository dependency scans, knowledge-base sync, provider model discovery, the run reaper, the orphaned-workspace sweep, the agent transcript and audit and activity retention sweeps, the model-call trace and workflow-run rollups, the weekly report digest, the skill-source update check, the automation-decision prune and the outcome report, by contrast, are on by default. Every system-wide schedule runs on the engineering-workflow task queue and is created with the skip overlap policy, so a fire that arrives while the previous one is still running is dropped (a manual consolidation trigger is allowed to overlap). The schedule settings are read at gateway startup, and the system-wide schedules are synchronized once the gateway’s Temporal connection is up, which may be later than boot (see the gateway-without-Temporal card). Schedules of a Slack channel or a scheduled work request are reconciled when their own rows are written, not at startup, and a write that needs one is refused with 503 TEMPORAL_UNAVAILABLE until the gateway’s first connection. After that connection a Slack channel write stands when its schedule sync fails (logged) and a channel delete tears its schedules down best-effort, while a scheduled work request syncs Temporal first or rolls its rows back. The scheduled-work list reports exists: null with unavailable: true for a schedule whose live state could not be asked, which differs from exists: false. Edits to a scheduled work request are compare-and-set on a row version and retry a few times when a competing write changed only the acting user or fire bookkeeping; any other competing change is a 409. When a repository share is removed or the repository moves, each schedule of a team left with no claim is deactivated and audited on its own (the acting user is the actor), before its Temporal schedule is paused; an audit failure is logged and does not skip the pause. The run reaper is one system-wide schedule (every 15 minutes by default) that finalizes runs whose Temporal execution is over; it is paused, not removed, when disabled. The skill-source check is one system-wide schedule (daily by default) that asks each tracked source’s host which commit its ref names and only flags a different one; it is paused, not removed, when disabled. A scheduled fire is a run like any other for budgets: it gets a ledger row and run connection at its first activity, and the pull request it opens links to that execution’s own ledger row so CI signals reach the right workflow. While a re-run (or any other non-fire run) of a schedule’s standing request is in flight, each fire is skipped as a refused execution with reason request-in-flight, logged at info and audited (event fire-skipped, action UPDATE) at most once an hour, and the schedule resumes on the first tick after the run ends. A re-run is refused with 409 WORKFLOW_ALREADY_EXISTS while any live ledger row of the request exists: a fire’s, an earlier run’s, or a child run that carries the request’s id. Both read the request’s non-terminal ledger rows, the schedule’s anchor excluded, and confirm each with Temporal before refusing: a finished or absent workflow has its stale row closed with the status Temporal reports (COMPLETED, TIMED_OUT, CANCELLED for terminated or cancelled, else FAILED) and does not block (closing the row is best-effort: a failed close is ignored and the next check asks again), a row written in the last five minutes is trusted, and when Temporal cannot be asked or does not answer within three seconds the row blocks and the refusal says so. The re-run also confirms the row its workflow id allocator refuses on, which reads only the ticket’s eng- family and never asks Temporal itself, and allocates again once that row is closed. A run ended by a SKIPPED terminate node closes its ledger row as COMPLETED, so it never reads as in flight. Between the read and the start there is no lock. The outcome report is one system-wide schedule (Temporal schedule id auto-swe-outcome-report; Mondays at 02:37 UTC by default (the schedule sets no time zone); OUTCOME_REPORT_ENABLED and OUTCOME_REPORT_CRON, read when the schedules sync once Temporal connects) that starts ScheduledOutcomeReportWorkflow with no arguments. Its one activity builds the outcome report from the deployment’s run data over the trailing 90 complete UTC days (the scheduled run passes no options, so the window is fixed), stores it as an outcome-report artifact and keeps the newest eight snapshots; an administrator-only route serves the newest snapshot, and another computes a report on demand over a windowDays of 7 to 365. It is paused, not removed, when disabled. The automation-decision prune is one system-wide schedule (daily at 04:37 by default; AUTOMATION_DECISION_PRUNE_ENABLED and AUTOMATION_DECISION_PRUNE_CRON, read when the schedules sync once Temporal connects) that deletes decision-ledger rows which started no run once they are older than workflow.automationDecisionRetentionDays (90 days by default, at least 7, GLOBAL scope only); it is paused, not removed, when disabled. Rows that started a run, and rows naming a commit the platform produced, are never deleted. A scheduled fire and a template webhook call also leave a row in that ledger (started, or refused with a reason, a refusal recorded once an hour per reason) so the Automations page can say what came of each; recording is best-effort and never fails the fire or the call, and no event-source guard reads these rows. Run callbacks are delivered by a system-wide sweep (every minute by default) and pruned daily (CALLBACK_DELIVERY_ENABLED / _CRON and CALLBACK_DELIVERY_PRUNE_ENABLED / _CRON, both on by default and read when the schedules sync); eval flake screens run as per-dataset workflows started when a dataset is created, when an eval run finds unscreened cases, and by the revalidation sweep. A template webhook may require signed calls (see that card).
features.title: Scheduled automation & webhooks

features.body: The gateway starts and serves while Temporal is unreachable, connecting in the background; routes that need a workflow client answer a retryable 503.
features.detail: The Temporal plugin registers at once and retries the connection with a doubling delay from one second up to thirty, logging the first attempts at warn and later ones at debug. Until the first connection succeeds, every call through the gateway’s Temporal helpers raises a dedicated error. Where a route does not handle it, the global handler answers 503 with the code TEMPORAL_UNAVAILABLE and a Retry-After of five seconds (logged at warn, not error); routes that handle Temporal failures keep their own answers (the GitHub webhook signal paths answer 503 SIGNAL_FAILED, an event-automation delivery whose run could not be started after three attempts answers 503 AUTOMATION_START_FAILED so the delivery can be sent again, Slack shows a temporarily-unavailable message, and the scheduled-work list degrades). That error is not a workflow-not-found error: callers that signal or look up a workflow treat it as could-not-confirm, roll back and ask for a retry. Routes that would persist a row whose consistency depends on a Temporal call check the connection first and refuse before writing: eval launches (so an outage is not recorded as a failed eval), Slack channel registration with a digest or poll, a change to a Slack channel’s active flag, digest or poll enablement or cron, and channel deletion (an edit that leaves those values as stored goes through), and the saves of system settings that synchronize a schedule. The Slack approval path answers a temporarily-unavailable message. A channel knowledge edit’s re-embedding is deliberately not gated on Temporal. System-wide Temporal schedules (lesson consolidation, repository dependency scan, knowledge-base sync, permission sync, model discovery, run reaper, orphaned-workspace sweep, skill-source check, automation-decision prune, run-callback delivery and its prune, agent transcript prune, model-call trace rollup, workflow-run rollup, report digest, outcome report, audit and activity prune, Slack channel sync, eval regression and revalidation) are synchronized once the connection comes up, each best-effort: a failure is logged. Only consolidation, eval regression and revalidation have an admin save route that re-syncs them; the environment-driven ones (repository dependency scan, knowledge-base sync, repository access sync, model discovery, run reaper, workspace sweep, skill-source check, automation-decision prune, callback delivery and prune, transcript prune, trace and run rollups, report digest, outcome report, audit and activity prune, Slack channel sync) are next synced at the following gateway start. GET /health always answers 200 with status ok while the process serves requests and adds temporal: connecting or connected, so a container healthcheck keyed on it does not depend on Temporal. The per-client request limit is read once at boot from RATE_LIMIT_MAX (default 200) and RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW_SECONDS (default 60); a value that is not a positive integer fails the boot instead of falling back to the default. The GitHub-signed webhook routes (git, access and ci) have their own per-address ceiling, WEBHOOK_RATE_LIMIT_MAX (default 6000, in the same window), because every delivery from one host shares an address and GitHub does not retry a 429; a 429 is logged as one warning line, not an error.
features.title: Gateway boots without Temporal

features.body: The dashboard lists work by request, with the latest visible attempt standing for each, and retries a request without losing its identity.
features.detail: Run visibility is applied first, then executions are grouped by request. A single-repository request is represented by its newest visible execution; a cross-repository request summarizes every visible child and keeps failed children visible while others run. Filtering and paging happen after grouping, so an old failure cannot resurface behind a successful retry. A retry starts a new execution of the same request from its recorded template version. Whether the request targeted a repository or not, it applies the template checks a fresh launch applies (the template must be ACTIVE and visible through the caller’s team membership, a recorded input is validated against its input schema); a repository request additionally re-checks repository access, and a connection-free or non-repository one re-checks the connection and the budget of the organization the request recorded (else the template team’s, which the retry then records). An agent re-run reuses the request id with a fresh delivery branch. Optional instructions are appended to the new attempt’s description only. A cross-repository request is not retried as a whole. Text search over runs, requests and tickets also matches the request’s launch label, held in a plain title column that a database trigger fills from the launch payload, trimmed and capped at 200 characters, and leaves empty rather than failing a launch on a payload it cannot read.
features.title: Request-centred work list and retry

features.body: Read and write Notion pages, Confluence pages, Zendesk comments, tracker issues, PagerDuty incident notes, Slack messages, HubSpot CRM objects and generic HTTP API endpoints.
features.detail: These have concrete worker connectors, and a step over a pair outside GENERIC_STEP_CONNECTION_TYPES fails with CONNECTOR_NOT_IMPLEMENTED. The HubSpot and http_api branches in genericActions call their own connectors (HubSpot CRM v3 objects through a private-app token; http_api through a guarded, https-only fetch confined to the connection’s base path) and, for writes, go through the approval check and outcome ledger. An mcp connection is executed through the MCP core, with approval checked after the server is contacted. A confluence connection is a team’s own, with its own credential; its connector reads, creates and updates pages through the guarded fetch with the connection’s private-network opt-in, escapes agent text into storage format, honours a supplied page version so a stale update is refused, and stops non-retryably on a response that is ambiguous or names a different page. A readSource node can name an issue with issueId. A pagerduty connection (a REST API key plus the fromEmail of a PagerDuty user) supports all three generic steps: readSource and the fetchIncident tool read an incident with its latest alerts, log entries and notes (a request takes an incidentId in the query or inputs, validated as a short uppercase-alphanumeric id), and writeOutcome and the addNote tool post a note, which needs the fromEmail user, is capped, and takes the draft pull request link or a short reason no fix opened when the step is given one. The PagerDuty requests go to the fixed api.pagerduty.com host with redirects refused and a thirty-second timeout, but through a plain fetch rather than the guarded one. A pagerduty_events connection holds only a routing key and is refused by all three generic steps with CONNECTOR_NOT_IMPLEMENTED. Requests either refuse redirects (Notion, Confluence, Zendesk, Slack and Linear; Jira treats a 3xx as a failure) or, for GitHub Issues, re-check every hop through a guarded fetch, so a credential cannot leave the configured origin.
features.title: Non-engineering API handlers

features.body: Connector requests to tracker and knowledge-base base URLs, and MCP server URLs, pass a text check and a connection-time resolve-and-pin check whose private-network opt-in is narrow, and connector requests refuse or re-check every redirect.
features.detail: Jira, GitHub Issues and Confluence base URLs are checked strictly first when those connectors run, and Jira field detection, an ADMIN call, runs the same check before it builds its client and answers 400 BASE_URL_REFUSED for a refused URL, whether it came from the stored row or the environment fallback. Only when that check refuses a private address and the connector’s allowPrivateNetwork opt-in is on is the refusal waived, and the waiver is logged. The same opt-in decides whether a resolved private address is accepted when the request connects (see the resolve-and-pin card). MCP connections use the same address check, with the flag stored on each connection (see the MCP card): every MCP save re-checks the URL, and the waiver is recorded in the audit trail rather than logged. A refused loopback, link-local or unspecified address is reported as such, with or without the opt-in, rather than as a private-network refusal that would suggest the opt-in could help. The opt-in never reaches loopback, link-local (IPv4 and IPv6), cloud-metadata or unspecified addresses, multicast or the reserved and documentation ranges, nor a malformed URL or a scheme other than http(s). The worker’s Jira path honours the opt-in only for the exact origin an ADMIN configured. The tracker and knowledge-base save routes apply the same check and answer 400 BASE_URL_REFUSED for a stored target the connector would refuse, but only when the write touches the provider or URL or turns the opt-in on, so a save that only turns it off is never blocked. Redirects are never followed unchecked. Linear, Notion, Slack, Zendesk and Figma requests set redirect: error, and the Atlassian client treats any 3xx as a failure it does not retry. GitHub Issues and the CI-log download, which GitHub answers with redirects, go through a guarded fetch: redirects are followed by hand for at most three hops, the guard runs on every hop, the credential is sent only to the configured origin, only a short allowlist of benign headers crosses to another origin, a write cannot cross origins, a 307 or 308 keeps the method and body, and every hop is also resolved and pinned. GitHub Issues waives private addresses only on its configured origin, follows a redirect only while it stays under the named repository’s path there (so a renamed repository or a transferred issue fails closed), and drops a fetched issue whose repository_url names another repository. The CI-log download waives them only on the credential’s and the repository’s GitHub origins, except for a repository on a GitHub Enterprise host (any web or API base other than github.com), where every hop of the download may resolve to a private address because its log storage usually sits on the same network; the token still goes only to the log URL’s origin. Figma has no opt-in: its host is a constant that is still run through the guard. The tracker, knowledge-base and Figma connection tests also accept unsaved form values. A blank token means the stored one, but a typed provider or base URL that differs from the saved one (for Notion, whose address is fixed, only a different provider counts) is refused unless the token is typed again, so a stored token is not sent to a target it was not saved for, and such a typed URL passes the guard first. Figma’s host is fixed, so a typed token can only go there. Knowledge-base test failures are fixed messages by class (credentials, not found, unreachable, failed), never text from the remote service, and the check uses a dedicated connection test that throws on a rejected credential instead of a search that returns nothing.
features.title: Connector base URLs and redirects are guarded

features.body: On the GitHub Issues tracker a ticket id names its own owner/repo, so the platform reads, comments on, links, closes or files issues under it only when that repository is one the request or run targets, on the tracker’s host; on Jira and Linear the same reads and writes are held to the operator’s allowed project keys.
features.detail: The id is user-supplied and the instance’s tracker token reaches any repository it can see, so a GitHub-tracker read or write that names a repository is checked first. The submit-time ticket fetch is checked against the one repository the launcher selected (a bare issue number resolves against it). The worker’s ticket fetch (the gather step and the validate/implement fallback) and every write are checked against the run’s own connection when it is a git repository, plus the repositories its launch was authorized against. The writes are postTicketComment, the tracker sync (pull-request links, CI and failure comments, and closing the issue when a run completes) from the pull-request and run-end steps and the merge and CI webhooks, and PRD issue creation, whose project key is checked as that repository when the request supplies one (a run with no project key files under the tracker’s configured default project, which is not checked); a workflow-started event writes nothing on GitHub and is not checked. Owner and repository compare case-insensitively, and the repository’s own GitHub URLs (the instance’s when it states none) must be on the tracker’s host, with github.com and api.github.com, and a GitHub Enterprise Cloud tenant’s web and API hosts, counting as one. An id or host that does not parse is refused, and so is a bare number on a write. A refusal happens before any request, writes nothing, logs a fixed line with ids only and never fails the run: a read is treated as a ticket that was not found, and a refused PRD item counts as failed. A refused run-end write is recorded on the run as out_of_scope (the id names a repository the run does not target) or no_repository (it names none), so the run page says the ticket was not updated. The provider also follows a redirect only while it stays under the named repository’s path on the configured origin, so a renamed repository or a transferred issue fails closed, and a fetched issue whose repository_url names another repository is dropped. A ticket kept in a different repository from the one the run targets (a separate issues repository, say) therefore gets no context and no tracker writes. The check runs when a ticket is fetched, not on one already stored on the request. Jira and Linear ids name no repository, so a read and a write are held instead to the operator’s tracker.allowedProjectKeys list (empty means unrestricted, and a key is matched case-insensitively). A ticket whose project key is not listed is treated as not found on a read, and the ticket comment, the tracker sync and its status transitions make no provider call for it, recorded on the run as out_of_scope; a list that cannot be read, or a scope that fails to load, writes nothing either but is recorded as an unknown failure rather than a refusal, and a skipped write records which tracker was in use so a run viewed after an operator switches trackers keeps its wording. PRD epic and story creation on Jira or Linear is gated too: the target key (the PRD input’s, else the configured default project, else BACKLOG) must be listed, and a refusal fails the step non-retryably with TRACKER_PROJECT_NOT_ALLOWED instead of skipping the epic. The list resolves at the contexts of the repositories the run targets, else at the launching template’s team; for a launch with no git repository and a platform-wide template, the gateway computes the contexts once and stores them on the run (RunInput.trackerScopeContexts), and the worker reads that recorded value, so a launcher who later leaves a team does not change a running run’s answer. A person’s contexts are each active team in an active organization plus any organization they belong to through no listed team; a service principal’s is its own team; each context’s list overrides GLOBAL rather than being unioned with it, and a recorded empty list means GLOBAL only. A launch whose context lookup fails is refused with 503 LAUNCH_SCOPE_UNAVAILABLE, and a recorded value that fails validation refuses instead of widening to GLOBAL. A run with nothing recorded (launched before the column, or by a path that records none) falls back to its template’s team, then the launcher’s active teams, then GLOBAL.
features.title: Tracker reads and writes stay inside the run’s repositories or the operator’s project keys

features.body: Requests to operator-supplied URLs resolve the host once, refuse the request if any answer is internal, and connect only to an address from that checked answer.
features.detail: The text guard reads only the URL, so a public name that resolves to an internal address passes it. createGuardedFetch closes that at connection time: it drives undici’s own fetch with a dispatcher whose connect lookup resolves the name once (bounded to 5 s), classifies every returned address with the text guard’s rules, and refuses the request if any one is refused; a resolver error, timeout or empty answer also refuses, with a fixed message. The socket is handed only addresses from that checked answer, so the check and the connection share one resolution. They are ordered IPv4 first and tried in turn with a 300 ms per-attempt wait, over HTTP/1.1 only, while TLS server name and Host stay the hostname. A literal IP never reaches the lookup, so it is classified before the request. Private ranges (RFC 1918, CGNAT, unique-local IPv6, and 198.18.0.0/15, which fake-IP proxy tools answer every name with) pass only with the call site’s opt-in. Loopback, link-local, unspecified and cloud-metadata addresses (GCP’s fd20:ce::254 and OCI’s 192.0.0.192 included), multicast, and the reserved, IETF protocol, documentation, 6to4 relay, Teredo and discard ranges never pass, whether written as a literal or returned by DNS. The call sites are bundle install-from-URL, the provider credential test, model discovery and the catalog refresh (strict unless the apiBase host is listed in models.privateNetworkHosts, which waives only the private-range refusal), the worker’s chat-model and embedding calls and the Claude Code model proxy’s upstream calls (the same listed-host rule, with redirects refused), the Jira and Confluence (Atlassian) and GitHub Issues connectors, the worker’s Jira connector, the worker’s MCP transports and the gateway’s MCP connection test, skill-source fetches, the CI-log download, the GitHub connection test when its API URL is typed and unsaved, the Confluence connector, run callbacks (with the endpoint’s opt-in) and the community price-list fetch (with the model host list). Pi’s model calls go through the worker’s model binding, so they take the model-call guard too. createOriginScopedFetch applies a private-network waiver only to named origins, which is how the MCP opt-in and the CI-log allowance cover the configured host while any other hop is strict; GitHub Issues does the same by choosing a permissive or a strict fetch per hop. A refused resolution carries the ESSRF_BLOCKED code: model discovery and the credential test report it as blocked address and the MCP test says the address resolves to a network the connection may not reach, never resolver detail. Under an environment proxy the guarded fetch dispatches through Node’s own fetch so the proxy’s routing is used; the host is still checked up front but the connection is not pinned. The repository’s invariant check fails a bare fetch (a call, a default parameter or a passed value) in the modules whose every request is operator-supplied, so an injectable fetch cannot silently default back to the text-only path.
features.title: Operator URLs are resolved and pinned at connection time

features.body: Package agents, skills, scanner patterns and templates for export/install and SDK authoring.
features.detail: Manifest v2 hashes identity and content; detached Ed25519 signatures are checked against deployment trust keys. Unverified install is denied unless allowed. Installing a skill over an existing one cuts a new revision when its text or description differs, always clears its verification, and scans it; a concurrent edit to that skill rolls back the whole install. Credentials and connection instances are not portable bundle content. An ADMIN installs a bundle inline (the CLI’s bundles install <path>, or a .json file picked or dropped in the dashboard) or from a URL (the dashboard or the CLI). The URL path text-checks every hop as public-only, resolves and pins it with no private-network opt-in, follows at most five redirects, times out after 15 s and caps the streamed body at BUNDLE_MAX_BYTES (5 MB by default); the inline preview and install routes accept a request body of that cap plus 64 KiB. The dashboard’s file flow parses the file in the browser (invalid JSON, a non-object or a file over the gateway’s cap — read from GET /platform/bundles/limits, 5 MB while that answer loads or is unavailable — is reported without sending anything), previews the parsed bundle and installs that same object; both install routes take an optional expectedContentHash and answer 409 BUNDLE_CHANGED when the bundle’s declared hash differs from it, and the install then re-derives the hash, so whatever the hash covers is what was previewed. The dashboard sends the hash on both paths; the CLI sends none and installs without a preview. Every template version an install writes gets the same WorkflowShellAudit rows a canvas save would for its authored code, with the installing ADMIN as author; a container node naming an image that is not a built-in shell image still installs, and the install and its preview each return a warning naming the template, node and image; the image is checked when the step runs, against the allowlist of the team that owns the run’s repository. Templates’ input schemas are checked as a save checks them, so a platform-filled text key cannot be typed as a connection.
features.title: Portable signed bundles

features.body: Price models from a catalog, and on a schedule ask each provider which models it lists, storing unreviewed suggestions instead of catalog rows.
features.detail: The gateway upserts one Temporal schedule, auto-swe-model-discovery, once the Temporal connection is up; it runs ScheduledModelDiscoveryWorkflow, a single discoverModels activity that lists models through every GLOBAL provider credential. It is on by default (MODEL_DISCOVERY_ENABLED, MODEL_DISCOVERY_CRON, read when the schedule is synchronized once the Temporal connection is up); disabling pauses the schedule rather than deleting it. Results go to model_suggestions (NEW: listed but priced nowhere; RETIREMENT_CANDIDATE: a priced model missing from a complete listing) and model_discovery_provider_status, never to catalog rows, so a suggestion cannot make a model known at $0. A failed provider changes only its status row; an incomplete listing (page cap, empty result, an unfollowable continuation) still records new suggestions but deletes nothing and flags no retirement candidates; a dismissal survives refreshes; deleting a provider’s GLOBAL credential removes only the credential: the next discovery pass, scheduled or on demand, removes that provider’s suggestion and status rows, and until then the suggestions endpoint still serves them. Every failure is reduced to a fixed string (HTTP <status>, timed out, request failed (<name>, <code>; the code is omitted when absent), credential could not be decrypted, blocked address, apiBase required, unrecognised response), so no fetch or provider text reaches the status row, logs or Temporal history, and a credential save rejects a key with whitespace or control characters and an apiBase carrying a username or password. An apiBase on a private network (any provider’s) is refused on the credential Test button, model discovery and the catalog refresh (which also check every resolved address) and, as URL text only, on credential save, unless its host (or host:port, as the URL spells it) is listed in the ADMIN-only, GLOBAL-only setting models.privateNetworkHosts; the listing waives only the private-range refusal, and loopback, localhost, link-local, cloud-metadata, unspecified, multicast and reserved addresses stay refused whatever is listed. A setting that cannot be read leaves the list empty, so the strict guard applies. The list also applies to the model and embedding calls agents make, and a call to an unlisted host that resolves to a private address fails before any request is sent; those calls refuse redirects, so a provider that answers with a 30x must be pointed at its final URL. The list is read per request behind the settings cache, so a client built earlier picks up a change, and an unreadable setting leaves it empty. A built-in provider (anthropic, openai, google) with an apiBase is probed and listed at that base instead of the vendor’s, keeping the provider’s auth style (a Google probe against a custom base sends the key in x-goog-api-key, not in the URL). Because a proxy exposes aliases rather than the vendor catalog, such a listing is never marked complete: it still proposes new models but never proposes retiring one. An apiBase carrying a query or fragment is rejected for every provider, since /models would land inside it. Admins read the suggestions in the Catalog tab, where the on-demand discover route refreshes the same rows. Nothing is added to the catalog or retired automatically. Adding a model can be prefilled from price hints: the provider’s own listing where it carries prices (an OpenAI-compatible listing such as OpenRouter’s), and a community price list in LiteLLM’s format at models.priceListUrl (on by default; empty turns it off), fetched through the model-host guard with redirects refused, a 32 MB cap and a six-hour cache. The hint routes write nothing; the discovery list shows each new model’s suggested price, and bulk add creates every selected row in one transaction, refused whole (409 MODEL_EXISTS) when any spec is already in the catalog. The price-list figures also reach the catalog refresh as a cross-check (see that use case).
features.title: Model catalog & scheduled discovery

features.body: Reach repositories on other approved GitHub hosts with that host’s own PAT or App, and never send a platform credential to a host it does not belong to.
features.detail: GitHubHostCredential holds, per approved non-instance host family, an optional PAT and/or a GitHub App (id and private key), encrypted with the platform envelope and managed by ADMINs through routes that return only whether a secret is set and its last four characters. resolvePlatformCredential returns instance, host, mismatch, misconfigured or installation-mismatch. A launcher’s own saved token still wins; a host’s set is built from its row alone (no instance PAT, App, auth mode or singleton installation) and lapses when the host leaves github.repositoryHosts. resolveGitHubToken refuses any API host outside the set’s credentialHost as a last line, for the PAT, installation tokens and the App JWT. GitHubInstallation is identified by (host, installationId) with the host fixed at creation, and a repository may point only at an installation on its own host: checked when the repository is written and again when a run token is minted (REPO_INSTALLATION_HOST_MISMATCH), The installation’s host is required wherever a token is minted: the repository types the worker’s SCM calls and the shared mint-time check take (RepoRef, InstallationScopedRepo) declare it without an optional, so a caller that does not load it fails to compile, and a repository with an installation but no host reads as a mismatch, failing closed. GitHub’s own installation lifecycle events (installation deleted, suspend and unsuspend, and installation_target renamed) are only a prompt: the gateway confirms with GET /app/installations/{id}, signed with the App JWT of the host the delivery’s secret proved, and applies only what GitHub answers (404 is deleted, suspended_at is suspended, otherwise active; a rename updates accountLogin). A host with no App credentials, a failed lookup, or an installation nobody registered changes nothing, so a forged or replayed delivery that GitHub contradicts is harmless; installations are never created automatically. GitHubInstallation.retiredReason records that a retirement came from a webhook, so a webhook reverses only its own retirements, an admin’s isActive change clears it, and the write is conditional on the row as read. Each applied change is audited with the state GitHub confirmed. The login-ownership check reads the account a login was recorded against (users.github_login_account_id) and asks that account’s host with that host’s credential; a non-github.com host with no credential is reported unverifiable, keeping the login, and a github.com account with no applicable credential is asked unauthenticated, so the check is rate-limited. A confirmed mismatch clears the login only if it and its source account are unchanged since they were read, and records a takeover. Unlinking a GitHub account clears the login only when it is the source account.
features.title: Per-host GitHub credentials & installations

features.body: A skill’s text is an immutable revision, and a run reads the revisions it pinned at start, so editing a skill mid-run does not change what a retry or replay sees.
features.detail: Every write that changes a skill’s text or description (create, edit, boot sync, bundle install) cuts a SkillRevision in the same statement, guarded on the revision number the writer read; a concurrent edit gets 409 SKILL_CHANGED (PUT also accepts expectedRevision), and the boot sync skips a race it lost. createWorkflowRun stores {skillId: revision} in WorkflowRun.skillRevisions for every skill visible to GLOBAL plus the run’s team and organization (a repo-less channel task uses its Slack channel’s). Skill reads for agents use the pinned text, and the pin is part of the resolveAgent cache key. isActive is deliberately read live (within the config cache window of about 30 s), so an admin can switch a harmful skill off under a running run. isVerified describes the current text. An admin edit or bundle install that cuts a revision clears it, and a pinned older revision never reports as verified. For custom and bundle-installed skills, only POST /platform/skills/:id/verify (ADMIN, naming the revision, 409 when stale) sets it; the boot sync re-verifies the seeded built-ins on every start, including when it cuts a revision from shipped text. Skill descriptions and text are scanned in full on create, edit and bundle install; the scan is advisory and is marked incomplete when a pattern is quarantined or the scanner fails.
features.title: Immutable skill revisions pinned per run

features.body: An ADMIN previews skills in a GitHub or GitHub Enterprise repository, then installs the chosen ones pinned to the commit that was previewed.
features.detail: Preview writes nothing: it resolves the ref to a commit and reads each SKILL.md under the path. The install request names skills and the previewed commit, never text; the server fetches again at that commit and fails with 409 if the ref has moved. A non-github.com host must be an approved repository host, and one on a private network must also be listed in a separate setting; the platform credential for that host is the only one used, and a host with none is read anonymously. Fetches are bounded in requests, bytes, skills and time. Skills with scan warnings are refused while the blocking setting is on (it is on by default). One transaction takes a name lock, checks name conflicts across the scopes the skill would be visible in, and writes the source plus every skill at revision 1, unverified, with its source commit. Markdown and text siblings are kept as reference text unscanned and nothing is executed. Wherever a model reads an imported skill’s text, it is labelled third-party with its source and short commit while the revision it reads carries a source commit; an admin’s hand edit cuts a revision without one, which drops the label, and a deleted source drops the repository name (the label reads external@sha7). Updates to an imported source are a separate, reviewed flow: a scheduled check flags a moved ref, and an ADMIN diffs and accepts it. A preview request that names one skill returns that skill’s complete incoming text and writes nothing; it is read at the previewed commit and fails with a moved-ref conflict only when the request names that commit (the field is optional), otherwise it reads what the ref names now. The dashboard’s External sources tab drives the flow, and it is the dashboard that requires a skill’s full text to be read at the previewed commit before it can be ticked and sends only skills it read; the create and install routes take skill names and require no earlier read. Skills the pinned commit holds that nothing installed uses can be installed later. The install is read by the pinned sha and never through the ref, so upstream ref movement does not affect it, and it takes a per-source lock plus the name lock and never moves the pin. It applies the import rules (ALREADY_INSTALLED for a folder already installed, NAME_CONFLICT, scan warnings blocked by the setting), refuses STALE_SHA when the sha is not the pin, DISABLED for a source disabled before the request and 404 for one deleted before it. SOURCE_CHANGED means the source was disabled, deleted, re-pinned by an accept or switched to another script mode while the install ran. Nothing is written on any refusal. A folder first added upstream after the pin is UNKNOWN_SKILLS until an accept advances the pin. The skill list marks each skill still attached to a source with that source and the commit its current text was cut from; the commit is empty after a hand edit. In the External sources views and the skill list, repository-derived text (names, descriptions, paths, diff lines, full text) is rendered as plain text, and each control, format, line or paragraph separator and default-ignorable character is shown as a ⟨U+XXXX⟩ marker, except the variation selectors and joiners that make up an emoji and, in text bodies, newline and tab; other look-alike spaces are not marked, and the skill editor shows stored text raw. The gateway stores names, descriptions, text and diffs as parsed and does not mask them; only folder and file paths and ignored frontmatter keys pass through the display function that replaces those characters with ? and cuts to 120 characters.
features.title: Skill import from an external GitHub repository

features.body: A schedule flags when an imported source’s ref names a different commit; an ADMIN reads a per-skill diff in the dashboard or the CLI and accepts it, which cuts new skill revisions. Nothing updates on its own.
features.detail: The gateway upserts one Temporal schedule, auto-swe-skill-source-sync, once the Temporal connection is up; it runs ScheduledSkillSourceSyncWorkflow, a single syncSkillSources activity. It is on by default (SKILL_SOURCE_SYNC_ENABLED, cadence SKILL_SOURCE_SYNC_CRON, default 41 5 * * *), read from the environment at gateway start, and paused rather than removed when disabled. The sweep visits each source that is not disabled, one at a time. A check resolves the ref to a commit and fetches no tree or file. It writes only latestSha, status, lastError and lastCheckedAt, guarded on the pinned commit and on the source not being disabled, so a concurrent accept or disable wins and the check’s write is dropped. A failing source does not stop the others; when a host answers that it is rate limited, only the source that got that answer has its check time moved; the host’s remaining sources are not asked and nothing is written for them until the next run. The same check runs on demand for one source. The diff reads the source at the checked commit (or a given one), by commit and never through the ref, and writes nothing. Per installed skill it reports unchanged, changed or unreadable, with a unified text diff against the live text, description and reference-file changes, scan warnings and whether an admin hand-edited it since import; installed skills whose folder left the source are flagged as removed and folders nothing installed uses are listed as added, each with the name conflicts and the scan block an install of it would meet. A skill whose diff passes a fixed size or work bound has no complete diff and its full text has to be read separately. The accept takes the commit and may name skills, each bound to the installed revision the admin saw; without named skills it is bound to the commit alone. It refuses unless the commit is still the source’s latest, refuses with SKILL_CHANGED and writes nothing if a named skill was edited since, never overwrites a hand-edited skill unless it is named, refuses a skill whose diff is incomplete (truncated or too large) unless it is named, and never updates a skill that no longer parses or whose folder left the source, naming it being refused as NOT_INSTALLABLE, and refuses scan warnings while the blocking setting is on. The accept transaction first takes the per-source lock that an install into the source also takes and re-reads the installed set; the accept compares the installed set it planned from with the set inside its transaction, so a skill installed into, or removed or detached from, the source since this accept read it refuses with SOURCE_CHANGED and the pin never moves past a skill this accept did not plan for. The same transaction cuts a new revision per updated skill, unverified and carrying the source commit, moves the pin only when nothing that changed upstream was left behind, and writes the audit entry; a latestSha that moved or a disable meanwhile rolls it all back. Runs already started keep the revisions they pinned. The CLI shows the diff, asks for confirmation (unless --yes) and, when skills are named with --skills, sends the installed revisions it showed. The dashboard’s Review update offers each changed skill for selection: one the scan blocks cannot be selected; one whose diff is incomplete or too large needs its full incoming text read at that commit and a confirmation that it was read; one hand-edited needs an explicit overwrite confirmation; those last two start unselected. A refusal meaning the reviewed state is stale (the source’s latest commit differs from the diffed one, an edited skill, an incomplete diff, a changed or disabled source, a source not yet checked) offers a Reload diff button rather than retrying.
features.title: Tracked skill-source updates: scheduled check, reviewed diff, bound accept

features.body: Track each pull request a workflow’s pull-request step or an Agent Run’s draft delivery opens, with its state, draft flag and title kept current from host webhooks, and list pull requests and tickets with per-row visibility.
features.detail: A PullRequest row, linked to the opening execution’s ledger row, records OPEN, MERGED or CLOSED (closed without merging), an isDraft flag, a title capped at 300 characters and opened, merged and closed times. Signed pull_request webhooks update only a row the platform already holds for that repository and number: closed, reopened, ready_for_review, converted_to_draft and edited (with a non-empty title) each update only that row. Close (only from OPEN) and reopen (only from CLOSED) are guarded by status, so a redelivery is a no-op; draft and title updates are not, so an out-of-order delivery can leave an older value. A pull request opened outside the platform is never created. An Agent Run with draft delivery inserts its row, on the run’s own ledger row, after the host accepts the draft. The row is only inserted, never updated, because an existing row with the same repository and number is a different pull request; the unique index refuses the collision. A failed write is logged and recorded on the run as a pr.record_failed event without failing it, since the branch is already pushed and the PR open. A workflow’s pull-request step links its own execution’s ledger row, or any ledger row of the same request when it has none. A re-push looks at the latest pull request on its own ledger row, whatever its status: an open one is updated, and a closed one fails the step before any other pull request is considered. When that one is merged, or there is none, the step adopts the newest open pull request of the same request and repository, and re-links it to the executing workflow’s own ledger row when that workflow has one, because CI webhooks signal the workflow a row names. The webhook lookups can match more than one connection row for a repository and take the newest. An id the platform generated names no tracker issue, so the tracker syncs for PR opened, workflow started, CI verdict, merge and run end are skipped for it, as is the knowledge-base page link write-back when a pull request opens, which also needs the flag to have been read and found false, so an unreadable flag skips it while the tracker sync is still attempted; the Slack merge note and merge evaluation row still run. Of the pull_request events only a merge signals the workflow (CI results arrive separately, through check_run webhooks). A merge is accepted from OPEN or CLOSED, so a reopen that was lost or late cannot strand it; a transient signal failure rolls the row back to its previous status, and a terminal one keeps MERGED. When the latest pull request on the executing workflow’s own ledger row (one it adopted included) was closed unmerged, the pull-request activity fails non-retryably with PR_CLOSED_BY_REVIEWER instead of opening a replacement or adopting another open one; a new run of the same request has its own ledger row and is not stopped. GET /api/v1/pull-requests (any signed-in person) lists newest first. A non-ADMIN sees a row only when the repository is reachable to them, and the ticket, request, cost and run on it come from its ledger row only while that row is on the same repository, the run only when the caller may see that run. GET /api/v1/tickets groups requests by external ticket id. A request counts for its requester, for anyone who can see one of its runs, and for anyone who reaches a repository it targets or holds a ledger row on; cost and pull-request aggregates count only repositories the caller reaches, so two teams can read one ticket differently. On the server, scope defaults to MINE (requests the caller submitted), pull requests to every state, and tickets exclude agent runs, channel tasks and requests whose ticket id the platform generated (an agent run, a channel task, a template launch that named no ticket, a PRD run, a scheduled work request, a PRD story the tracker gave no id) unless includeAutomated is set. The dashboard’s Pull requests page, by contrast, opens on OPEN.
features.title: Pull-request lifecycle & ticket views

features.body: Summarize the pull requests the platform opened in a window — merge rate, time to merge, CI state — export them as a file, and measure how long human steps wait for an answer.
features.detail: The outcomes summary and its export need only a signed-in caller and use one filter: a non-ADMIN reaches only repositories they may reach, narrowed by repository, team (owning or shared), template or the caller’s own requests. Merge rate is merged over merged plus closed unmerged, so open pull requests do not count and it is empty when nothing resolved; time to merge is the median and 95th percentile of merge minus open time, skipping a merge with no time or one dated before the pull request opened. A pull request carries its run, template and template version as columns the worker stamps. The workflow’s pull-request step looks up the run of a ledger row and uses it only when that row’s repository is the pull request’s own: a create may fall back to the request-wide row when this execution has none, an update uses only this execution’s own row, and an update that finds no run leaves the existing stamp alone. An Agent Run’s own delivery stamps its run, template and version with no repository check. The summary breaks merge rate and median time to merge down by template, and a pull request with no stamp, or one whose template a non-ADMIN caller may not see, falls in an Unattributed row. The template filter matches the stamped template in the query before the row cap, and a non-ADMIN who names a template they cannot see gets a 404. The export streams CSV or NDJSON for the current window only, in batches, at most a fixed number of rows (a header states the limit and whether more matched), with repository, number, status, draft and CI state, timestamps and the attributed template’s id and name (empty where a non-ADMIN may not see the template) but no title or ticket; CSV text cells that start like a formula are prefixed so a spreadsheet does not run them.
