Once streaming starts a database failure can no longer become an error status. The export is recorded as an activity export event, and the in-app assistant may not call it. Workflow-template analytics add approval latency over the human steps requested in the window, of runs in the caller’s report scope (runs attributed to their teams, to organizations they administer that have org-wide reporting on, or to repositories they reach, plus runs they launched; every run for a platform ADMIN): only answered steps have a wait (median and 95th percentile), while timed-out, cancelled and pending steps are counts only, overall and for the templates with the most steps; the read is capped and says when it was truncated.
features.title: Pull-request outcomes, approval latency and export

features.body: Report the runs started in a window as a delivery funnel, gate and review quality, automation health and approval load, and project each organization’s month-end spend against its cap.
features.detail: Five read routes under /api/v1/reports back the Reports page’s tabs (a separate pair serves the weekly outcome reports), which navigation offers to every signed-in person and which refreshes every 30 seconds while its date range includes today. Delivery, quality, automations and approvals need only a signed-in caller (the scope below does the narrowing) and accept a team filter. A run is attributed once, when it is created, to a team and organization: the team of its connection, else of its work request’s connection, its Slack channel, its requesting service principal or its template, else the team the work request was billed to, and that team’s organization, else the work request’s billing organization. A platform ADMIN reads across tenants. For delivery, quality and approvals anyone else reads the runs attributed to their teams, to organizations whose reports they hold (org.reports.read, an organization ADMIN) while the organization has analytics.orgWideReports switched on, or to a repository they can reach, plus the runs they launched themselves, so a run with no attribution is visible only to its launcher and a platform ADMIN; delivery masks repository and template labels they could not otherwise see (Inaccessible repository, Private template), while quality returns no repository or template labels; approvals apply the same scope to each step’s run and add the team filter. For a non-ADMIN a team filter answers 403 unless the caller belongs to the team or the team’s organization is one whose reports they hold with org-wide reporting on. Automations are scoped like the automation list, to automations on a repository the caller may reach or repository-less ones of a team they belong to, and a team filter keeps those of that team or on its repositories. Budget is gated on org.reports.read: a platform ADMIN sees every organization, an organization ADMIN the ones they administer (whether or not org-wide reporting is on), and anyone else gets 403. The window is a 7, 30 or 90 day preset or a custom range; budget ignores it and covers the current UTC month. Delivery’s cohort is the runs started in the window, read from the daily run rollup for each day older than the recompute horizon (30 days by default) that the nightly sweep has built and live from the run table for every other day, where the live read is newest first and flagged as truncated past 10,000 runs: runs started, succeeded and with at least one pull request, then pull requests with CI passed and merged (pull requests, not runs). Cost per merged pull request divides the cohort’s whole spend by merged pull requests, time to merge is the median from the run’s start, estimated from duration buckets, and CI-fix rounds are averaged over runs with a pull request; the same funnel is sliced by template, repository and team. A run’s spend is its accrued cost, or its ledger row’s when that is zero, and a pull request counts toward a run through the run id the worker stamped on it when it opened or updated the pull request: the workflow’s pull-request step stamps only from a ledger row whose repository is the pull request’s, while an Agent Run’s own delivery stamps its run without that check. Quality groups gate steps per run and gate, a first-attempt pass being a pass with no failure and a final pass any pass; it counts fix-loop attempts per fix step, a CI self-heal rate (runs with a finished CI-fix step whose pull request passed CI or merged), and per-reviewer verdicts parsed from the cohort’s reviewer trace rows (errored rows, and rows whose output has no approved field, skipped and not counted; rows that do not parse as a verdict or name an unknown reviewer counted as non-verdict rows), and compares how many runs with a pull request merged with and without a rejecting verdict; those two figures come from the same rollup and live split as delivery. Budget reads month-to-date spend through the same orgMonthSpend the cap guard uses, projects it linearly over fractional elapsed days (low confidence under one day), reports no cap when the organization has none, else over, projected over, alert or ok in that precedence, and lists the month’s five costliest runs attributed by the billing precedence. Automations count fires by outcome and reason, starts, failed starts and suppressions, and flag noisy (ten or more fires, more than half suppressed) and broken (a failed start, or three or more starts with no successful run). Approvals give the wait median and 95th percentile of resolved steps requested in the window, timeouts, counts by kind and status, waits per resolving user with how many of each user’s resolutions came interactively (web, Slack) or automatically (API token, MCP, assistant), a count of every resolution by how it arrived, autonomy decisions by event and risk class, and the steps pending now with the oldest one’s age. Each report tab except Digests exports what it shows as a CSV built in the browser, with formula-like cells prefixed and the range and any team in the file name. The in-app assistant may call all five routes.
features.title: Delivery, quality, budget, automation and approval reports

features.body: Summarize runs, cost, autonomy and time saved across the templates a caller can see, compare one template’s versions, and export the rollup and the usage report.
features.detail: Cross-template analytics need only a signed-in caller, over the runs in the same report scope as the Reports page (attributed to the caller’s teams, to organizations they administer that have org-wide reporting on, or to repositories they reach, plus runs they launched; every run for a platform ADMIN). The headline, per-template, per-workspace-type and per-integration figures come from one database grouping of the window’s runs and one of the equal-length window before it, so they are not capped; a run’s workspace type is its template’s workspace provider, recorded when the run is created. Time saved sums the estimate snapshotted on successful runs only. A run whose accrued cost is zero takes its ledger row’s cost instead, from a read of at most 50,000 such runs that is flagged when cut, and the daily series and the duration percentiles come from the daily rollup for each built day older than the recompute horizon plus a live read of at most 50,000 runs for each of the two windows, flagged when the current window’s read is cut. One template’s analytics break its runs down by version: success rate over decided runs and merge rate over merged plus closed-unmerged pull requests, each with a 95% Wilson interval, plus average cost, median duration and open pull requests; that read is capped at 10,000 runs and 10,000 steps and says when it was truncated. GET /workflow-templates/analytics/export writes the per-template rows and GET /platform/usage/export the usage report’s rows by model, agent and node, each as CSV or NDJSON and built by the same function as its JSON report, so the same scope checks apply (the usage report is a held scope: team.usage.read for a team’s report, held by its leads, org.reports.read for an organization’s, or platform.reports.read-all); formula-like text cells are prefixed, and the in-app assistant may not call either export. The usage export leaves out the per-person and per-run rankings and the series.
features.title: Workflow analytics and exports

features.body: Each agent runs on the platform’s Mastra tool loop, the Claude Code harness or Pi, and a run never switches an agent’s loop partway through.
features.detail: Resolution order: a caller-supplied pin (an eval side’s override), then the run’s own pin in WorkflowRun.agentRuntimes (an empty pin means the default, without reading the Agent), then the Agent version’s runtime (inherited along inheritsModelFrom, through the usual scope cascade and GLOBAL version pin), then the caller’s default. The implementer family and eval cases default to the run-pinned workspace.implementerRuntime setting; agent runs and checkout agent nodes default to the run-pinned workspace.agentRunRuntime setting (Mastra unless an admin sets it per team, organization or workflow template), read with the repository’s owning team while an agent run’s agent is never resolved at team scope. A run, a channel-assistant turn included, snapshots every visible agent’s own runtime at start, resolved in the run’s scope under its version pins; an agent the snapshot lacks (one created later, or an agent run’s) is pinned at its first resolution with a compare-and-set, so parallel activities agree on whichever pinned first; code outside an activity, and an eval, which has no run, pin nothing. The run page shows what each agent ran on. Generic agent nodes resolve and pin their runtime the same way, defaulting to workspace.agentRunRuntime. Without a workspace they run on Mastra and trace agent.runtime_not_applicable when their agent is pinned to the harness; a node with workspace: true clones the run’s repository (the run’s branch once pushed, else the run’s base branch: payload.baseBranch when the launch named one, otherwise the repository’s default branch) and runs the pinned runtime there, harness included, committing and pushing nothing and destroying the checkout afterwards. A node’s @version ref does not choose its runtime: the pin is per agent key. Every runtime other than Mastra is served by a registered harness (Claude Code, or Pi, whose loop runs in the worker): a runtime value no harness serves fails non-retryably with HARNESS_UNAVAILABLE, and the implementer family, agent runs and checkout agent nodes select the harness and bind the agent’s model before building it (agent runs and checkout nodes before cloning).
features.title: Per-agent runtime, pinned per run

features.body: The worker decides every harness tool call, verifies the harness binary before each turn and treats an undecided call as a refusal.
features.detail: Each harness tool call is translated into a canonical vocabulary (read, search, write, shell) and decided in the worker by the same checks that guard the Mastra workspace tools: the shell-command scanner and audit line for shell, the sensitive-file block and pre-write content check for writes. File paths must be absolute; writes stay inside the checkout, reads and searches inside the checkout or the harness’s own .claude home directory, and search patterns may not be absolute or contain “..”. Tools the agent’s grant leaves out are left off the harness’s tool list and refused by the policy, as is any tool outside the six the harness maps, except the agent’s relayed MCP tools, which run in the worker. A harness is selectable only if it declares that the worker decides each of its tool calls; the registry refuses one that does not. A tool call the worker does not answer within the decision deadline, or whose decision throws, is refused, and writes to the harness’s own configuration (.claude/, CLAUDE.md, CLAUDE.local.md, .mcp.json) are refused. Managed settings make the harness ignore the repository’s permission allow rules and disable bypass mode. The harness retries a failed model API call at most workspace.harnessApiRetries times (4 by default, overridable per template, team or organization), so a call the API keeps refusing gives up after about 20 seconds of backoff rather than about three minutes; only implementer-family turns read the setting, and agent runs and generic agent nodes use the default. Before every turn the container’s copy of the binary is compared by SHA-256 with the worker’s, re-copied on a mismatch, and a turn whose copy still differs fails with HARNESS_BINARY_UNVERIFIED. Pi’s agent loop runs in the worker and awaits a policy hook before every tool call; its read, write, edit, ls, grep and find tools and its shell act on the container through worker-issued commands, a path is resolved to an absolute path before it is decided (a leading @ or ~, or a Unicode space, is refused), the repository’s AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md that the run reads into the prompt is protected from writes, and its model calls and credential stay in the worker.
features.title: Claude Code harness confinement

features.body: The three-persona review rejects only on what its reviewers said; a reviewer that cannot run is not a rejection of the code.
features.detail: Each persona’s output is schema-checked, and a CRITICAL verdict never approves. Each persona’s model is bound, and checked for a price under a USD cap, once before the three start, so an edit while they run changes neither the model called nor the price recorded; a budget, unpriced-model or missing-configuration failure in any persona fails the review activity, and all three failing throws a retryable REVIEW_NETWORK_UNAVAILABLE. When only some fail, the review stands and each missing persona is a critical REVIEWER_CRASH finding that asks for a human look. The summary a review-fix session starts from lists each finding’s reviewer, severity, description and suggested fix, and names a rejection that came with no findings.
features.title: Review failures are not verdicts

features.body: A repository’s team can attach rules that start a template when a signed GitHub delivery matches (a failed Actions run, a label added to an issue or to a pull request, review feedback on a pull request, commits pushed to a branch) or when a Jira filter the gateway polls shows a new ticket or a status change; a team can attach rules to signed events posted to its own endpoints.
features.detail: An Automation row holds the when (an event source and its filters), the what (a template and its options) and the limits (a cooldown, 30 minutes by default, and a daily cap, 10 runs by default). An automation belongs to a repository, or, for a source that targets a team, to a team. The sources are inbound.event (team-owned; see the inbound events card), github.workflow_run.failed (a completed, failed or timed-out run of a push, pull-request or scheduled workflow, from a branch of the repository itself, never a fork) and github.issues.labeled (a person labelling an open issue; bots, Apps and pull requests are ignored before any query), github.pull_request.labeled (a person labelling an open pull request of the repository itself, never a fork; its default template is ticket-to-merge, and its title and body are untrusted text written by whoever opened it), github.push (a person pushing commits to a branch the automation names, optionally narrowed by changed-file globs; it has no default template, so the automation must name one, and the head commit message is untrusted text), github.pull_request.feedback (a review requesting changes or a /auto-swe fix command from a member of the repository, an allowlisted Qodo review, or explicit DB-backed review_findings from a blocking review run; see the review cards), and the two polled sources jira.filter.new_issue and jira.filter.status_changed, which decide what a poll of Jira returns rather than a delivery (see the Jira filter card). A signed webhook is normalized into an occurrence. Event text comes from those facts, but a person's actor check can make a live host-permission lookup when the repository access gate is enabled; feedback enrichment may also reread the host. Temporal confirms potentially in-flight runs. A push reaches the gateway for every repository whose webhook or App subscribes to Push, and one to a repository with no push automation skips the engine's settings and decisions after a repository lookup; independent knowledge-base push synchronization may still run. It takes the first matching enabled automation (oldest repository row, then oldest automation), so one occurrence starts at most one run however many rows match. Before the limits, the source’s own ignore rule applies (the platform’s own work branches never react, and a push source never selects a branch under the work-branch prefix whatever its branch patterns say), the per-team or per-organization kill switch must be on (github.ciFailureTriggersEnabled is on by default; github.issueLabelAutomationsEnabled, github.prLabelAutomationsEnabled, github.pushAutomationsEnabled, github.prFeedbackAutomationsEnabled and workflow.jiraPollAutomationsEnabled are off), a source precondition holds (a pull-request failure needs an open pull request), a source that acts for a person finds one, the organization is within its monthly budget, and the automation’s template (its own, or the source’s built-in default) is active and one its source can start. The limits are then judged under an advisory lock on the decision’s owner (a repository, or a team’s endpoint) across that owner’s whole ledger: not a commit the platform itself produced (for a push source, a commit a CI-fix or pull-request-feedback run pushed onto a person’s own pull-request branch counts as that output), not a subject (a commit, an issue, one labelling of a pull request) that already started a run, not inside the cooldown for its scope (a branch, an issue, a pull request), no earlier run for that scope, started within the source’s lookback (36 hours for CI, 14 days for issue labels, pull-request labels, pushes and Jira tickets, where the two Jira sources count as one, 24 hours for pull-request feedback and inbound events), still open (the ledger row is confirmed against Temporal, and a Temporal that cannot answer counts as running), and the automation’s rolling 24-hour cap. Each decision is one AutomationFire row: STARTED, a SUPPRESSED_* outcome or FAILED_TO_START. The workflow start is tried three times; if it never lands, the row becomes FAILED_TO_START and the delivery answers 503 so it can be sent again (a Jira poll instead stops and leaves the issue unseen for its next poll), and a redelivery or a manager’s retry takes a FAILED_TO_START decision again. A manager can retry ordinary event decisions that started no run; every limit applies again and the earlier row stays, marked retried. Review-findings fixes instead take the review-specific retry path: only eligible transient decisions can be retried, with fresh attempt identities, findings reread from the review run and the same push guards. One builder makes a run’s options at save time and at fire time and checks them against the template’s input schema; a fire also decides every connection those options declare with the owning team’s reach and re-runs the source’s template check, so a template retyped after the save cannot let an event choose a connection. Saving an enabled automation, or enabling one, is a launch decision for the saver; managing needs ADMIN, or a LEAD or ADMIN member of the owning team, and reading needs repository membership, a shared team included, and, under an enforcing access gate, a current host permission.
features.title: Event automations start runs from GitHub events, signed inbound events and polled Jira filters

features.body: The gateway polls each enabled Jira filter automation’s JQL with the platform’s Jira credential, narrowed to the projects an admin allows, and starts a template (ticket-to-merge by default) for each issue, or each issue and status, the automation has not seen.
features.detail: Every gateway replica runs a self-rescheduling timer: the first tick 15 seconds after boot, the next one workflow.jiraPollIntervalSeconds after a tick ends (300 by default, one GLOBAL value read before each wait). A tick does nothing unless the configured tracker is Jira; it polls the automation polled longest ago first, re-reads each automation just before polling it, gives one poll four minutes and the whole tick ten. Replicas take turns through a five-minute lease, a compare-and-set on the automation’s AutomationPollState row. A poll is skipped, and its baseline forgotten, while the repository or its installation is inactive or workflow.jiraPollAutomationsEnabled (ADMIN, off by default, overridable per team or organization) is off for the repository’s team, recording REPOSITORY_INACTIVE or SWITCHED_OFF; filters that fail validation at poll time, or JQL with unbalanced parentheses, stop the poll with INVALID_FILTERS, and with no project in workflow.jiraPollProjectKeys it stops with NO_ALLOWED_PROJECTS. The JQL (at most 2,000 characters, parentheses balanced outside quotes, a trailing ORDER BY dropped) is sent as project in (allowed) AND (jql), and results outside an allowed project are dropped again. A search Jira rejects as a bad request (HTTP 400) stops the poll with JQL_REJECTED, any other failed search with TRACKER_UNAVAILABLE, and more than 1,000 matches with FILTER_TOO_BROAD. The first poll, and the first after the narrowed query changes or polling resumes, records what already matches and starts nothing. After that up to 50 unseen issues per poll are decided in key order: each is read again, its title and description are placed in the run description inside a block marked as data, and the occurrence goes to the automation engine with its usual kill switch, limits and ledger. An issue Jira refuses to show (404), one that now answers under another key, and one whose facts fail validation (an issue key of an unexpected shape, an empty project key or one over 50 characters, or in status mode a blank status or one over 100 characters) are marked seen without a decision, the last logged by key only; any other failed read (a 403 included) or a start that fails ends the poll with TRACKER_UNAVAILABLE or START_FAILED and leaves the issue unseen for the next poll. lastError only ever holds one of eight fixed codes (NO_ALLOWED_PROJECTS, SWITCHED_OFF, REPOSITORY_INACTIVE, INVALID_FILTERS, JQL_REJECTED, FILTER_TOO_BROAD, TRACKER_UNAVAILABLE, START_FAILED), never text from Jira, and a poll that ends without an error clears it. jira.filter.status_changed remembers (issue, status) pairs instead of keys, so each status a ticket reaches is one occurrence; its run works on a branch of its own (the ticket branch plus a digest of the status, kept by a re-run), the two Jira sources count as one ticket for the in-flight check, and a ticket in In Progress, In Review or Done that has any non-synthetic run is recorded as SUPPRESSED_OWN_OUTPUT, because the platform’s own tracker sync writes those statuses. Saving or switching on an enabled Jira automation needs an allowed project and a configured Jira and, while polling is on for the team, asks Jira once whether it accepts the narrowed JQL (creating an event automation, POST /automations/events, and updating one, PATCH /automations/events/:id, are each limited to 20 requests a minute, whatever their source); a retry from the ledger re-checks the allowlist. Ledger reads never return the ticket description, and return the title only to those who manage the automation. The run carries no launchedById and uses the platform credential.
features.title: Jira filter automations poll a JQL and start a run per new ticket or status change

features.body: Every commit the platform makes carries the git.authorName and git.authorEmail identity, and git.launcherAttribution can credit the person who launched the run as co-author or author.
features.detail: The identity resolves through the setting cascade (workflow template, team, organization, global; auto-swe and auto-swe@localhost by default) once per workspace, before any container exists, and once per shell step, and is written as the user, author and committer git config, each value shell-quoted. Changing the name or email needs ADMIN; launcher attribution (none by default, co-author-trailer or author) needs LEAD. The launcher is WorkflowRun.launchedById on the row with the activity’s workflow id, read only when that row records a temporalRunId equal to the activity’s own run id; a row with none or another execution’s gives no launch context at all, so neither a launcher nor template-scoped identity settings apply, and a webhook, schedule or automation run has no launchedById, so it credits no one. A launcher is credited only with a verified email, used exactly as stored, and only as a member of the team the run resolves for; otherwise the configured identity stands. In author mode the launcher is the author and the configured identity stays the committer; in trailer mode each commit message the platform writes (implementation and fix, shell-step, decomposition and agent-run commits) ends with a Co-authored-by line. A database failure throws and the activity retries rather than commit under a fallback identity.
features.title: Commits carry a configurable identity and can credit the launcher

features.body: A failed GitHub Actions run is diagnosed from its logs; in fix mode a code-fixable failure gets a draft pull request into the branch that failed.
features.detail: ci-triage-and-fix is library content: an ordinary spec the interpreter runs, started by a CI-failure automation or by hand with a run id. Its first step, triageCiFailure, takes the run by id, never a URL, and reads the run, its failed jobs and their logs from the run’s own repository. It ends SKIPPED, posting nothing, when the run belongs to another repository, did not fail, was triggered by something other than a push, pull request or schedule, comes from a fork commit, is for a branch other than the payload’s, is a tag or a deleted branch, or is a pull-request failure whose pull request is no longer open from that branch. Log text is redacted for common token shapes, screened with the INJECTION patterns (every character of the tail given to the triager, about 40,000 characters shared across the failed jobs), and given to the ciTriager agent (no tools, model inherited from the planner), which returns a typed verdict. Code, not the model, decides fix or report, so the model can veto a fix but cannot start one the rules refuse. Code reports instead of fixing when the mode is not fix (the default mode is triage, diagnose only), no log could be read, the logs look like injection or the screen did not complete, a pull request’s head has moved since the failure, the category is not regression, test_bug, configuration or dependency (flaky, infrastructure and unknown are never fixed, and a trigger can only narrow that set), or confidence is below the trigger’s floor (0.6 by default, between 0.3 and 1). On the fix path the implementer receives the diagnosis fenced as untrusted data, and a change touching .github/workflows or .github/actions, or adding a symlink or a submodule, is refused before anything is pushed. Lint, typecheck and tests follow, then verifyCiFix labels the fix, then a draft pull request opens into the failing branch. Its CI is waited on by signal or poll and the fix is revised while that CI fails, up to maxCiFixAttempts times (2 by default, at most 5), with the draft’s own CI logs redacted, screened whole and fenced; a first attempt that changes no file ends the run as a report, and a revision that changed nothing counts as a spent attempt instead of waiting out CI. For a failure on a pull request the platform posts or updates one marked comment (unless the trigger turns commentOnPullRequest off), rendered from structured fields with model text neutralized (no markdown structure, links or mentions). Nothing is merged, and the template has no approval node.
features.title: CI failure triage and draft fix

features.body: For a failing pull request, a trigger may ask that the fix land as a commit on the author’s branch instead of a draft; a setting that is off by default and several refusals stand between the request and the push.
features.detail: pullRequestDelivery: push is a request, not a grant. An automation cannot save it unless the built-in template is its template and github.ciFixPushToPullRequestEnabled is on for its team (default off). pushCiFixToPullRequest then pushes only if all of these hold at the moment of the push: this execution is the one a CI-failure automation started (its ledger row names this request and workflow id, so a re-run or a hand-started run never qualifies, and a run with a launching user is refused); the run’s template is the built-in one and the automation, not the payload, asks for push; the setting is on; the failure is a pull-request run whose pull request is still open from this repository with the failing branch as its head; the branch is not the default, not protected and not matched by github.ciFixNeverPushBranches (main, master, develop, trunk, release/**, releases/** and hotfix/** by default); the commit is on the run’s own work branch and is a fast-forward of the branch tip; and it touches no workflow file. Anything else returns pushed: false with a reason and the template opens the draft instead. The ref moves with force: false. The commit is recorded on the ledger row before the push, so its later CI failure is suppressed as the platform’s own output (SUPPRESSED_OWN_OUTPUT) even if the activity dies right after pushing. The run then polls the pull request’s CI on the pushed commit; on failure it makes at most one follow-up (none when the trigger allows no revisions, whatever maxCiFixAttempts is above 1), then reports and leaves the pull request to a person. The work branch is deleted afterwards unless a follow-up could not be pushed.
features.title: A CI fix can be pushed onto a pull request’s own branch

features.body: The command the triager says reproduces the failure is run on the failing branch and on the fix; the result labels the fix and never blocks it.
features.detail: The command is model output read from untrusted logs. It runs only if it is the whole run: of a step the host reports as failed in a failed job, read from the workflow file in the workspace, contains no ${{ }} expression, is at most 1,000 characters (a longer one is dropped, never cut) and is cleared by the shell command scanner. The fix branch is fetched before the command runs, so no credential is used after the branch’s code has run. The command runs on the failing branch, the tree is reset and cleaned, and it runs again on the fix, each with an 8-minute limit; both outputs are stored as an artifact. The status is verified, not_reproduced, still_failing or unverified, shown as a Verified or Unverified line in the pull request and the run result. Nothing is installed first, so a command that needs the workflow’s setup steps fails both times; that is reported, not read as proof the fix is wrong. The step is a warning-on-failure node, and delivery proceeds whatever the status.
features.title: A CI fix is reproduced before and after, but only labelled

features.body: A launch may name payload.baseBranch; the checkout, the diff and the pull request target follow it.
features.detail: The gateway validates it on template launches, template webhook calls and retries (agent runs refuse a work branch with the same error, while an invalid name fails request validation): it must be a valid git branch name and must not be one of the platform’s own work branches, otherwise 400 INVALID_BASE_BRANCH. The work-branch rule is decided once, at launch, so changing the branch prefix mid-run cannot fail a run part-way. The worker re-checks the name in every activity that clones for a run (BASE_BRANCH_REFUSED, non-retryable), because the clone is single-branch and every activity must agree on which branch it holds. The payload is the one place a base is recorded, so a retry or re-run of a fix for release/1.4 is still a fix for it. CodeResult.baseBranch carries it into fix sessions and makes the pull-request step open into the branch the change was cut from. A CI-failure automation sets it to the failing branch.
features.title: A run can be based on a branch other than the default

features.body: One row-based coverage model decides whether every agent and the embedding model can reach a credential; the same model refuses a credential delete that would strand one and fails the credentials item of setup readiness on gaps in the agent set the worker’s boot gate resolves, plus a missing apiBase on a custom provider, which boot does not check (the embeddings item fails on any embedding gap).
features.detail: credentialGaps derives, from rows alone and without decrypting any key, which agents and the embedding model have no credential they can call. An agent’s model comes from its own spec or its inheritsModelFrom chain. A pinned credential counts when it exists, is for that provider and is reachable from the agent’s scope; otherwise the TEAM, ORGANIZATION, GLOBAL cascade picks the first reachable credential, as the worker does, and an unusable pin falls back to the cascade. A provider that is not built in also needs an apiBase on it. A channel or workflow-template agent runs for whichever team owns the run, so any credential for its provider counts. The embedding model follows the worker’s own rules, including that a pin to a credential of another provider is used as-is and is therefore a gap of its own. Deleting a credential answers 409 CREDENTIAL_IN_USE with the dependents unless force=true; a forced delete records what it left uncovered in the audit entry, and a team admin is refused, and shown dependents, only for its own team’s agents. GET /credentials adds usage.leavesWithoutCredential for the same question, and the dashboard’s delete confirmation lists it and then sends the forced delete; a delete that would strand an agent or remove the last platform credential for its provider also asks for the provider name to be typed first. The admin-only readiness route reports four items (credentials, embeddings, GitHub access, a real repository connection) and computes the agent set the worker’s boot check resolves from the same shared code: the steps of every installed template’s active and experiment versions, plus channelAssistant when a Slack channel exists. The credentials item fails only on a gap in that set or a required key with no platform-wide agent; every other gap, at any scope, is returned in gaps with a blocking flag. The same route lists each provider with the GLOBAL agents that call it and whether any of them lacks a usable credential. The embedding model is counted toward its provider only when the provider is what is missing: no credential at all, or a custom provider with no apiBase on an embedding that pins no credential. A spec the platform cannot embed with, no embedding config, or a credential pinned to another provider (or pinned and lacking an apiBase) is reported on the embeddings item and does not mark the provider as uncovered. The worker, for its part, refuses to start until assertConfigReady has resolved each of those GLOBAL agents for real (decrypting its key) and checked the embedding model’s rows only.
features.title: Credential coverage, delete guard and setup readiness

features.body: An agent’s pinned credential is used for its model call only if it exists, matches the model’s provider and is in the run’s scope; otherwise the provider cascade runs.
features.detail: The resolver uses the agent’s own pin or, if it has none, the pin on the row its model was inherited from; one unusable pin goes straight to the cascade. A pin is accepted only when the row exists, its provider (trimmed, lowercased) equals the provider the spec routes to, and its scope is GLOBAL, the run’s organization or the run’s team. A miss logs that the pin is not usable and falls back to the provider-name cascade (TEAM, ORGANIZATION, GLOBAL), so a stale pin cannot send one vendor’s key to another vendor’s API. The gateway checks reachability when an agent is created, edited or restored, and the client cache is keyed on a SHA-256 digest of the whole key and bounded with least-recently-used eviction.
features.title: A credential pin is honoured only where the run could reach it

features.body: Chat, embedding and Claude Code proxy calls resolve the provider host, connect only to a checked address and refuse redirects.
features.detail: modelCallFetch wraps the list guard: each connection is resolved, every answer checked and the socket pinned to a checked address, with redirects refused because a model call carries the prompt and the API key. Every built-in client (anthropic, openai, google) and every OpenAI-compatible client is constructed with it whether or not the credential sets an apiBase, as are the embedding clients and the Claude Code model proxy’s upstream fetch. A host that is, or resolves to, a private address is reachable only if it is listed in models.privateNetworkHosts; loopback, link-local, cloud-metadata, unspecified, multicast and reserved addresses stay refused whatever is listed. Saving a credential checks its apiBase as text only; the resolve-and-pin happens at the test, discovery, refresh and call. The list is read on every request behind the settings cache and an unreadable setting degrades to empty, so an unlisted in-cluster model server fails before any request is sent. This closes the gap between the text check at credential save and the call: a name that later resolves, or redirects, to an internal host no longer receives the prompt and the key.
features.title: Worker-built model, embedding and proxy calls go through the outbound guard

features.body: Agents may sit on different providers at once; adapters make structured output, proxied OpenAI and embeddings behave across them.
features.detail: OpenAI-compatible providers (OpenRouter, Ollama, vLLM and others) are wrapped by schemaInPromptMiddleware: the adapter sends plain json_object mode and drops the response schema, so for a structured call the middleware appends the JSON schema and a return-only-the-JSON instruction to the system prompt, while built-in providers, which enforce schemas natively, are untouched. An openai credential with an apiBase uses Chat Completions (most proxies serve nothing else); without one it uses the Responses API. Agent saves and the embedding config require <provider>/<model-id> and store the provider lowercased, so pricing, the catalog and the harness check read one canonical form. Embeddings accept openai, google and OpenAI-compatible endpoints, requested 1536 wide (except at an OpenAI-compatible endpoint that refused the parameter); on a 400 from an OpenAI-compatible endpoint the call is retried once without the dimensions parameter and the endpoint remembered as refusing it, so only a model natively 1536 wide still works there (an openai or google 400 is not retried). Anthropic is refused as an embedding provider. An agent’s reasoning level is bound into the model so every call honours it, but it reaches only a model its installed adapter can make think (Claude 3.7 and later, Gemini 2.5 and 3, OpenAI without an apiBase); an OpenAI-compatible provider, or OpenAI behind an apiBase, is sent nothing, and off is sent only where the adapter knows the model accepts it, so a level never makes a call fail. A model that cannot be built (a non-built-in provider with no apiBase) throws a non-retryable MODEL_CONFIG_INVALID.
features.title: Providers side by side: structured output, OpenAI endpoints and embeddings

features.body: Agent repository workspaces start with the resolvers in WORKSPACE_DNS, public by default.
features.detail: The Docker backend adds one --dns flag per entry, each shell-quoted, to the docker run that creates a workspace. The list is read from the worker’s environment (comma-separated IPs): unset or empty gives 1.1.1.1 and 8.8.8.8, and an invalid list falls back to that default with one logged warning. At worker boot the environment check stops the worker on an entry that is not an IP, is zoned IPv6, is loopback or unspecified, or, while WORKSPACE_BLOCK_METADATA is on, is one of the metadata addresses the workspace blackholes. It exists for split-horizon repository hosts whose public answer is unreachable from the cluster. Like the other workspace infrastructure settings it is environment-only: not a registry setting and not an admin form. Only repository workspaces made by createWorkspace on the Docker backend are described here; Kubernetes workspace pods use cluster DNS and do not apply the list.
features.title: Workspace containers get a configurable list of DNS resolvers

features.body: Dashboard pages keep explanation out of the way: inline help tips, and a Help panel (the “?” in the top bar) holding a page’s longer help, its doc links and a lifecycle overview; plus a first-run checklist, an optional tour, node help and a run verdict, with a built-in docs reader and and a command palette that finds pages and the work a person can see.
features.detail: A help tip is a small button that opens a popover on hover, focus or click, showing either a glossary definition or the text its caller wrote, plus a link to the matching doc. The glossary and the table of doc links are constants compiled into the web app: opening a tip reads that local table and a doc link only builds an in-app URL, so neither calls the gateway or reads platform data (the link is a Next.js Link, which may prefetch the static doc page from the web server). A doc link is an ordinary in-app route into a docs reader, which serves only the top level of the repository’s docs directory; its pages are generated statically, so they show the docs as they were when the web app was built. The reader’s index also searches the doc text: once typing pauses, the browser asks a route of the web server (behind the web proxy’s sign-in redirect, which checks only that a session cookie is present, as for the docs pages themselves; the query is cut to a bounded length) for the best matching sections, which return as highlight segments rather than HTML, so only those few results are downloaded. The server builds the index once per process from the same files, begins it at start-up without delaying start-up, logs once when it is ready (or logs the failure), and does not keep a failed build; if the request fails, title and summary matching still works and the next edit retries. Longer explanations, a page header’s doc link and the request-to-merge lifecycle overview are not drawn on the page: the page declares them and they appear in the Help panel opened from the “?” in the top bar, for as long as that page is mounted, and a page that declares none shows a link to the docs. Home, Start work and the run page carry the lifecycle overview there. The node palette and admin pages carry tips of the same kind, and some forms carry static help text and doc links. The OAuth consent screen opens its docs link in a new tab so the reader does not navigate away from the grant. Home also shows people who are not admins a first-run checklist whose steps tick from data the person can already read (a visible repository, a request of theirs, a gate they answered, a merged pull request from their request; it hides itself once all four are ticked, and shows nothing while any of those reads is loading or has failed), and shows admins a governance guide once the setup readiness check passes; each can be dismissed, the dismissal is kept in that browser’s local storage only, and a line at the foot of Home offers to show a hidden guide again. A Take the tour button on Home starts a short role-dependent tour that points at the sidebar and its links (one step points at nothing and is centred); the Help panel offers the same product tour, and on the run page and in the workflow editor also a Tour this page that points at elements the page itself marks. A tour never starts by itself; ending the product tour is recorded as seen in the same browser storage, ending a page tour is not, and a page tour ends quietly when its page unmounts. In the workflow editor, selecting a node shows its type’s help, with an Output line and a link to the type’s section of the node reference; the library’s starter gallery offers specs built from node types only. Each run page opens with a verdict banner derived from the run record and the run’s visible open gates (a guide to reading the page sits in its Help panel): it names a cause only for an error the dashboard classifies, otherwise says none is stated, and for an open gate it says whether the viewer can answer now and otherwise states in general terms who can (the owning team’s members with repository access, whoever launched the run, platform admins), because a gate records no approver or assignee. Start work offers a chooser between modes and a sample-task button that only fills fields and never launches; the workflow, agent-run, epic and PRD-run forms each show a review step listing the inputs before they launch, and a goal-driven plan is shown as a preview before it can be approved. The command palette opened from the top bar matches page names, Start work and the theme and palette choices in the browser and, once typing pauses at two characters or more, searches (at most five of each) requests, runs and workflow templates through the same list routes their own pages use, so it sees only what those pages would show: the run and template lists take an optional text filter (trimmed, at most 200 characters) that is ANDed with the visibility filter and so can only narrow a list. A failed search leaves its group empty rather than blocking the page results. Standing warnings on the platform settings, workflow defaults and autonomy policy pages, and the models page’s mid-run notice, are fixed text shown at page load as notes rather than live announcements; they do not read the settings they describe.
features.title: In-app guided help

features.body: A command an author wrote, in a container node or a gate or eval step, needs the shell authoring role and leaves an audit row naming who wrote it, on every path that can make it run.
features.detail: Two shared predicates decide what counts: container code (shell, containerStep, or a step naming the shell-category step) and authored commands (a gate step’s command, a runQualityGates gate’s, an eval gate scorer’s, or any inputs binding of one). Every template save route and the read-only check require the shell authoring role for both — a platform ADMIN, or an ADMIN of the template’s team; on a global template only a platform ADMIN — and write one WorkflowShellAudit row per container node and per command (an authored command records the agent workspace as its image); only container code takes the image allowlist. Review, promote, activation and making a version an experiment arm re-check the version against its rows by node, image and command, require the role for whatever is uncovered, and record it with the caller as author in the same transaction, so a version audited at save stays promotable by any lead who can write the template. A bundle install records rows for every version it writes, and the built-in sync records the built-in versions it writes, and the latest built-in version while it still matches the shipped spec, with no author. Rows of active and draft templates are kept as long as the template, since any of their versions can be promoted again. The shell-audit prune route deletes rows older than a requested number of days only when their template is ARCHIVED (a dry run counts them first, and a real delete writes an audit-log entry), and the Audit page offers a platform administrator a preview followed by a confirmed delete. The worker’s generation and channel drafting paths refuse both kinds outright.
features.title: Authored code is gated when it is saved and when it starts serving

features.body: Every connection a launch’s payload declares takes the launch decision; the run pins that set, and the generic connector steps and workspace resolution refuse a connection outside it.
features.detail: A launch decides the run’s own connection and every connection-typed field its template declares that the payload fills, with the same rule (reach, the declared connection type, an active GitHub installation); the git-repository retry and an automation fire decide them too. createWorkflowRun pins the set (the run’s connection plus those fields) on WorkflowRun.authorizedConnectionIds, computed from the input schema the run’s template version snapshotted, so editing the template’s inputs cannot widen a run under way, and an experiment arm or rollback is judged by its own version’s schema. readSource, writeOutcome, runTool and workspace resolution refuse a connection outside the pin before decrypting its credential (CONNECTION_NOT_AUTHORIZED), whichever node resolved it. A template schema may not type ticketId or description as a connection, since the platform fills those from text. An mcp node’s literal connection is in no pin; it is checked against the run template’s team when the node runs. A channel-assistant run row is created elsewhere and carries no pin, and an Agent’s own bound MCP connection is not in the pin either: it is checked against the run’s team instead (see the pin-gaps card).
features.title: Payload-declared connections are pinned and checked where the generic steps use them

features.body: Store reviewed, versioned summaries owned by a team and an organization, publish them deliberately, and let explicitly granted agents and steps search them or submit evidence-backed learnings.
features.detail: A KnowledgeItem is a learning, reference, decision or policy with an owner and origin team, an organization, an optional repository, a status (unreviewed, approved, rejected, superseded), a visibility (repository, team, selected teams, organization) and a version; every lifecycle action is version-checked and evented. A team lead or admin approves for its repository, team or selected teams (recipients must be active teams of the same organization), an organization admin for the organization, and a platform ADMIN for any. A reader sees, locally, approved items and unreviewed learnings, and shared items only once approved. A workflow’s authority is the stored Temporal execution and its WorkflowRun, never the payload, and its source repository is re-checked against the launcher’s recorded access when the repository-access gate enforces. Governed search and submitLearning require explicit toolKeys grants; pinned repository KBs can independently enable the same searchKnowledge tool without granting governed search. commitToMemory writes legacy MemoryItems, not an automatic governed-learning mirror. Governed search is bounded, semantic over current embeddings with a text fallback, labelled untrusted, and drops items an INJECTION pattern matches. A learning must name the current node, passes the memory injection gate before it is stored, and may cite as evidence only passed quality-gate records of the same execution with their artifacts. It sits beside MemoryItem and does not change lesson recall.
features.title: Governed knowledge items

features.body: Team-owned machine identities start and follow runs with scoped tokens of their own instead of a person’s token.
features.detail: A ServicePrincipal belongs to a team and carries allowlists of connections and templates (empty allows nothing) and two limits: runs per day and runs in flight. Its tokens live in api_tokens with scopes, need an expiry, and set a principal, never a user. A route accepts one only if it declares service scopes (runs:agent, runs:launch, runs:read, runs:cancel), answering 401 SERVICE_TOKEN_NOT_ALLOWED otherwise and 403 INSUFFICIENT_SCOPE for a missing scope, and a route opting in behind a role a principal cannot hold fails at registration. A launch goes through the same handlers as a person’s; inside the ledger transaction, under the principal’s row lock, it re-checks that the principal is enabled, its team active, the target still allowlisted and still reached by its team, and both limits. The run uses the platform credential and records requestedByServiceId; a repository-free run is billed to the principal’s team’s organization. ADMINs or the team’s leads manage principals and tokens, audited without the token.
features.title: Service principals for machine callers

features.body: A launch may ask to be told how its run ended, or that it waits for a person, by a signed POST to an endpoint its team registered.
features.detail: A team registers callback endpoints (an origin, a path prefix and the events it wants), managed by its leads or an ADMIN; only an ADMIN may turn on an endpoint’s private-network opt-in, and while it is on only an ADMIN may move it. An agent run, a template run or a template webhook call (the last only for endpoints that accept webhook launches) may name an endpoint or a URL under one; the URL is stored encrypted and a re-run does not inherit it. The run.completed row is written in the transaction of the run’s winning terminal write, and run.waiting_for_human with the human step, so each event is recorded once. A sweep claims due rows with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and sends each through the guarded fetch with redirects refused, a ten-second timeout and an X-AutoSwe-Signature (two during a secret rotation); only the status and a fixed error class are kept. Retries back off from a minute to six hours for 24 hours, after which the row is DEAD; a row whose endpoint was deleted, disabled or changed goes DEAD when the sweep next tries to send it; a DEAD row can be redelivered. The payload carries the run’s outcome, who launched it and the caller’s context, never transcripts.
features.title: Signed run callbacks to team-registered endpoints

features.body: A team’s event endpoint accepts signed events from another service and hands them to the team’s inbound.event automations, under the same decision ledger and guards as GitHub events.
features.detail: An endpoint verifies with the platform’s own scheme, an HMAC-SHA256 header in a configurable shape, or a shared secret compared in constant time; its secret is sealed, and a rotated one keeps working for 24 hours. The receiver reads the body as bytes: a request carrying the platform’s own delivery header (a callback pointed back) is dropped with 202, an unknown endpoint answers 404, then the signature is checked before the body is parsed or any other check runs, and only after it a disabled endpoint, an inactive team or the workflow.inboundEventsEnabled switch (off by default) refuses with 409. Event fields are located with JSON pointers, structured CloudEvents are read natively and binary-mode CloudEvents are refused. An automation filters by event type and simple match rules and maps pointer values into template inputs, never into the run’s own keys (connectionId, description, ticketId, baseBranch), a connection-typed or an array input; only the mapped values are recorded, capped. Each event starts at most one template run, deduplicated by endpoint and event id; a target repository the team reaches can be named, and its team’s switch and organization budget are checked too. The endpoint form offers presets for known senders (a signed JSON body, CloudEvents, an HMAC GitHub-style header, Snyk project snapshots and PagerDuty v3 webhooks) that fill in the signature and pointer settings, and an endpoint can list event types that cancel the runs it started, as described in the run-cancel card.
features.title: Signed inbound events start team automations

features.body: A template webhook call can carry an X-AutoSwe-Signature over its exact bytes; a template, or policy, can require it.
features.detail: The signature is HMAC-SHA256 over the timestamp and the raw body, within a five-minute tolerance, with several v1 entries allowed during a rotation and a constant-time comparison; the SDK exports the signer and verifier. Signing is required when the template’s own switch is on or workflow.templateWebhookRequireSignature resolves true for its team (off by default); then an unsigned or bad call is refused with 401 SIGNATURE_INVALID, or 409 WEBHOOK_SIGNING_NOT_CONFIGURED when the template has no secret. When it is not required a present signature is still checked. Once the template is found by its token, the signature is checked before any other check on the call, over bytes kept before parsing, and a refusal is recorded in the decision ledger at most once an hour per reason. A signed call’s run identity is its signed timestamp and body hash in its own namespace, so a replay inside the window, whatever Idempotency-Key it carries, finds the same run. Secrets are rotated or removed by whoever may edit the template, audited without the secret, and each write is conditional so racing writes cannot leave signing required with no secret.
features.title: Template webhooks can require signed calls

features.body: A dashboard panel answers questions about the platform, its configuration and the page in view, acting as the signed-in user and citing the docs.
features.detail: Off unless assistant.enabled is set. Each conversation is one Temporal workflow that runs its turns in order, completes after 30 minutes idle and continues as new periodically; a turn runs the appAssistant agent for at most assistant.maxStepsPerTurn steps and streams into its reply row. A conversation is titled by its first message until the person renames it (from the panel header or the history list) or, while assistant.generateTitles is on (the default), the tool-less assistantTitler agent names it alongside a turn from the person’s first message and their latest three, trying on each of the first three messages and then on the 5th, 10th, 20th and so on while it is still untitled; a rename made meanwhile wins, a title the model wrote is not revisited, and a failed or declined naming leaves the title and never fails the reply. Auto hands a title back: it returns to the first message and, with the assistant and model titles on, starts a one-off title workflow to name it at once (if that cannot start, the next turn names it). Its tools are searchDocs over the docs the worker image ships (a long section is clipped, keeping the table rows that match the query when the section is mostly a table), workflowInventory over the same code-derived catalog as the generated inventory page, getPageContext, describeApi and a GET-only callApi that reaches the gateway with a short-lived token bound to the user and the conversation. Every gateway route carries an assistant decision — read, confirm or never — with no entry, every DELETE and deprecated aliases refused; a confirm route runs only with an action the user confirmed for that exact method, URL and body, spent by one conditional update. No assistant tool proposes such an action yet, so it only reads. A failed reply records a redacted cause, and its trace rows are tagged with the reply, which an ADMIN-only failures view reads (its filter and most-common-causes summary cover only the page of failures loaded); the assistant itself is refused that view.
features.title: In-app assistant panel

features.body: pi is a third runtime for the implementer family and agents: Pi’s loop runs in the worker while its tools act on the workspace container.
features.detail: Pi drives any model the worker can bind (a built-in provider, or a compatible one whose credential has an apiBase; anything else fails with HARNESS_UNSUPPORTED_MODEL), through the worker’s own model binding, so its calls take the model-call guard, honour the agent’s reasoning level, and are debited per call as they end; the credential never enters the container. Its tools are granted from the agent’s toolKeys like the Mastra implementer’s, its MCP connection is relayed from the worker, and every call passes the same scanners. The conversation persists across turns and is fitted before each model call to workspace.harnessContextTokens (estimated at three characters per token with the prompt and tool definitions): old tool output and old file content in write and edit calls become stubs, then the oldest whole exchanges are dropped, then the newest exchange is stubbed oldest first, never its latest result; a write that copies a stub into a file is refused, and a turn that compacted records a pi.context_compacted event. A script runs one real Pi turn in a hardened throwaway container for manual checks.
features.title: Pi runs its agent loop in the worker

features.body: The shipped compose file gives the worker a DOCKER_HOST on a repository-owned policy broker, ahead of HAProxy and the Docker socket.
features.detail: The Node/TypeScript broker validates methods, canonical/versioned paths, query schemas, bounded duplicate-free JSON, container profiles and object ownership. Its private label and persistent state retain owned containers, volumes, exec IDs and root phase state across restart; it serves nothing until reconstruction succeeds. Ordinary image repositories are operator-allowlisted and privileged helpers use exact references. Host binds, privileged mode, devices, host namespaces and unconfined security options are refused, except a target hosts-file bind derived by the broker itself. Root exec admission is a phase-state heuristic, not proof of execution provenance. The worker cannot reach HAProxy's separate internal network. HAProxy alone mounts the socket and retains its path filter as defense in depth. Neither API port is published. The worker requires a signed privileged-create denial probe unless an operator explicitly disables it for direct-socket development.
features.title: The worker reaches Docker through a policy broker and socket proxy

features.body: A worker can run agent repository workspaces as Kubernetes pods instead of Docker containers, chosen by its environment.
features.detail: WORKSPACE_BACKEND=kubernetes selects the backend per worker process (any other value is Docker, and the boot check refuses a value that is neither); its namespace, kubectl binary, runtime class, user id, storage limit, maximum lifetime and image pull secrets are environment-only too. Before polling, the worker checks it may create, read, list, watch, delete and exec into pods and create and delete secrets, and, unless an operator turns the check off, starts a probe pod and refuses to start if that pod reaches the cloud metadata address or, when the worker itself runs in the cluster, the cluster API address (a worker outside the cluster probes metadata only and logs that), because without an enforcing NetworkPolicy the namespace’s policy is inert. A workspace pod passes the restricted PodSecurity profile: non-root with an explicit user, every capability dropped, no privilege escalation, the runtime-default seccomp profile, no service-account token, no service links and no host namespaces; requests equal limits for CPU, memory and ephemeral storage, the working tree is an emptyDir of the storage limit, the GCP metadata names resolve to 0.0.0.0 and the kubelet ends the pod at its hard lifetime even if the worker dies, and a scheduled sweep then deletes the dead pod object. Commands run through kubectl exec; secrets go on the exec’s stdin, never in its arguments, and a secret that is empty or contains a line break is refused. A secret the pod needs for its whole life (the registry proxy’s token) is kept in a per-pod Secret owned by the pod, which the Pod object only names, and a plain environment pair that looks like a credential is refused before it reaches an exec command or the Pod. An archive copied into a pod is read by the worker first and refused if an entry could write outside its destination (absolute or climbing paths, hard links, devices, writes through a symlink the archive made, escaping symlinks). On this backend the worker also refuses to start without the model proxy, and refuses a model, registry or egress proxy URL that pods cannot resolve (unset, the Docker host alias, the worker pod’s own name, localhost or another loopback or unspecified address); the registry and egress proxies themselves stay optional. Requiring the model proxy is what keeps the provider key from the harness. The worker also refuses to start without an enforcing workspace admission policy, and without the configured RuntimeClass when that is required (see the Kubernetes admission card).
features.title: Kubernetes pods as agent workspaces

features.body: Git credentials, the registry proxy token, container-step inputs and a credential-bearing model base URL reach workspace commands as named secrets that stay off every docker and kubectl command line, and both backends refuse a plain environment pair that looks like a credential.
features.detail: Every authenticated git call (the workspace clone, dependency checkouts, fetches and pushes, and a shell step’s clone, base fetch and push) uses the credential-free URL and reads its http.extraheader value from ASW_GIT_AUTH, delivered as a secret; a call that expects the credential and finds the variable unset or empty aborts rather than going out unauthenticated, and the hardened flags also turn off automatic gc and maintenance, which could detach and keep the header in a background process. A secret is passed by name only: on Docker as -e NAME with the value in the docker client’s own environment, on Kubernetes as NAME=value lines on the exec’s stdin that a wrapper exports before the command runs. A secret the container needs for its whole life, the registry proxy’s token, is split off the registry environment: Docker passes it the same way to docker run, and Kubernetes keeps it in a per-pod Secret the Pod names through secretKeyRef, created already owned by the pod so it is garbage-collected with it, deleted by the worker on removal and on a failed create, and scrubbed, with its base64 form, from kubectl errors. A shell step’s registry files and token, a container step’s CONTAINER_STEP_INPUT, and a Claude Code base URL used without the model proxy that has a path, query, fragment or userinfo travel as secrets too; for that URL the pinned settings layer is written to a private file in the harness home instead of passed inline, and credential-named SDK variables are not forwarded to the harness. Wherever a backend renders a plain env list (docker exec, run, helper and sandbox arguments, kubectl exec arguments and the Pod spec) a guard refuses a pair whose name looks like a credential, whose value carries URL userinfo, or whose value has a well-known token shape, naming the variable but never the value.
features.title: Workspace credentials travel by name, never on a docker or kubectl command line

features.body: Private npm, Go, PyPI and Maven registries are fronted by a read-only worker proxy, so a workspace installs packages without holding the registry credential.
features.detail: When the worker’s environment configures the proxy (REGISTRY_PROXY_PORT), a workspace whose run has a team registers with it and gets the proxy’s address and a random per-workspace token in place of the credentials of the registries resolved from the active rows that are the team’s own or global; with no proxy, no team or no row there is no wiring. Rows are managed by platform ADMINs only, their tokens are write-only, and a row is npm, Go, PyPI or Maven. A Maven registry is served in open mode only: Maven has no committed lockfile, so it has no lockfile scope. A Go registry is wired only into a workspace whose repository uses Go, and serves modules as GOPROXY paths, in lockfile mode only those the base ref’s go.sum lists. A PyPI registry likewise serves a rewritten simple index for pip and uv, in lockfile mode only the files whose name and version the base ref’s Python lockfiles pin; the registry credential is sent only under the registry’s own path. The npm proxy serves packuments, per-version manifests and tarballs over GET and HEAD; its only POSTs are audit queries, so a vulnerability-scan gate can run through it: the bulk advisory endpoint npm audit and yarn npm audit use, and the two legacy audit endpoints pnpm audit sends its dependency tree to. Every audit goes to the registration’s default registry (404 when it has none), whichever registry the URL names. A bulk body is accepted only as a map of package names to version lists; pnpm’s tree only with its fixed keys, empty install, remove and metadata, and names, versions and integrity hashes in their own charsets, and the proxy forwards the re-serialised validated tree, not the bytes it received. Both are size-bounded, gzip included. Every package an audit names must be one the default registry serves, so a private scope’s package names are not disclosed to a registry that does not own them; such a body is refused with 403 rather than trimmed. In lockfile mode a registry serves only the package@version pairs committed in the base ref’s lockfiles, and an audit naming any other pair is refused. Packument, manifest and audit requests buffer their bodies, so each workspace’s registration runs at most eight at once and queues up to 64 more, each waiting at most 30 seconds before a 503 with Retry-After (npm and Yarn retry it); a slot is taken only after the request’s cheap checks and is held across the upstream fetch and the body read, which have a 20-second deadline and stop when the client hangs up. Tarballs stream and are not counted. These bounds are built-in constants, not settings.
features.title: npm registries are reached through a per-workspace worker proxy

features.body: A connection marked as Qodo's binds only Qodo's read tools, and what its tools return is screened and fenced before an agent reads it.
features.detail: Qodo's catalog mixes read tools with tools that approve, comment, label and change rules, so a Qodo connection is an ordinary MCP connection with a marker (config.integration) that only an admin can set. The marker implies a read-only allowlist. A marked connection with no stored list gets Qodo's read list; a stored list is intersected with it, so a write tool in it binds nothing, and a stored list that is not valid binds nothing at all. Create and edit refuse a write tool on a marked connection with a 400 that names it. An edit rebuilds only the config keys the route owns and carries the rest over, so renaming a connection cannot drop the guard. The allowlist travels with the resolved connection target into the loader, so a caller cannot connect without it; the harness relay and the mcp node enforce it too, and the node refuses before connecting. Results of a marked connection, and of any connection that sets scanResults, are screened with the INJECTION patterns string by string, object keys included. A flagged string is replaced by a fixed placeholder, the rest of the result is returned, and every string kept is fenced as untrusted. A scan that throws withholds the whole result. The connection test lists tools and calls none, and also reports how many advertised tools match the read list. resolveQodoConnection returns the oldest active Qodo connection the repository's team owns; no template, agent or run input names a connection. The MCP connections page has an allowlist editor for a Qodo connection: it offers only Qodo’s read tools, shows names in a stored list that are outside that list as never binding, can only narrow the default, and never saves an empty list (an empty stored list would bind nothing), and its Test action shows which tools the server advertises.
features.title: Qodo as a read-only MCP connection

features.body: The platform reads Qodo's review of a pull request, never asks for one, and a workflow step and a built-in template route on it.
features.detail: Qodo's MCP catalog has no tool that starts a review, so the platform only reads the one Qodo's pull request bot produces. One client calls a single tool for a pull request's URL. It checks qodo.enabled before it touches the connection or the network, resolves the repository team's connection, and turns every failure into a fixed reason with no error text. The awaitQodoReview step polls that client, with a heartbeat, until Qodo has completed a review of the exact head commit it was given or its wait runs out. The wait comes from qodo.reviewWaitSeconds, and the step gets its own single-attempt activity group. It takes the repository from the run, so no step config or input can point it at another team's connection. Its result is typed and bounded and the step never throws: reviewed, pending, stale, unavailable and disabled are statuses. blocking is true only for a completed review of the given head with an open action_required finding. Nothing is blocked unless a template routes on it. The qodoReview authoring helper builds the node and its gate, with an optional fail-closed form. ticket-to-merge-qodo is ticket-to-merge with that step between green CI and the merge wait, so the review it reads is of the final head. A blocking review asks a person to continue or stop; stop ends the run FAILED, no answer within a day ends it TIMED_OUT, and every other result goes on to the merge wait. No lesson is stored for the Qodo ends.
features.title: Waiting for Qodo's review in a workflow

features.body: A Qodo bot's review on a pull request the platform opened can start a feedback round, and the worker pulls Qodo's findings instead of reading the bot's comment.
features.detail: The qodo_findings trigger of the pull-request feedback source is opt-in per automation. A review, review comment or discussion comment from a sender of type Bot whose numeric account id is in qodo.prFeedbackBotAccountIds, on an open pull request from the same repository that the platform opened, is only a nudge. The id is matched, never the login, and the bot's text is never copied or read as a command. Every delivery for one head commit shares one decision subject, so a review that posts many comments starts one round, and a fix push moves the head. A nudge that arrives while the run that opened the pull request is still working on it waits, up to qodo.prFeedbackRunWaitSeconds, for that run to park, and skips silently if the pull request closes or stops being eligible meanwhile. If a CI fix moved the head, the round follows the head the run left, because Qodo's comments on that head arrived while this round was in flight and were suppressed, so no later nudge would come for it. The worker then asks Qodo for the findings and goes on only when Qodo's completed review is of the pull request's current head, read again just before the brief is built. Only findings that are still pending, at or above qodo.prFeedbackMinActionLevel, are briefed. They pass one injection-screen batch and are fenced like human review text. Every other outcome is a silent skip with a fixed reason. A person's /auto-swe fix command can also include Qodo's findings, but only when qodo.enabled and qodo.prFeedbackIncludeOnCommand are both on and the pull request is the platform's own. It reads Qodo once and never waits, and any outcome that adds nothing leaves the round on the human threads with one recorded reason.
features.title: Qodo's findings fix a pull request, pulled and not scraped

features.body: A repository's preview recipe starts its app inside the run's executor container; a headless Chromium visits each smoke path and the optional e2e command, and a navigation failure, console error, 5xx or e2e exit fails the gate. Every visit keeps a screenshot; each check keeps a recording (unless turned off), a Playwright trace and the app log as run evidence, served through short-lived user-bound links and summarised in the pull request.
features.detail: The recipe is the connection’s previewConfig as a whole, else the trusted .auto-swe/preview.yml on the base commit, else none. A previewConfig on a git_repo connection holds: setup and start commands, readyUrl/baseUrl, readyTimeoutMs, environment values, allowed browser hosts, smoke paths with an optional waitFor, an e2e command with its results directory, and up to four service sidecars. uiVerify starts the preview in the run's executor image, drives the in-container Chromium through a unix-socket driver, blocks every host but localhost and the recipe's allowedHosts, and treats a driver error as a page failure rather than an empty result. Evidence is an artifact (ui.screenshot, ui.video, ui.trace, ui.log) plus a RunEvidence row carrying kind, source (uiVerify or agent), spec node, attempt, caption, page URL and dimensions; the gateway lists ready items and mints a signed link whose content route re-checks the viewer's live account and run visibility. The agent browser toolset (browser_start_app, browser_navigate, browser_click, browser_fill, browser_press, browser_select, browser_wait, browser_snapshot, browser_screenshot, browser_console) is bound only when an Agent names 'browser', and its screenshots are evidence under source 'agent'. Workspace agent nodes can bind the browser tools on Mastra, Claude Code or Pi when their Agent grants browser; non-workspace nodes have no such checkout toolset. The preview starts detached; stop() signals its process group and scans /proc for descendants retaining the preview's random environment marker. Signals and process inspection are best-effort, not proof that every descendant exited; the daily sweep applies the evidence retention, removes the public copies a pull request published, and reaps ready ui.* artifacts whose RunEvidence row was never written. browser_screenshot also returns a viewport-only JPEG to the agent’s model, on Mastra, Claude Code (as an MCP image item) and Pi, when uiValidation.agentScreenshotImages is on (the default; turn it off for a model without image input); the image is dropped, with an imageOmitted note, when it is over uiValidation.maxScreenshotBytes or unreadable, and when the output screening blocks the page text, and the image bytes are stripped before tool-call traces are stored. The evidence PNG is kept either way.
features.title: Verify the app in a real browser

features.body: Off until an ADMIN enables it, the platform classifies each pull request it opened as LOW, STANDARD or HIGH risk by fixed rules and publishes a commit status and a reviewer brief; in auto mode, behind further ADMIN switches, it asks GitHub to auto-merge a LOW change and a separate App can approve it.
features.detail: prEvaluation.enabled is an ADMIN, GLOBAL-only setting that defaults to false; a repository then chooses off, advisory, enforce or auto, falling back to prEvaluation.defaultMode, which cannot be auto. Only a pull request whose PullRequest row links a workflow run is evaluated: a branch name is not evidence, because anyone can name a branch auto/. A GitHub delivery starts one evaluation, in a workflow named for the repository, pull request and delivery so a redelivery does not evaluate twice, when a pull request is opened, reopened, pushed to, marked ready, converted to draft or has its base branch edited, or when a review is submitted, edited or dismissed. With evaluation off for the repository or by prEvaluation.enabled, or the repository deactivated, a delivery still starts one for a pull request that holds a standing auto-merge or approver App approval, so the worker can withdraw it; a failure in this handler is logged and does not reach the delivery’s other handlers.
