The class comes from fixed rules over the changed files, the repository policy and two earlier signals, the scanner findings and the review severity (model output); no model chooses it. Any exclusion makes the change HIGH and never auto-eligible; among them are an evaluation error, an invalid or changed repository policy file, a sensitive path, a too-long path, invalid line counts, a removed test, a skip or only marker added to a test, a test patch too large to scan, a changed file or test file with no patch to inspect, a scanner finding, and a missing review result or one at WARNING or CRITICAL. Without an exclusion, a high-risk path or more changed lines than highLines is HIGH, a change over the LOW size limits, one with no changed content to evaluate, or one that changes source with no test is STANDARD, and only what remains is LOW. Each class carries an approver count, and a policy file read from the base branch can add paths, lower size limits and raise counts but never loosen a rule. The commit status (prEvaluation.requiredStatusContext) is always success in advisory mode; in enforce and auto it is pending until enough distinct people have approved the exact head, and failure when the evaluation itself errored. Only each person’s latest review counts, never the author, a bot or anyone who launched or requested the work, and only people whose write access on the repository could be read (the first twenty distinct approvers are looked up, and one whose standing cannot be read is not counted). The row also counts when a person first reviewed the head, changes requested, and where inline comments landed against the brief (flagged, skimmed or elsewhere), keeping no names or text. An evaluation re-reads the pull request just before it publishes and stands down when the head or base branch moved, since the newer head has its own evaluation, and after a merge a recount rewrites the stored approver count at the merged head with the same trust filter, writing 0 on any failure. Auto mode arms auto-merge only behind prEvaluation.autoMergeAllowed (off by default), an evidence gate over the last 90 days of merged LOW evaluations that recorded a requester, a minimum amount of change and a trusted approval (deployment-wide volume, no bad merge and several distinct requesters, plus the repository’s own volume and no bad merge), and only when GitHub itself will hold the merge until the platform’s status is green: the repository allows auto-merge, the status is a required check pinned to the platform’s own GitHub App, and either the branch requires an approving review or the approvals the change needs are given. It also needs the status accepted by the host, a pull request that is not a draft, and every launcher and requester matched to a linked GitHub account. The platform does not turn auto-merge back on after a person turned it off. The one merge-capable call is enableAutoMerge, which asks GitHub to squash-merge later and only for the evaluated head; a source tripwire (yarn invariants:check) fails other merge calls it can recognise. A second, separate GitHub App (the approver App) can submit an approving review on a LOW change, which then merges with no human approval once auto-merge is armed. It does so only while every condition holds: prEvaluation.autoMergeAllowed and prEvaluation.botApprovalAllowed, the repository’s auto mode and its bot-approval flag are all on; the App is configured, differs from the platform’s App and is installed on the repository with access to selected repositories and pull-request permission alone; the change has no exclusion and passes the evidence and launcher checks; it is within the bot’s own caps (changed lines and files, paths on an allowlist, no net test deletion); no reviewer has a standing request for changes and no person dismissed an evaluator approval earlier; the base branch provably allows auto-merge, requires the platform-pinned status and dismisses stale approvals on a push; and the change needs exactly one approver, so a higher required count refuses it. The approval makes the status success for a LOW change only; the conditions are re-read just before and after it is submitted, and an approval that stops qualifying is dismissed with the platform credential. A repository’s mode is set through a route open to the owning team’s LEAD or an ADMIN; choosing auto, or turning bot approval on, is ADMIN-only and is refused with every unmet reason listed (auto also needs the switches, the evidence and an earlier evaluation that read the branch rules; bot approval also needs a configured approver App that differs from the platform’s), and the database keeps bot approval inside auto. A save of the approver App that completes its id, slug and key is stored only after GitHub confirms them as one App, and the slugs of replaced Apps are kept so their earlier approvals stay recognisable. Moving a repository out of auto, withdrawing its bot approval, deactivating it, switching off a deployment-wide switch (prEvaluation.enabled, autoMergeAllowed or botApprovalAllowed), changing the bot-approval paths or size caps, or replacing or removing the approver App starts a re-evaluation of the open pull requests that hold an arming or an approval, so the worker withdraws what the policy no longer wants.
features.title: Platform pull requests are risk-classified and handed to reviewers with a brief

features.body: A GitHub App installation token minted for work on a repository is restricted to that repository, rather than every repository the App is installed on.
features.detail: resolveGitHubToken sends the installation-token request a repositories list when its target names one. installationTargetFor builds that target from the repository’s name for the worker’s SCM client, the repository permission check and the gateway’s connection probe, check-run lookup, pull-request file reads and pull-request-feedback reads; the name is a required field, so a caller that did not load it fails to compile. The token cache key holds the installation, the API host and the case-folded, sorted repository set, so a narrow token is never served for a wider request nor the reverse. When GitHub answers 422 that the stored name does not exist or is not accessible, the minting process mints a full-scope token for the lookup (a rename redirect is followed only within the same origin), checks that the resolved owner matches, and mints once more restricted to that repository’s id; the full-scope token is not returned to the caller, but it stays in the process token cache under the unscoped key until it expires. A repository the App cannot see (not selected for it, transferred to another owner, or stored with no owner to look it up under) raises a typed not-visible error. Work that spans an installation, such as listing its repositories, still asks for the full scope.
features.title: GitHub App installation tokens are minted for one repository

features.body: While capture is on, each outbound request an activity makes through the worker’s fetch is stored as one row tied to the run, step and attempt; where the egress proxy is configured, the workspace’s proxied traffic is also stored as metadata-only rows, whatever the capture setting says.
features.detail: The worker replaces the global fetch at boot and wraps the guarded fetch that connector, source-control, MCP and callback code uses; an activity interceptor opens a capture for each attempt when workflow.httpCaptureEnabled (ADMIN, GLOBAL-only, on by default) is true. Each call becomes a WorkflowHttpCall row: purpose (model, embedding, scm, connector, mcp, callback, egress or other), method, scheme, host, port, path, status, duration, request and response sizes, error, the run, node, step attempt and Temporal attempt, the OpenTelemetry trace and span ids, and the team and organization the spend belongs to. Headers are never stored, and a query parameter whose name looks like a credential is dropped from the path. Model and embedding calls keep no bodies here and name the attempt’s agent transcript instead. Other calls keep a request and response body only for text-like content types, redacted and cut at workflow.httpCaptureBodyMaxBytes (8192 by default, at most 65536; 0 turns body storage off); a JSON body that no longer parses once cut is dropped and the row flagged truncated, and reading a body is abandoned after two seconds. A call the outbound guard refuses is recorded as blocked with its reason, and so is a workspace request the egress proxy refuses for a host outside the team allowlist or an address it will not reach. Rows are buffered and written in batches of up to 100, mostly when the activity ends: a persistence failure is counted and logged and never fails the activity, and at the end the capture waits up to five seconds for pending bodies and then writes what is buffered, while the activity stops waiting after ten seconds, so the close can delay it by up to that long. The egress proxy writes its own rows as each exchange ends, whatever workflow.httpCaptureEnabled says. A scheduled sweep deletes rows older than workflow.httpCaptureRetentionDays (90 by default) in bounded batches; it runs with the agent transcript retention sweep.
features.title: Activity HTTP exchanges are recorded as a run action log

features.body: A run page lists one time-ordered activity feed across its steps, tool calls, model responses, activity events, HTTP calls and human steps, and exports it.
features.detail: The feed is read for any signed-in person, never a service principal, through the run visibility filter, and can be narrowed by kind, spec node, recording or a start time; it pages by cursor and, while the run is live, the page also tails new rows every three seconds and merges them by id. An HTTP call opens to its metadata for anyone who can see the run, but its captured request and response bodies only for a caller who can control the run; a service principal is refused there too. The export is an NDJSON file of the same items (HTTP metadata, no bodies) for the same filters that needs that control, writes a log line, and ends with an end-of-file line the dashboard checks before saving, so a file cut short is refused rather than saved.
features.title: The run page shows one activity feed and exports it

features.body: When the worker’s environment configures an egress proxy, repository workspaces and egress-enabled container steps send HTTP(S) through it with a per-workspace credential, so each proxied connection is recorded and the effective host allowlist (the platform baseline plus the team’s list) is applied.
features.detail: EGRESS_PROXY_PORT (with its URL and bind address) is environment-only; Compose and Helm set it to 8792. Without it a GLOBAL restricted policy, the default, refuses worker boot, and a restricted workspace or step that needs the proxy fails as unenforceable. Under restricted whenever the effective allowlist (the live platform baseline in workspace.egressBaselineAllowlist plus the team’s list) is non-empty, and under open whenever a proxy is configured, a repository workspace, and an egress-enabled container step or sidecar, receives HTTP_PROXY and HTTPS_PROXY (both cases) holding a random per-workspace token as secret environment, plus NO_PROXY for localhost, the registry and model proxies and, for a workspace, the repository’s own git host, which is therefore neither audited nor filtered. The proxy keeps only a digest of each token, answers 407 without a live registration, drops a registration and aborts its open exchanges when the workspace is torn down, accepts 32 concurrent exchanges per registration (429 beyond that) and closes an idle tunnel or upstream after 60 seconds. A request is checked against that effective list: exact host names or *.suffix wildcards that match subdomains but not the bare domain. Under the open policy an empty team list means no baseline and every host allowed, so a team with no list gets auditing and no filtering; under restricted only an empty effective list proxies nothing, and the workspace is locked down as for blocked. A refused host answers 403 and is recorded as blocked. The proxy then resolves the name itself, refuses any address the outbound guard refuses (private ranges included) and connects only to that checked address. The workspaces the repo-onboarder agent drafts in get a wider list than their team’s in a seeded repo-onboarding run. On every activity of that agent the worker checks that the agent key is repo-onboarder, that the agent definition that resolved has the seed’s content (a GLOBAL row with no team, organization, channel or template owner whose system prompt, tool list and skill refs (as sets), MCP binding, runtime, harness profile and model inheritance equal the seeded definition’s; its model and reasoning may differ, so a team or organization override or a global version with other content does not qualify), that the node’s loop is the default one (a runtime pinned at run start refuses, even after the override that set it is gone), that the credential its model is called with is not one a team could point at a server of its own (the credential row is GLOBAL, or it is a team or organization one with no custom API base, so a team’s own vendor key against the provider’s default endpoint still qualifies, while a team or organization credential with a custom API base, or one whose scope is not known, refuses; the credential is the agent’s pinned one or the team, organization or global one the provider cascade picks), and that the run belongs to the global starter-origin repo-onboarding template at a version no user wrote or generated, so a team’s own template, or an edited or generated version of the seeded one, does not qualify; an onboarding trial never takes this path. A refusal is logged with the first differing condition. A widened workspace runs only the definition it was widened for: if a different agent definition resolves later, or the model credential at that later resolution is not a trusted one (the same rule: global, or team or organization without a custom API base), the node fails without retry, and no MCP server is bound; a credential that changed but is still trusted does not stop the run. A team or organization credential without a custom API base supplies only the key: its owner does not choose the endpoint or the model, but does control the vendor account the call is billed to and governed by (retention, limits, organization policies). The draft workspace already runs repository code under the wider list by design. Under open, when no proxy is configured (logged), or when the combined set of added hosts is empty, nothing changes. Otherwise the workspace is held to restricted, with the hosts of the onboarding.draftEgressHosts setting (package registries and GitHub download hosts by default, overridable per team or organization), the upstream hosts of active package registries (global or the team’s) and the download hosts of non-revoked tool-catalog entries added to its allowlist; setup inherits that policy instead of running under a wider one, and a configured draft run is audit-logged. Where the run’s policy was restricted the live baseline and team list stay in force, and where it was blocked only those added hosts are reachable. The repository’s git host is exempt from the proxy as in any workspace. Each exchange lands in the same table as the worker’s own calls with source egress_proxy: for a plain HTTP request the method, host, path with credential parameters removed, status and byte counts; for a CONNECT tunnel only host, port, bytes, duration and outcome, because the proxy cannot read inside TLS. No body is stored.
features.title: Workspace HTTP(S) traffic can pass an audited egress proxy

features.body: A nightly sweep rebuilds each recent UTC day of run, approval and reviewer figures into rollup tables, and a weekly sweep emails or posts a digest of the last full week to subscribed organizations and teams.
features.detail: The rollup workflow (nightly by default; its window, schedule and backfill are environment-only WORKFLOW_RUN_ROLLUP_* values) rebuilds the most recent window of complete UTC days (30 by default) from runs, the pull requests and CI-fix steps linked to them, reviewer verdict traces and human steps into the daily run, human-step and review-verdict rollups. Each day is replaced in one transaction that deletes its rows, inserts the rebuilt ones and stamps the day built, so a reader never sees half a day and a day with no runs still counts as covered. A day older than the window is rebuilt in two cases: an optional backfill of a configured number of days (off by default, at most ten uncovered days per sweep) and a dirty day, one holding a run, pull request, CI-fix step, reviewer trace or human step updated since the previous successful sweep (with an hour of overlap). At most sixty dirty days are rebuilt per sweep and the rest wait in RollupSweepState. The watermark advances only after a sweep finishes, is kept if the clock moves backwards, and does not exist on the first sweep, which therefore finds no dirty days. The digest workflow (weekly by default) takes the previous ISO week, Monday to Sunday UTC, and for each enabled subscription of an organization or a team requires all fourteen days of that week and the one before to be stamped built; otherwise it records rollup_incomplete, sleeps fifteen minutes and tries again, up to three attempts and six when a rollup was incomplete. An organization subscription is skipped while organization-wide reporting is off for it, and a period that starts less than six days after the last sent one, or before the newest delivery, is skipped. The digest sets the week against the week before from the rollups, adds the approvals pending now, the worst quality gate (only one with ten or more run-gate pairs, and not when the gate read hit its 50,000-row cap) and, for an organization, the budget state and percent used, with month-to-date spend and its projection only when the creator and every email recipient still hold org.budget.manage on the organization (an organization ADMIN of it, or a platform ADMIN) and no Slack channel is a target, otherwise the digest carries the state and percent used alone; a team digest carries the state and percent of whichever cap, team or organization, has used more. Recipients are the subscription’s addresses minus opt-outs, re-checked at send time as active members of the scope, plus an optional Slack channel. A delivery row per subscription, week and target records attempts: a target is tried up to three times in total, an optimistic claim keeps overlapping sweeps from sending twice, and a period counts as sent only when every target has been. Email goes by SMTP, else Resend, with a signed unsubscribe link and a one-click List-Unsubscribe header; a test send skips the period checks, writes no delivery row and tries once.
features.title: Daily rollups and weekly digests are built by scheduled worker sweeps

features.body: The dashboard home reads GET /me/summary: the caller’s own teams, each with what is waiting on them, how much is running or queued, and the tighter of its budgets.
features.detail: The route needs only a signed-in person and builds the summary from active team memberships only, so a platform ADMIN’s desk is member-scoped too; with no membership it returns empty. Needs-you items are pending approvals the caller can answer (the same filter as the human-step list with mine=true, so a badge and its list count the same steps), failed attempts the caller launched or a team lead assigned to them (an assignment counts only while the assignee is still on the assigning team and that team owns the run), and pull requests awaiting a human merge on requests they made. Items are ordered with due-soon approvals first by deadline and capped at 25, while the total counts every item. Attempts are read over a 30 day window, a running attempt whatever its age, and channel assistant and task runs and runs with no work request are left out so running and queued counts match the request list. Each team card carries its own running, queued and needs-you counts and a budget state with a percentage that is the tighter of the team’s cap and its organization’s. Sources are queried once and bucketed by team in memory. Preference slugs (pinned and last team) are hints that are not checked against membership; the web resolves them through the member team list, so a stale or foreign slug resolves to nothing.
features.title: A personal desk across the teams you belong to

features.body: Each team has a space at /teams/<slug> whose overview adds sections by the viewer’s team role, and the team switcher navigates between spaces instead of filtering global lists.
features.detail: GET /teams/:id/overview answers 404 to a non-member exactly as to an unknown team (a platform ADMIN passes). The viewer level comes from the caller’s team role (MEMBER, LEAD, ADMIN); the platform role never raises it, except that a platform ADMIN outside the team is shown the admin level. An engineer gets counts, the needs-you total with a link to the actionable list, recent activity, the last 7 days, repositories, and 30 day pull-request outcomes; a lead adds open pull requests, overdue approvals and failures nobody owns; an admin adds month cost in dollars. Those sections are not queried for a lower role and their keys are absent. The dollar figure is attached to a team ADMIN when the binding cap is the team’s own; when it is the organization’s, only someone holding org.budget.manage (an organization ADMIN or platform ADMIN) gets it, and anyone else receives the admin section without it. The space has Overview, Work, Automations, Reports, Knowledge, Members and Settings tabs, plus a Manage tab for team.attention.read (team LEAD or ADMIN); each tab and control shows only what the server’s effective permissions say the caller holds on that team (Settings for team.settings.manage, the budget for team.budget.manage), and the Members tab badges open join requests for those who may decide them. The overview also carries pendingJoinRequests and needsAdmin (a team with no ADMIN) only for someone holding team.members.manage. The switcher lists the caller’s member teams with role and needs-you count and opens the chosen space; the in-memory team filter store is gone. Global pages narrow with ?team=<slug>, resolved through the caller’s member teams (a platform ADMIN may also resolve any team); an unknown or foreign slug is ignored. On the server, the teamId filter on human steps, workflow runs, the request workspace, repositories and pull-request views is checked against membership and answers 404 TEAM_NOT_FOUND to a non-member, so an empty list cannot confirm that a team exists; it only narrows what the caller could already see.
features.title: A team space with a role-aware overview

features.body: A team can hold a monthly USD cap of its own: launches on its repositories are refused once it is spent, and a running run stops at its next model call, including Claude Code and Pi turns, which ask before each call they send.
features.detail: The cap and an alert threshold are columns on the team row, set at PATCH /teams/:id/budget by a team ADMIN, an organization ADMIN of the team’s organization or a platform ADMIN (team.budget.manage); dollars are readable by the same roles, while any member reads only a status. The launch decision checks the organization’s cap and then each spending team’s, refusing with 402 TEAM_BUDGET_EXCEEDED; the refusal carries no amount, and names the team only to its members. Where the caller could launch, the repository list and the team overview carry the owner’s binding cap as a state and percentage (never dollars), so launch pickers can disable a repository whose cap is spent and say who can lift it. The spending team is the OWNER of the repository, also when the caller launches through a share, so a sharing team’s members spend the owner’s cap and key. Spend is finalized runs this month and in-flight ledger cost by attributedTeamId, plus this month’s runless traces by trace team. The worker checks the same cap before each budgeted model call beside the organization’s and fails with the non-retryable BUDGET_EXCEEDED, through a cache of one config window; a run with no attributed team is counted in no team’s spend and capped by none. Before each model call a Claude Code turn (through the model proxy, which answers a non-retryable 400 and never contacts the provider) and a Pi turn ask the same caps; only a genuine refusal (BUDGET_EXCEEDED, MODEL_UNPRICED, MODEL_PRICE_UNAVAILABLE) ends the turn, any other error is logged and the call goes through, and a pass is remembered until the next debit lands or one config window passes. A model with no catalog price is refused when the attributed team has a cap. The in-app assistant and its titler are attributed to a team when the person is an active member of exactly one team and one organization (a person in several teams is attributed to their organization only, so no team cap binds them), and a repository-less run resolves its settings, agents and credentials at the team it was billed to when no repository names one. A connection-less launch that is gated against a team records it on the work request (RunInput.billingTeamId), which attributes the run to that team when no repository, channel, service principal or template team does. The percentage shown to members is the tighter of the team’s and the organization’s caps, with the scope named; it says over exactly when launches on the team’s own repositories would be refused; launches on a repository shared to it follow the owner’s cap.. In the first day of a month a pace projection is replaced by the threshold, as the pace is not reliable yet. A team earns one Slack notice per UTC month when its spend first reaches the alert threshold and one when it reaches the cap, posted to the team’s notify channel through the broadcast-defusing sender and sent only when a budgeted model call refreshes that team’s cached spend. Organization report digests carry the organization budget in dollars only when no Slack channel is a target and the creator and every email recipient are organization ADMINs or platform ADMINs; otherwise they carry a percentage, and a team digest carries only a percentage line for the tighter cap.
features.title: Per-team monthly budgets beside the organization’s

features.body: When a Claude Code agent calls AskUserQuestion, the step saves its working tree, the workflow opens an INPUT human step, and a fresh container restores the tree and continues with the answers.
features.detail: Four surfaces can pause: an agent node with a checkout, an agent run, the implementer’s TDD loop and the fix sessions. The activity validates the question (at most four, each with two to four options), stores the tree as one binary patch against the commit the checkout began from (nothing is committed, pushed or scanned, and a tree over 20 MiB fails the step), and returns the questions with a digest of the work so far instead of a result. The workflow loop turns that into an INPUT human step, waits for the signal, maps the answers onto the questions and runs the same activity again with allowPause set and the saved state. Each round has a recording id derived from the dispatch key and round number, so a replayed dispatch names the same step. An answer that fits no question re-asks the same round up to three times, cancelling the superseded step. After the round limit (workflow.maxNeedsInputRounds, default 5) the activity runs once more with the ability to ask removed and a note to finish on its own judgement; a further pause fails NEEDS_INPUT_LIMIT. No answer within workflow.needsInputTimeoutSeconds (default 24 hours) fails NEEDS_INPUT_TIMEOUT. A cancelled wait closes the open step. Both settings are pinned to the run. A resumed agent run carries the steps and wall-clock time it already used, so the caps apply across rounds. Before the implementer or a fix session pushes, a resumed branch that moved while the person decided is fetched and the run’s commits are replayed onto it (never force-pushed), a conflict fails with NEEDS_INPUT_PUSH_CONFLICT, and the result is checked against the step’s path guard again. The loop is behind Temporal patch markers, so executions that began earlier replay without it.
features.title: An agent can stop to ask a person and be resumed

features.body: Git pushes, pull-request creation, tracker syncs and PRD ticket creation, knowledge-base page writes and non-read-only MCP tool calls each write a RunEffect row with a status of DONE, FAILED or SKIPPED.
features.detail: A row holds the kind (MCP_TOOL, PULL_REQUEST, GIT_PUSH, TRACKER, KNOWLEDGE_BASE), the action, a target (id, URL, branch or tool name), the path it took (harness relay, Mastra MCP binding or an activity), the node and agent, and a failure message. The call’s input is stored only as a SHA-256 of its redacted canonical form; detail and error are redacted and capped. An MCP tool counts as a read only when its server declared readOnlyHint, so an undeclared tool is recorded. Recording is best effort: it never throws, is raced against a five-second timeout and, outside an activity, writes nothing. A git push is recorded after it ran, failures included, and the original result or error is returned unchanged. A tracker sync is FAILED when the tracker refused a write, SKIPPED when it had nothing to write, otherwise DONE. A retried pull-request step does not record a second create for the same URL. GET /runs/:id/effects returns the newest page of a run’s rows to a caller who can see the run, and rows outlive their run. audit.runEffectRetentionDays (ADMIN, default 0 = forever, otherwise at least 30) lets the daily sweep delete old rows.
features.title: An effects ledger records what a run changed outside the sandbox

features.body: An ADMIN reads a folder of a GitHub repository at an exact commit, reviews and approves it into an immutable, hash-pinned profile version, binds one or more profiles to an Agent version, and each run pins the version it started with.
features.detail: The folder must contain a strict profile.json: a description, an optional instructions file, up to 20 plugin directories and optionally the extra built-in tools Skill and Agent. Reading reuses the skill-source machinery (host policy, outbound guard, scoped token), downloads nothing when there is a symlink, submodule, unsafe path or over-limit folder, and shows structure and scanner warnings that approval acknowledges. A version stores the commit, a content hash over the sorted file hashes plus the parsed manifest, and the gzip archive. A profile is disabled, never deleted. Which profiles apply come from the resolved Agent version’s list, not from inheritsModelFrom; marketplaces, the hook switch and team enablement are described in the plugin lifecycle card; which version comes from a caller pin, then the run’s pin (taken at run start for every bound agent and otherwise at first use), then the latest. Resolution fails closed: a missing or disabled-and-unpinned profile, a missing version row or an archive that no longer reproduces its hash raises a non-retryable failure rather than running without it. The Claude Code harness rewrites the approved snapshot into the container outside the checkout before every turn, loads the plugins from that copy, adds the profile’s tools, and appends the instructions behind a provenance line; instructions that spell the provenance marker are refused.
features.title: Admin-approved harness profiles give Claude Code plugins and instructions

features.body: A request can only name a catalog row; a row pins an https download per architecture with a SHA-256, so a workspace installs a checksummed binary instead of an arbitrary one.
features.detail: Rows carry a key, version, per-architecture download, the member path in the archive, a libc and a status of ACTIVE, DEPRECATED or REVOKED. Requests come from a list on the connection and from a tools file in the repository, read from the base ref with git show and never from the agent’s branch or working tree, capped by workspace.toolInstall.maxTools. Nothing is requested unless workspace.toolInstall.enabled resolves true. An agent may ask for more tools in a running workspace when the connection allows it; a denied key, a different version of one already installed, a catalog that cannot be read and a locked network all refuse. Any signed-in user can read the catalog; every write is ADMIN-only, and built-in rows are seeded and kept in step with code until edited.
features.title: A tool catalog lets a workspace install pinned binaries on demand

features.body: Optional node fields replace flat plumbing nodes: storeAs copies an output into context, onFailure routes a finally failed node, status stamps domain status on entry, maxVisits with onExhausted bounds a loop, and resetVisits zeroes other nodes' counters.
features.detail: Absent, a node behaves as before, so stored specs parse and run unchanged. onFailure takes a node id or a terminal status with a message; it applies to the dispatched node types after retries are exhausted and wins over onFail block, warn and continue, while cancellation bypasses it. storeAs writes the output to a second context path, also on a warn or continue outcome. status is set once per visit through a best-effort call and is not repeated on a retry. maxVisits counts entries to the node, and the entry after the limit routes to onExhausted or fails the run. resetVisits lists up to a fixed number of node ids whose visit counters are set to zero when the node is entered, before the node's own count; it is not an edge, and validation rejects unknown ids and a bounded node that resets itself. The authoring helpers and the built-in templates use these fields, so a template's graph has fewer set, cond and updateDomainState nodes than its behavior implies.
features.title: Nodes can store output, route on failure, bound their own loops and reset counters

features.body: The sidebar, top-bar title, breadcrumb and page headings read one list of pages, and each entry shows only when the server’s permission answer says the signed-in person holds its access.
features.detail: The sidebar has a persistent Start work button, then the groups Home, All teams (Approvals with a pending badge, Requests, Epics, Campaigns, Orchestrations, All runs, Pull requests, Tickets), Teams and insights, Build, Connect, Knowledge and Admin; a My teams list (the person’s pinned teams, else up to eight of their member teams, each with a needs-you count) follows Home. Admin is one entry that opens its own settings area with a sub-navigation grouped into sections. Every entry declares an access: anyone, a platform administrator, or a capability key. The sidebar filters the list with the answer from GET /me/permissions: until that answer loads only entries open to everyone show, and LLM usage additionally needs a usage scope. Route layouts can repeat the check on the server (AccessLayout, which says so when it cannot confirm access instead of redirecting), and a unit test reads each layout and requires the entry’s declared access to match it, with a short named list of entries deliberately narrower than their layout. Detail pages (a run, request, pull request, workflow, team) publish their entity name and the top bar draws a breadcrumb through the parent list. The team switcher is drawn only on a fixed list of pages and inside team spaces, where it navigates to a team’s space. The sidebar collapses to an icon rail, kept in the browser’s local storage, and is a drawer on narrow screens. While the readiness check has incomplete items a platform administrator also gets a Setup n/m button in the top bar that opens the checklist. Addresses from earlier layouts (/workflows, /govern, /studio, /inbox and others) are permanent redirects, applied before sign-in redirection.
features.title: The dashboard’s navigation is one capability-filtered page map

features.body: The workflow picker lists active workflows a person can launch by hand, grouped by purpose with the team’s default preselected, and summarises the chosen workflow’s phases, outputs and human steps before any input is typed.
features.detail: A template is offered when it is ACTIVE, has an active version, is not system-managed (the channel assistant’s), is not a review-kind template (those start from a finished run’s Reviews panel) or an automation-kind one (started by an automation or integration), and, with a team scope, is global or that team’s. The preselected workflow is the scope team’s default, else the global default. The searchable list shows up to three templates with the most recent last run first, then the built-in catalogue’s groups (ship code changes, put people in the loop, gate a release, product, support, content and comms), then the team’s own workflows and the rest; a catalogue title replaces the template name where the catalogue knows the name. A deep link to a template the picker excludes shows a warning with the hand-launch reason, or says it may be inactive, archived or not visible to the team. Below the picker the chosen version’s spec is parsed in the browser and summarised as phases (the distinct node group labels in flow order), declared outputs (keys of terminate results), human steps (nodes whose type starts with human) and external signals it waits for; a spec that does not parse says the summary is unavailable. A side panel adds general points and says no built-in step or template merges a pull request. Large graphs elsewhere open folded into phase cards (see the workspaces card).
features.title: Start work offers only hand-launchable workflows, grouped, with a process summary read from the spec

features.body: One page starts a workflow, a single agent, an orchestration, a goal that is turned into a reviewed plan, a multi-repository epic or a PRD run, each with a review step or preview before anything launches.
features.detail: Epic and PRD run are disabled with the reason unless the person holds team.launch.multi-repo (team LEAD) on the scope team or, with no scope, on at least one team, and the form then offers only those teams’ repositories; the epic and PRD routes ask it of every repository’s owning team (a share does not count), and orchestration needs a signed-in account. The workflow, agent, epic and PRD forms each show a review step listing the inputs before they launch. The PRD form collects a title, the PRD text, an optional tracker project key and repositories (view-only shared repositories are not offered), and says the agent analyses the PRD and a person reviews the analysis and the breakdown before tickets or work requests are created. It posts one request with an Idempotency-Key that the page keeps while the body is unchanged, so a retry after a lost response reaches the run the first call started (the gateway answers 409 PRD_RUN_ALREADY_EXISTS) instead of starting a second decomposition, and a 403 lists the repositories where the person is not a lead. The goal mode first asks for existing templates that fit the stated goal and offers them; only on request does it generate a plan, polls the generation job (a person can leave and reopen it from My plans), and shows the plan with its expiry, cost estimate, warnings and agent pins. There the person approves it, which starts a run of exactly that stored plan under one idempotency key per approval, rejects it, regenerates it, or saves it as a draft workflow template where the plan allows. Generation, scrubbing and approval on the server were not reviewed for this card.
features.title: Start work has six modes, and epics and PRD runs are for team leads

features.body: A workflow opens as a read-only Definition canvas with Settings and Versions tabs, and a run opens as linked Events, Graph, Timing and Transcript views that share one selection beside approvals, evidence, activity and details.
features.detail: The workflow page has Definition, Settings and Versions tabs. Definition draws the stored version read-only with a node inspector for anyone who can open it, and the visual editor, which shows a palette, canvas, inspector and a Check workflow button, appears only on edit and for someone who may write the template; saving creates a new immutable version and promoting it is a separate action, and Settings and Versions stay mounted after the first visit so a webhook token shown once is not lost. A graph larger than twenty nodes opens folded: bookkeeping nodes hidden and each connected group of two or more nodes (or macro use) collapsed into one phase card, except that a group holding a failed, running or pending step, a diff marker or the selected node stays open. The folding is a display copy, never saved, run or offered in the editor, and a static graph only (a run’s graph with statuses does not start folded). The run page keeps Events, Graph, Timing and Transcript over one node and attempt selection and holds Overview, Evidence, Activity and Details as further views; Overview is the opening view while a gate needs a decision. A footer says whether the page shows the live edge, a paused snapshot (full-payload mode stops polling) or a final state, and Review history replays the already loaded steps and traces up to a chosen time with a speed control. Views that cannot be rewound (outcome, cost, approvals, evidence, activity, details) say they show latest or final information.
features.title: A workflow is a canvas workspace and a run is one linked investigation workspace

features.body: The page puts the changed files read live from GitHub beside the stored evaluation’s risk class, findings and brief, remembers which files each person viewed and what moved since they last looked.
features.detail: The cockpit route needs a signed-in person who can reach the repository; one they cannot reach is a 404 before the host is asked. Changed files are read live with the platform credential for the repository’s host: the pull request first (asked with the last ETag so an unchanged one costs no rate limit), then its files in pages up to a ceiling of 3,000, held in memory for a few minutes keyed by head. Patches are never stored, and a patch over 200,000 characters is treated as absent (the page says no patch to show). A repository that is not on GitHub, on an unapproved host or without a usable credential makes the read unavailable and the page degrades to what is stored. The latest stored evaluation supplies the risk badge, findings placed on the lines they name (the rest listed apart) and the reviewer brief. A viewed mark stores the file’s patch digest, so a push that changes the file puts it back among the unviewed and lists it as changed since viewed. Filters (all, to verify, unviewed, skim), j and k to move between files, v to mark viewed and a unified or split layout (unified on a narrow screen) are in the page; moved blocks are found in the browser by comparing removed and added lines across the loaded patches. Opening the page records the head the person saw, so the next visit says which commits came in, calls out a rewritten branch, or says the host could not say. Findings and commit subjects are drawn as text, never as markup.
features.title: A pull request the platform opened has a review page read live from the host

features.body: From the review page a person can keep line-comment drafts, send a review or send the pull request back to the agent, but only with their own saved GitHub token and only against the head they were looking at.
features.detail: Writing needs a GitHub token the person saved for that repository, and the platform must have saved tokens enabled; with none, an unusable one (the repository moved host or provider, or the person left its team) or an unreadable one, the page explains why and offers no form. The platform credential is never used for a write, so the review and its audit row are the person’s. Line comments are drafts kept per person and pull request (at most 100), each tied to a path, a side (the new side or a deleted line), a line or a line range, the head and the file’s patch digest; a draft whose file changed or whose line left the diff is flagged outdated and blocks sending until it is deleted or redone. A review (comment, approve or request changes; request changes needs text) names the head the page showed, and the gateway reads the pull request live and refuses with 409 when it is no longer open, when the head moved (STALE_HEAD) or when a draft is outdated. It posts once and never retries; when the outcome is unknown the page holds further sends until the person asks it to check, which looks for a matching review on the host with the same token and, if it finds one, clears the drafts and writes the same audit row marked confirmed. Text that starts /auto-swe fix, that carries the platform’s reserved marker or that is over 4,000 characters is refused. Send back posts the comment /auto-swe fix with an optional note as the person; it is refused while pull-request feedback automations are off for the repository and starts nothing itself, since the webhook path then applies its usual checks (the commenter’s linked account and write permission, the round limit and the kill switch). The page warns that an approval from someone who launched or requested the work is set aside by the platform.
features.title: Reviews, line comments and send-back are sent as the person with their own saved token

features.body: The Manage tab shows failures nobody owns with an assign control, overdue approvals with a Nudge, open pull requests, and the team’s repositories, schedules, automations, budget and service principals.
features.detail: The tab shows for someone who holds team.attention.read on the team (a team LEAD or above in the capability catalogue); anyone else gets not-found. Failures with no owner are failed attempts of the team’s own requests within the desk’s 30-day window, on runs the team owns (a repository merely shared to it does not count), whose launcher is unknown or no longer an active member and which no active member has been assigned; the overview count and the list read the same function. A person with team.attention.manage can assign one to an active member (POST /teams/:id/failure-assignments): the assignment is a separate record that never rewrites the run’s launcher (per-user credentials key on it), lapses when the assignee leaves, replaces a lapsed one, and puts the failure on the assignee’s desk while they remain on the assigning team. Stale approvals are the team’s pending human steps past their deadline; Nudge appears only for a step announced in Slack and overdue, replies once in that message’s thread with fixed text that carries only the escaped step title and the date it was requested, and a step can be nudged at most once every four hours. The budget section shows the meter; a lead who cannot change the cap can send a change request, a reason of up to 500 characters with no amount, one pending per team, recorded with an audit row and listed under Pending requests in the team’s Settings for those who may set the cap. The route that records it sends no message.
features.title: A team lead’s Manage tab lists what needs a hand: unowned failures, overdue approvals and budget

features.body: A signed-in person can browse the team directory and ask to join; the team’s managers decide, a team in another organization also needs that organization’s admin, and the CLI mirrors the flow.
features.detail: The directory lists active teams of active organizations with public fields only (name, slug, description, organization, member count and the viewer’s own relationship), across the whole platform unless the platform setting teams.directoryScope is organization, which limits it to the viewer’s organizations. A request carries a message of up to 500 characters and is refused for a member, for a second open request to the same team (409), within teams.joinRequestCooldownHours (default 72) of a rejection (429) or beyond teams.maxOpenJoinRequests open requests (default 5, 429). A request to a team in an organization the person does not belong to needs a second step. The team step is decided by someone who holds team.members.manage; it cannot decide the approver’s own request and cannot grant a role above the approver’s own rank, and for a cross-organization request it moves the request to an organization step that an organization admin (org.members.manage) decides, which creates the organization membership and the team membership together. Requests can be withdrawn while open, and every state change is a conditional update on the request's current status inside a transaction, and approvals also hold the organization and team row locks, so a withdrawal and a decision cannot both win. The Teams page also offers team creation to organization admins and, when teams.selfServiceCreation is on (default off, with teams.maxCreatedPerUser per creator), to any member of an organization; the Members tab of a team shows a count of pending requests to someone who may manage members. The CLI has teams directory, request, requests (list, withdraw, pending, approve, reject) and orgs requests (list, approve, reject).
features.title: The Teams page is a directory where a person can ask to join, and managers decide

features.body: The admin PR evaluations page lists evaluations across repositories with filters, shows the stored brief as plain text, and sets a repository’s evaluation mode and bot-approval switch, printing the gateway’s refusals.
features.detail: The page sits behind the platform-admin layout. Filters (repository, risk class, merged) live in the URL; rows show the class, mode, commit-status state, whether auto-merge is armed, merged, and a bad-merge marker with its reason, and opening a row loads the stored brief and draws it as plain text, never as markup. The list route itself answers any signed-in person for the repositories they can reach, so the page is the admin entry rather than the only reader. A row links to the pull request’s review page only when the page can find the pull request id, which it does by listing each repository’s newest 100 pull requests; an older evaluation shows no link. The repository policy card offers inherit, off, advisory, enforce and auto and a bot-approval toggle, sends them to the route that decides who may choose auto or bot approval, and prints the reasons the route lists when it refuses; it says whether bot approval is allowed on the deployment and whether the approver App is configured, and calls auto mode and bot approval GitHub-only.
features.title: A platform-admin page lists every pull-request evaluation and sets a repository’s mode

features.body: A platform administrator can now create an eval dataset with its cases, add judge rubrics, import a repository’s lessons, re-screen cases and change a case’s stack from the dashboard, but eval runs still start only from the API or CLI.
features.detail: Everything here is admin-only. Creating a dataset (name, slug, description and cases with a prompt, repository URL, baseline commit, golden test command, optional reference and tags, and a stack of node, python, jvm, go or none) always uses the GLOBAL scope. Cases can be supplied only at creation, because the API has no route that adds a case to an existing dataset, and the form has no per-case rubric field. A rubric (slug, scale, prompt) is created at global scope. On a dataset page an admin can import the newest active lessons of one repository, up to a fixed ceiling, as the dataset’s lesson corpus, choose the repository whose setup secrets the cases use, re-screen every case or one, and change a case’s stack; after a confirmation a stack change sends the case back to not checked, takes it out of quarantine and starts the screen again. Runs are listed and read in the dashboard; the CLI’s evals run is the launcher and takes --candidate-memory and --against-memory (on, shadow or off).
features.title: The Evals admin pages create datasets, add rubrics, import lessons and re-screen cases

features.body: plan and orchestrate are thin clients over the gateway: nothing runs until a plan is approved, the human decisions of an orchestration are made under the launcher’s own account, and the CLI enforces no authorization itself.
features.detail: plan route ranks the templates the person may already launch for a goal; plan create starts a generation job and --wait polls it (600 seconds by default); plan show prints the outline and the generated spec only with --json; plan approve asks on a terminal and refuses non-interactively without --yes, and an --idempotency-key makes a retried approval find the run it started; plan save stores the plan as a DRAFT template (team lead; another person must review it before promotion); plan run, also spelled run --describe, creates, waits, shows and approves in one step but approves only with --yes. orchestrate start sends a task with agent keys (a key may pin key@version), a repository or a team, MCP connection ids, a budget tier and a delivery mode; list, show, messages, say, steer, cancel-agent, cancel and end act on it, and --wait or --follow read the server-sent event stream, resume from Last-Event-ID and fall back to polling every three seconds. attach, decline, approve and deny are decisions only the launcher can make; the help says the in-app assistant and service principals cannot make them and that the gateway enforces both. run accepts --ticket without --description when the ticket can be read from the issue tracker, and prints the launch warnings the gateway returns; the runs list gains an INITIATED BY column; bundles install needs --acknowledge-warnings once the plugin warnings it printed have been read. The clients do not enforce authorization, limits or isolation locally.
features.title: The CLI can generate and approve a plan, steer an orchestration and launch from a ticket alone

features.body: definePlugin names a plugin folder, the exact commit and the expected content hash, and bundle validation applies the plugin-reference gate before signing; the SDK fetches nothing.
features.detail: A bundle can carry plugins by reference: the folder at a source, read at a commit sha, with the harness-profile content hash the installer must reproduce, a profile name and the GLOBAL agents (by key) it is appended to. defineBundle leaves the plugins field out when empty so a bundle without plugins keeps one spelling and one hash, and validateBundle runs the same plugin-reference gate (names, bindings, source coordinates) as install. The installing deployment reads the commit and refuses a mismatch; the CLI says it approves an installed plugin with hooks off, prints the plugin’s warnings and needs --acknowledge-warnings. The SDK remains pure and I/O-free.
features.title: The bundle SDK can reference a Claude Code plugin by folder and commit

features.body: WORKSPACE_RUNTIME names an OCI runtime for agent workspaces, and the worker proves at boot that the runtime is in use and that network locks hold before it takes work.
features.detail: The setting is environment-only. When it is set on the Docker backend, every untrusted workspace container is created with --runtime=<name>. The boot probe (assertDockerRuntime) starts a throwaway container and requires Docker to report that runtime, creates a real workspace through the backend and requires the same, checks that a peer container on the workspace network is unreachable after first proving the peer serves HTTP, checks that public TCP to 1.1.1.1:443 is reachable before a blocked lock and closed after it (an unreachable pre-check is refused as inconclusive), and round-trips a file through docker cp; any failed stage refuses the boot and names the stage. Any runtime name other than runc or runsc-host takes the Kata network path. The network namespace is held by a runc holder container, a Kata sandbox container joins it, and a runc NET_ADMIN helper applies tc and nft rules on the holder's tap and veth interfaces. Detection accepts only the tcfilter topology (a tap named tap0_kata and a veth named eth0, each with exactly one Kata redirect) and refuses anything else. A drop-all nft guard on the holder is installed and checked before the sandbox starts and deleted only after the first policy is in place; each policy install or change adds a drop-all tc filter for the transition, installs the new filters under a fresh conntrack zone, reads the filter set back as JSON and compares it rule by rule, then removes the transition drop and verifies it is gone. A failed or concurrent replacement destroys the sandbox and then the holder. Workspace containers and service containers join the holder only while the group is ready, carrying the CRI annotations that bind them to the sandbox. The same path serves ephemeral shell and container steps. Trusted delivery workspaces use the default runtime instead.
features.title: Docker workspaces can run under a Kata runtime with a stateful tc network lock

features.body: A Docker workspace runs as UID 1000 by default, starts with private-range and metadata destinations blocked whatever the egress policy, and can carry a per-container storage cap.
features.detail: The container is created with --user 1000:1000, HOME under /workspace/.home, no capabilities, no-new-privileges, an init process and memory, CPU and PID limits; the workspace directories are copied in with archive ownership so the unprivileged user owns them. WORKSPACE_RUN_AS_ROOT=true (only that exact value) restores root and switches the setup-process cleanup to a mount-namespace path. Right after start, before any service container, a NET_ADMIN helper in the container's network namespace installs an iptables and ip6tables OUTPUT chain that blocks the IPv4 and IPv6 private, link-local, CGNAT, multicast and embedded-IPv4 ranges (and 127.0.0.0/8 off the loopback interface; the container's own loopback stays open) and the cloud metadata addresses, with exceptions for the resolved addresses of the git host, the model, registry and egress proxies, the configured DNS servers and any WORKSPACE_PRIVATE_EGRESS_ALLOW networks; only the literal value false disables WORKSPACE_BLOCK_PRIVATE_EGRESS or WORKSPACE_BLOCK_METADATA. The installed rules are read back and compared with what was intended, and a mismatch removes the container. On the non-Kata path the GCP metadata names also resolve to 0.0.0.0. WORKSPACE_DISK_LIMIT, when set, adds --storage-opt size=<limit> to workspace containers; at worker boot a probe container must start with that option and its storage driver must be overlay2, devicemapper, btrfs or zfs, otherwise the boot is refused because the size could be silently ignored. This baseline is separate from, and underneath, the restricted and blocked locks.
features.title: Docker workspaces run unprivileged, behind a baseline network block, with an optional disk quota

features.body: workspace.setupEgressPolicy lets repository setup use open or restricted networking while the run policy stays strict, then swaps in the run lock before the agent runs.
features.detail: The setting is inherit by default, which keeps the run policy and the existing order. It is run-pinned and resolvable at template, team and organization scope with ADMIN write access; a launcher cannot set it. The rule (effectiveSetupEgressPolicy) ranks open below restricted below blocked and applies the setup policy only when it is looser than the run policy, so a setup policy that is equal or stricter is ignored, and a restricted setup phase that gets no egress proxy registration (an empty effective allowlist) falls back to the run policy. Trusted workspaces, onboarding drafts that receive the widened draft allowlist, and callers that ask to inherit never use a separate setup phase. When there is a phase, provisioning and the setup lock come first, the repository setup runs under it (with proxy variables cleared in an open phase), and finishSetup then waits for setup, runs a script that stops and kills workspace processes other than PID 1 and the keeper, then fails the transition if any remain or cannot be inspected (a mount-namespace path under root), applies the run policy as a replacement lock, and for a blocked run releases the egress proxy registration. A failed transition removes the workspace and raises an egress-policy failure. A caller that defers setup to move onto the work branch triggers the transition after setup; the shell and container steps are not affected.
features.title: Setup can run under a looser network phase than the agent, replaced before agent code starts

features.body: Each worker records its egress capability, and the gateway uses fresh reports to warn when a policy or a team allowlist cannot be enforced.
features.detail: On start a worker probes its capability. On Docker it creates a throwaway workspace on the helper image and applies a blocked lock; success sets networkLock, failure stores the first 300 characters of the diagnostic, and a failed cleanup also clears it. On Kubernetes it reports a lock when K8S_REQUIRE_NETWORK_POLICY is enabled (the boot NetworkPolicy check does the proving) and says so in the detail when it is not. The report also records whether an egress proxy and a registry proxy are configured. It is written to a worker-capability row keyed by host, queue, process and a random id, refreshed every ten minutes and deleted on graceful shutdown. The gateway ignores reports older than 30 minutes; a lock counts as enforceable only if every fresh worker reports one, and restricted with a non-empty allowlist also needs an egress proxy on every fresh worker. Saving workspace.egressPolicy at a value other than open and saving a team's egress allowlist return those warnings with the successful response, and the admin readiness endpoint includes the summary. With no fresh reports there are no warnings.
features.title: Workers report whether they can enforce network locks, and settings warn when they cannot

features.body: The Helm chart ships a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy for workspace pods, and the worker will not start unless it finds that policy enforcing.
features.detail: The chart creates a policy and Deny binding named <namespace>-pods for pods and ephemeral containers in the workspace namespace, with failurePolicy Fail. Its rules require the asw/role=workspace label, a service account token that is explicitly not automounted, the default or one designated service account, only emptyDir, configMap and downwardAPI volumes (or projections of those), no envFrom and a secretKeyRef only to the pod's own -env Secret, no container that explicitly sets runAsUser 0 or adds capabilities, except one exact sidecar profile for preview services (pod-level and image-default users are left to the namespace's PodSecurity profile), and, when the namespace carries asw/required-runtime-class, a matching runtimeClassName. Before polling, and unless K8S_REQUIRE_ADMISSION_POLICY is false, the worker reads the policy and binding and refuses to start unless the policy fails closed, is scoped to the workspace namespace, has validations and no type-checking warnings, and the binding denies in that namespace. With K8S_REQUIRE_RUNTIME_CLASS true it also requires K8S_WORKSPACE_RUNTIME_CLASS to be set, the RuntimeClass to exist and the network-check pod to report that runtimeClassName, and, while the admission check is on, the namespace label to name it., the RuntimeClass to exist, and the network-check pod to report that runtimeClassName. The chart can create a Kata RuntimeClass (off by default; the nodes must already provide the handler), and pods run as UID 1000 unless K8S_WORKSPACE_RUN_AS_UID says otherwise.
features.title: A Kubernetes worker requires an enforcing admission policy and can require a RuntimeClass

features.body: The agent workspace never runs an authenticated git call: a short-lived trusted workspace fetches and pushes, and only a size-capped git bundle crosses between them.
features.detail: Implementation, implementer-session and decomposition workspaces are created with bundle delivery, which records the checked-out commit as the delivery base. Their gitAuthed does not inject the clone credential; each call creates a new workspace from the authenticated URL (open stays open, any other policy becomes blocked, so only the git host and platform proxies are reachable; default runtime, no Kata) and destroys it afterwards. Only three command shapes are accepted: ls-remote --heads origin, fetch origin with +refs/heads/x:refs/remotes/origin/x refspecs, and push origin <commit-or-ref>[:<branch>]; text that is not plain shell-quoted words is refused. A fetch runs in the trusted workspace, deepens it only if the base is not an ancestor, bundles each ref and copies it (512 MiB cap) into the agent workspace, which fetches from the file. A push bundles the commit the agent holds on top of the base, copies it to the trusted workspace, verifies the bundle, imports it to a private ref and requires the imported commit to equal the requested one, runs fsck --strict, requires the remote branch to be unchanged since it was listed and to be an ancestor of the commit, and pushes by commit id with no force option. Every git call there runs with hooks, fsmonitor, global config, replace objects and credential helpers disabled.
features.title: Fetch and push for implementation sessions run in a fresh trusted workspace that holds the credential

features.body: A team admin stores named secrets on the team and grants each to specific repositories the team owns; setup and preview recipes then name them like repository secrets.
features.detail: Values are encrypted with the same envelope as repository setup secrets and are write-only; at most 50 per team. The team routes (GET, PUT and DELETE under /teams/:teamId/secrets and PUT .../:name/grants) need the team.secrets.manage capability, and audit entries carry names only. Names that steer the shell, loader, git, TLS or proxies (PATH, HOME, NODE_OPTIONS, LD_*, GIT_*, SSL_CERT_*, *_PROXY, ASW_* and similar) are refused, because a team secret is injected wherever a grant reaches. A grant can name only repositories the team itself owns, up to 200, not ones merely shared to it, and moving a repository to another team deletes its grants. When setup or an app preview resolves a name, the repository's own secret wins; otherwise a granted team secret fills it when the repository's current team, read from its connection row, and that team's organization are active. A name that neither supplies fails setup with a missing_secret blocker, and a new grant closes the matching blockers. Eval runs and the repo-onboarding trial are called with team secrets refused.
features.title: Team secrets are stored once and reach a repository only through an explicit grant

features.body: A setup failure that carries a typed reason is stored per repository, counted when it repeats and closed when a later setup succeeds.
features.detail: The worker reads a blocker from the failure details and upserts it by repository, kind and subject, incrementing an occurrence count and clearing any earlier resolution. Kinds are missing_secret, secret_decrypt_failed, missing_tool, egress_denied, git_auth, git_fetch, lfs_missing, step_failed, step_timeout, invalid_config, secret_leak and internal, each with a fixed remedy sentence. A failed step is classed missing_tool from exit 127 or a command-not-found message, and egress_denied when the egress proxy recorded a blocked host after the step started. A setup run that finishes, or a workspace with no definition, resolves the repository's open blockers. People with repository-management or gate-command authoring rights list them (optionally with resolved ones) and resolve one by hand; the unresolved count is what the repository checklist uses as setup health. Recording is best-effort: a failure to write is logged and ignored, and the onboarding trial does not record.
features.title: Workspace setup failures are recorded as typed blockers with a remedy

features.body: A repository may keep .auto-swe/gates.yml and .auto-swe/preview.yml, read from the base commit and never from the agent's branch.
features.detail: Files are read with git cat-file at the base commit recorded during provisioning, with replace objects off, or, before a workspace exists, through the source-control provider at the resolved base-branch commit. A resume run reads them from the base branch, not from the snapshot pin that may contain agent commits. Gate precedence per gate is the step's command, the connection's gate commands, gates.yml, the stack default, then the built-in; the preview recipe is the connection's previewConfig as a whole when set, otherwise preview.yml, otherwise none. Each file is capped at 64 KiB, YAML aliases are limited and the content is schema-validated; a present but invalid file fails, as an invalid_config setup blocker inside a workspace and as REPO_CONFIG_INVALID before one, rather than being treated as absent. A command that came from the file is reported as a repo-file source in test evidence. A command in these files needs no platform shell-authoring role: whoever can land a change on the base branch controls commands that run in the agent workspace with its network access.
features.title: Gate commands and the preview recipe can live in trusted repository files

features.body: An orchestrator agent holds a durable conversation and starts, steers and cancels allowlisted sub-agent runs, while fixed code decides what actually happens.
features.detail: The orchestrator's four tools (spawn, message, cancel, request a repository) only record intents, up to a per-turn cap; after the turn fixed code applies each one through the gateway and writes a notice for every refusal. A spawn must name an agent on the launch-time allowlist (the orchestrator cannot spawn itself, and the default list is a registry setting), declare a reader or a writer, and stay inside the child-count, concurrency and writer-count bounds that were frozen into the orchestration at launch. A writer needs an attached repository, a branch or draft-PR delivery, and path scopes that do not overlap another running writer or each other; the scopes are enforced at delivery, which refuses and pushes nothing when any changed path (both sides of a rename) falls outside them. A writer also needs the launcher's own GitHub push permission, except when a service principal launched it. A child starts through the ordinary agent-run launch as the launcher, so budgets, admission and repository reach apply to it. A child's final result returns to the orchestrator only as a fenced, entity-escaped, truncated block. The launcher can message a child (a steering message on the child's run, which the orchestrator is told about), cancel it, attach or decline a repository the orchestrator asked for, and approve or deny the MCP writes the children attempt. The workflow ends on cancel, end, a quiet idle period with nothing in flight, a turn limit or the lifetime cap; the lifetime cap cancels running children and leaves pushed branches. Launch is refused until an admin turns the kill switch on (default off).
features.title: Orchestrated agent runs with sub-agents

features.body: Inside an orchestration, an MCP tool call that is not provably read-only waits for the launcher to approve that one call.
features.detail: One guard is consulted at every MCP binding point (the Mastra wrapper and the harness relay that Claude Code and Pi call through). A tool counts as read-only only when the server lists readOnlyHint: true as an own data property; a missing, inherited or malformed annotation is treated as a write. A write does not run until the launcher approves; denial, a timeout (a registry setting) or any failure to find out is a refusal that reaches the model as a tool error. The approval row stores a digest of argument names, types and sizes, never values. Agents bound to an orchestration also have their MCP results screened. A run that belongs to no orchestration gets no guard and is unchanged. Who approves is a person: the in-app assistant is barred from the approval, attach and decline routes by its route policy.
features.title: Launcher approval of MCP writes in an orchestration

features.body: A launcher states a goal, the platform generates a constrained workflow plan, shows it with a cost estimate, and only an approved plan starts a run pinned to exactly that spec.
features.detail: A router agent ranks only templates the caller may launch; a user can pick one or ask for a generated plan. A delivering plan is a canonical core, compared node for node with a fresh construction of the shipped core, with model-authored free nodes allowed only before it and after the merge wait. Free steps come from a code-classified allowlist (every registered step is free, skeleton or denied, with a reason for each denial), a plan may not contain shell, container, MCP, eval or fan-out nodes, writes only under context, and cannot reset a visit count. Free agent nodes take only fixed inputs, and one designated notes channel feeds the implementer's guidance. Generation is a bounded repair loop through the skeleton policy and the strict spec parse, with an attempt cap. Approval is a human decision by the plan's owner: it re-checks the stored hash, reach to the repository, agent launchability, agent version drift, a settings snapshot and the step-catalog hash, refuses rather than regenerating, and flips PENDING to APPROVED in one conditional update that opens a launch window. The worker re-runs the policy and pins the spec when it creates a run of a hidden Planned Run template, naming the plan as the run's trigger reference. A planned run's pull request is evaluated as advisory even on an auto-mode repository, so a human merges. Every agent node is held to the agent-run step and wall-clock ceilings and fails non-retryably on reaching one. Per-user generation and routing quotas, a pending cap and a kill switch are registry settings.
features.title: Run plans: generate, preview and approve at launch

features.body: A pending or launched plan can be saved as a DRAFT template, and launched plans lose their goal and body after a retention period while the row stays.
features.detail: Saving needs the plan's owner and template-authoring rights on the plan's team; the stored spec goes through the same strict parse and shell gates as any save, and the result is a DRAFT version marked generatedBy run_plan that is never the default and needs review before activation. A scrubbed, rejected or expired plan cannot be saved. A scheduled sweep expires unlaunched plans past their expiry, deletes old expired and rejected ones, and scrubs launched plans after runPlans.launchedRetentionDays (0 keeps them): it removes the plan row's goal, spec, router summary, stored reports and node-level cost lines in one guarded update; copies of the goal in the run's work request, spec snapshot and traces stay until run-history retention removes them., and keeps agent pins, the settings snapshot and metadata so run provenance still resolves. Launched plans are never deleted because runs name them.
features.title: Run plans: save as a template, and scrub after launch

features.body: A team lead launches one dependency or framework change as a campaign: a child run per repository, bounded in parallelism, each attempt ending at a draft pull request.
features.detail: A campaign names a description (the agent brief), an optional versioned recipe with strict parameters, and a bounded repository list; the caller must lead the owning team and each target repository's team (or be an admin), and every repository must exist and be active. It runs as a Temporal workflow that starts the dependency-upgrade-campaign template as one child per repository, at most the configured parallelism at a time, in input order. Before each batch starts the workflow re-authorizes the targets through an activity; a target that is refused ends SKIPPED with the reason, and a re-check that cannot be made fails closed. A child that fails never stops the others, and a campaign-wide cancel cancels the children in flight. Each target records its path (recipe, agent, recipe then agent, or none), a verification result and a failure reason, and the campaign ends COMPLETED, COMPLETED_WITH_FAILURES or CANCELLED. Inside a child, a code-owned recipe (an exact npm package version or a Go module version, validated against strict patterns in the gateway and again in the worker) makes the change in a sandbox; a repository the recipe does not affect ends successfully with no pull request, and a layout it cannot handle falls through to the agent. Every change is verified by the repository's original tests with the test files the change touched put back first, an agent that weakens tests is stopped, a failed verification gets one fix attempt, and the run ends at a draft pull request, never a merge. The feature is off by default behind a registry setting.
features.title: Campaigns: one planned change across many repositories

features.body: A spec may record that a block was built by a versioned macro; the flat nodes stay canonical and the macro record is checked against them.
features.detail: A top-level uses map names, per use id, a versioned macro (for example ciLoop@2) and its JSON arguments, and each node that expansion produced carries a use tag. The interpreter and the worker never read uses; they run the flat nodes, which are what is stored, hashed and diffed. The save path materializes the nodes of any use that has none, a use whose nodes are already present is never silently repaired, and validation reports an unknown macro, bad arguments, orphan tags, a missing expansion or drift between the stored nodes and a fresh expansion; the editor can then re-expand or detach the use. A changed helper output is a new macro version, so a stored use cannot change meaning silently. The built-in templates are written through the macros, and the workflow author's prompt documents them so a generated spec may declare uses instead of writing those nodes. The author's output is materialized and strictly parsed before it is accepted. Generated run plans ignore the macro metadata when judging what a node is.
features.title: Versioned workflow macros beside the flat spec

features.body: A built-in template that is merged into another is archived at start-up, but only when nobody has taken it over.
features.detail: The sync archives a retired built-in's global row only when it is still active on its latest built-in version, is not the default, runs no experiment, and no automation, schedule, template webhook or service principal still points at it; otherwise it is left as it is and a warning, logged once per process, names its replacement. Rows are never deleted, and runs that pinned a version are unaffected.
features.title: Retiring a built-in template

features.body: Each run records what started it, who or which service principal initiated it, and which run it repeats.
features.detail: Every launch door stamps a trigger from a closed set (work request, template run, agent run, planned run, service token, Slack, webhook, automation, schedule, epic, code review and others), an initiating user or service principal, an optional trigger reference and an optional earlier run it re-runs; the worker writes them once onto the run. The record is descriptive only: it is never read for a decision, and the credential key stays the separate launcher field.
