An id that no longer resolves, or an unknown trigger, is dropped to null with a warning instead of failing the launch. A planned run overrides the reference with its plan id.
features.title: Run provenance

features.body: A daily sweep deletes finished runs older than an admin-set number of days, and does nothing while the setting is 0.
features.detail: workflow.runRetentionDays defaults to 0 (keep forever) and otherwise must be at least 30. The sweep selects only terminal runs whose start and end are past the cutoff, with no step or trace newer than it, not under a transcript legal hold, not the child of a live orchestration, not the source of a review launch still being retried, and whose artifact backend this process can reach. Before deleting a run it removes artifact payloads and public evidence copies outside Postgres (a failure keeps the run), and it keeps a run whose ledger row is still live or has an open pull request, with a pending callback, or with LLM spend not yet rolled up, counting each reason. Deletion cascades to steps, traces, artifacts and other run-owned rows and sets null on memory items, transcripts and similar references. Batches are small and bounded by runs deleted, batches read and a wall-clock budget; a failing batch ends the sweep and the next scheduled one continues.
features.title: Opt-in run-history retention

features.body: Two seeded graphs read a PagerDuty incident: one diagnoses it against the repository, the other drafts a postmortem for a resolved one.
features.detail: incident-triage reads the incident with its alerts and log entries, has a triage agent diagnose it in a workspace, checks the reply as structured output, and posts the diagnosis as an incident note through the autonomy policy gate (an internal write, so it posts without waiting under the default policy, or waits for a person where a team requires approval). Fix mode is off by default: when on, a diagnosed code defect at or above a minimum confidence gets an implementer attempt, lint, typecheck and tests, and a draft pull request linked from the note; a failed or empty fix still posts the diagnosis. incident-postmortem reads the incident, alerts, notes and timeline, drafts and checks a postmortem, posts it as a note and, when a Confluence connection is named and the draft parsed, publishes a page, an external write that waits for approval under the default policy. Both are written to be started from an inbound-event automation that maps the incident id from the event.
features.title: Incident triage and postmortem templates

features.body: The dashboard groups a large graph into phases from its group labels; the engine ignores them.
features.detail: A node's optional group label is presentation only. The phase overview lists the distinct labels in flow order, breadth-first from the entry, and a node without a label belongs to no phase. The run, launch-summary and library views use that list to name the current phase and fold or summarize the graph; nothing in the interpreter or the worker reads the label.
features.title: Phases for reading large workflows

features.body: A signed PagerDuty webhook can start the incident-triage template, which reads the incident, diagnoses it against a throwaway checkout and posts the diagnosis as an incident note; a resolved incident can start incident-postmortem, which drafts a postmortem note and optionally a Confluence page.
features.detail: Nothing starts these runs until a team creates an event endpoint from the PagerDuty v3 preset and an inbound.event automation that maps the incident id (/event/data/id) into the template’s incidentId input; the preset reads the event type from /event/event_type, scopes the cooldown to the incident’s service, and verifies an HMAC-SHA256 header that may carry one signature per secret during rotation. A pagerduty connection holds a REST API key and the fromEmail of a PagerDuty user; its Test connection looks that user up. The run reads the incident, its latest alerts, log entries and notes through the connector (at most 25 of each, the notes endpoint being unpaginated so only the newest are kept, alert bodies and note text cut at 4,000 characters, the incident id validated against a short uppercase-alphanumeric shape). The seeded incidentTriager (file, directory and bash tools in a checkout that is discarded, and a prompt that treats incident text as data) answers as JSON with a category, confidence and fixable flag. The reply is parsed by code: only a code-category diagnosis counts as fixable whatever the model says, and a reply that does not parse is still posted, marked unstructured, and routed away from any fix. The note is an internal_write, so the default autonomy policy posts it without waiting and a team can require approval for that class. Fix mode is off by default; when set, a fixable diagnosis at or above minFixConfidence (0.7 unless the run sets one) is handed to the implementer as fenced untrusted data, then runs the lint, typecheck and test gates in warn mode (a failing gate is recorded and does not stop the run) and opens a draft pull request that the note links, and a fix that fails or changes nothing still posts the diagnosis. The postmortem writer drafts a blameless summary (impact, timeline, root cause, resolution, follow-ups) from the incident, its notes and the checkout and posts it as a note first; only when a Confluence connection is named and the draft parsed does it publish a page, which is an external_write and waits for approval under the default policy. The PagerDuty note is attributed to the fromEmail user, and the diagnosis is model output about production, so it is a hypothesis for responders, not a finding.
features.title: PagerDuty incidents can start a triage run, and a resolved incident can start a postmortem draft

features.body: A repository can link a pagerduty_events connection, and when the merge webhook records a merge of a pull request the platform opened, a change event goes to PagerDuty so responders see the merge on the service’s timeline.
features.detail: The link is a field on a git repository, and saving it checks that the target is a pagerduty_events connection of the repository’s own team. The send runs in the merge webhook after the Slack notice and the tracker sync, and only on the first delivery of a merge (a duplicate returns earlier). It decrypts the connection’s routing key, builds a change event (summary "Merged org/repo#N: title" cut to PagerDuty’s 1,024-character limit, a link to the pull request, the pull request number, repository and ticket id as custom details, source auto-swe, the merge time) and posts it to PagerDuty’s change-events intake through the guarded fetch (public addresses only, redirects refused, a five-second timeout). It is best effort: an inactive connection, a missing key, an unreachable host or a non-2xx answer is logged as a warning and never changes the merge’s recording or the webhook’s response. The pull request title is sent to PagerDuty as written. A pagerduty_events connection is only a routing key: the generic read, write and tool actions refuse it. Its Test connection sends a real change event marked as a test, because the Events API has no read-only check.
features.title: Merges of pull requests the platform opened are sent to PagerDuty as change events

features.body: An event endpoint can list event types that cancel the still-running runs its own automations started for the same subject, so a PagerDuty incident.resolved stops that incident’s triage.
features.detail: cancelOnTypes holds at most ten fixed event types per endpoint, and the PagerDuty preset sets incident.resolved. It acts only after the signature, the enabled endpoint, the active team and the inbound-events switch have passed and the event has been parsed, and before the event is decided as usual, so an automation that selects the same type still evaluates it. The cancel looks up the endpoint’s own STARTED automation fires whose subject key equals the event’s subject, keeps those whose run is RUNNING, asks Temporal to cancel each, marks the run CANCELLED (a status predicate never overwrites a terminal state) and writes an audit row with no actor. An execution Temporal no longer knows is simply marked; any other Temporal failure leaves that run RUNNING and the endpoint answers 503 RUN_CANCEL_FAILED so the sender’s redelivery tries again. It cannot reach runs another endpoint or a person started, and anything the run already wrote (a posted note, a draft pull request) stays.
features.title: A signed event can cancel the runs its endpoint started for the same subject

features.body: A Snyk webhook endpoint preset and the vulnerability-remediation template let a new vulnerability in a project start a run that makes the smallest dependency change, scans, tests and opens a draft pull request.
features.detail: The preset verifies an HMAC-SHA256 digest in X-Hub-Signature, uses a constant event type because Snyk names its event only in an unsigned header, takes the Snyk project id as subject and scope so the cooldown counts per project, and keys each delivery by a digest of its body because the payload has no event id. Its description tells the team to give every automation two match rules (a first new issue exists and is a vulnerability) because otherwise every snapshot and ping would start a run, bounded only by the cooldown and the daily cap. The automation maps advisory fields into scalar inputs (advisory id, package, severity on a four-level lowercase scale, vulnerable and fixed versions), each bounded in length and alphabet; there is deliberately no title, summary or URL field, since those are free text the sender writes, and the run’s description presents the mapped values as data the agent checks against the repository. The template validates, has the implementer make the smallest change that removes the advisory, and ends SUCCESS with no pull request when nothing changed (the repository is not affected). Otherwise it runs a vulnerability scan and the full test suite, both in warn mode (a failure is recorded and the run continues), opens a draft pull request and fixes CI failures from the logs up to three times, writing a lesson if CI stays red. A person still merges.
features.title: Snyk project snapshots can start a vulnerability-remediation run that opens a draft pull request

features.body: When a launch gives a Ticket ID and leaves Description blank, the gateway reads the ticket and builds a fenced brief from it; text the person typed is scanned for injection phrasing, advisory only.
features.detail: The template-run route, the legacy work-request route, the Slack run modal and the MCP submit tool share one brief builder. It runs only after every authorization check, goes through the same tracker scope rule as other ticket reads, and never carries provider error text: any failure is a refusal with DESCRIPTION_REQUIRED. Typed text always wins and causes no fetch, and the ticket id comes only from the payload’s ticketId, never inferred from a task name. The brief’s first line is "Ticket <id>" followed by the ticket link when it is http or https; the title (cut at 500 characters) and body (12,000) sit inside a <ticket> block with every angle bracket replaced by a look-alike so it cannot close the block, behind a line saying it is data written by someone else. A preview route returns only the title, status and link for a repository the caller can reach. A typed description, never the derived brief, is scanned with INJECTION patterns only (the exfiltration set would flag most tickets that contain a URL): it never blocks a launch, the audit row records the matched pattern labels but not the text, the response carries a DESCRIPTION_INJECTION_SUSPECTED warning, and the web form stays on screen with the warning until the person continues. Scanning is capped and incomplete scans are recorded, so a clean result is not proof the text is safe.
features.title: A launch can take its brief from the ticket, and typed text gets an advisory injection scan

features.body: Repository lesson recall is a pinned per-run mode: on injects lessons, shadow retrieves and traces without injecting, off skips retrieval, and an optional holdout puts a share of otherwise-on runs in shadow so the arms can be compared.
features.detail: memory.lessonRecall (on, shadow or off; overridable at workflow template, team and organization) and memory.lessonHoldoutPercent (0 to 50, default 0) are read when a run is created and stored on the run as its arm and a held-out flag. A run whose mode is on is assigned to shadow when a SHA-256 bucket of its run id falls under the holdout percent; a configured shadow or off run is never counted as held out. Recall for the implementer family, the fixers and review personas reads the run’s arm: shadow still embeds the query and searches, records a lessons.shadow_retrieved trace with the lesson ids and similarities, and returns an empty block; off records a recall_skipped event; the searchLessons tool answers with an unavailable note outside the on arm. A lesson manager (team.lessons.manage: a platform admin, a LEAD or ADMIN of the owning team, or an ADMIN of that team’s organization) can read GET /lessons/recall-experiment for a repository or a team over a window (30 days by default; more than 5,000 matching runs is refused). It summarises each arm’s success and failure rates, gate pass rate, merge rate, mean cost and mean fix-loop iterations, then the on-versus-shadow differences with Newcombe intervals over Wilson bounds, both overall and among runs that actually retrieved at least one lesson. The response says it is an observational comparison and flags fewer than 30 runs per arm.
features.title: Lesson recall runs on, shadow or off per run, with a deterministic holdout and an experiment report

features.body: Enough distinct flags on a repository lesson, or a manager’s decision, quarantines it: it stays stored and listed but the recall query no longer returns it.
features.detail: memory.lessonFlagQuarantineThreshold (default 2, 0 turns automatic quarantine off) is resolved at the repository’s owning team and organization. Adding or removing a flag runs under a per-lesson advisory lock and recounts: reaching the threshold sets the quarantine with source FLAG_THRESHOLD and a reason naming the count; falling back below it restores only a lesson that a flag quarantined, never a manual one. A lesson manager can also quarantine with a reason (source MANUAL) or restore it, and a restore deletes every flag on the lesson; each change is written to the audit log, and a restore's entry carries the flags it deleted. The recall query excludes quarantined repository lessons in SQL before the limit, and the explanation lookups that follow merged and superseded sources also require a lesson that is not quarantined. Changing the threshold does not sweep lessons already flagged, and a lesson list can be filtered to quarantined ones.
features.title: A lesson can be quarantined by a flag threshold or by a manager, and a quarantined lesson is not recalled

features.body: An eval run can give each side a lesson-memory mode (on, shadow or off) over an isolated lesson corpus stored with the dataset, so the effect of lessons on fixture cases can be measured without touching production memory.
features.detail: Each dataset can hold up to 50 corpus lessons in their own table, authored or imported by an admin from a repository’s active, non-quarantined, non-superseded lessons; production recall, search and consolidation never read the corpus and eval recall never reads memory items. Starting a run takes a candidate and a baseline memory mode (both off by default, so existing behaviour is unchanged) and pins them with a deterministic hash of the corpus’s content and failure types; on or shadow with an empty corpus is refused with EMPTY_EVAL_CORPUS. The worker re-reads the corpus, fails the run if its hash changed since launch or its embedding model no longer matches the query’s, and scores similarity with an exact cosine scan in the worker. In the on arm the implementer receives the same fenced lesson block production recall uses plus corpus-backed searchLessons and explainLesson tools; shadow retrieves and traces but injects nothing; off does nothing. Corpus text passes the same injection-pattern filter recall applies before use. The run summary records both modes, the hash and how many cases each side saw at least one lesson in, and the CLI takes --candidate-memory and --against-memory. Scheduled evals pin both sides to off.
features.title: Offline evals can compare lesson memory arms against a fixed per-dataset corpus

features.body: The repo-onboarding template has an agent explore a repository and draft its setup, gate commands and optional preview recipe, runs that draft in a fresh checkout, asks a person to review the result, and only then opens a pull request with the files.
features.detail: Launching it needs the team repository-onboarding permission on an active git repository and the seeded, platform-wide repo-onboarding template; onboarding.autoRunOnConnect (off by default) can start it when a repository connects, under the creating user’s normal launch authorization, and a failure to start never undoes the connection. The repo-onboarder agent works in a checkout and must return one fenced JSON draft, which code parses and validates; optional-tool presence checks in draft setup steps (docker, kubectl, a cloud CLI) are rewritten to warn rather than fail. A valid draft goes to a trial in a new workspace: setup runs without team secrets, but a repository setup secret the draft names is still injected into the agent-written setup steps before anyone approves them; then each gate command with a ten-minute limit, then preview readiness if a recipe was drafted., then each gate command with a ten-minute limit, then preview readiness if a recipe was drafted. A failed trial that is not operator-only loops the report back to the agent, up to three drafts, after which the run goes to review; missing secrets, egress denial, git auth or fetch failures, missing LFS objects and internal errors mark the trial blocked and go straight to review. The approval step (seven days) shows the draft and trial and lets the person approve even when the trial failed or was blocked; request changes returns to the agent, rejection or timeout ends FAILED. Approval runs a delivery step that needs a verified run launcher and opens the pull request with the rendered files, and the run result carries the PR link. The files take effect only when that pull request is merged. During the draft, a seeded repo-onboarder may reach extra package and download hosts (onboarding.draftEgressHosts) when the egress proxy is configured, but only if the node runs on the default loop, the agent row equals the seeded definition (no override, runtime, harness profile or MCP binding) and its model credential is global or has no custom endpoint; its MCP tools are never bound, and an override or untrusted credential that appears mid-run fails the step rather than running in the widened workspace. The trial never receives the widened allowlist.
features.title: A seeded onboarding workflow drafts a repository’s configuration, trials it, and opens a pull request after approval

features.body: A heuristic guard reads the diff a CI-fix, quality-gate-fix or pull-request-feedback session committed and, depending on the setting, records or refuses a change that reaches green by removing or weakening tests.
features.detail: github.ciFixTestIntegrityGuard is off, warn (the default) or block, set per team or organization and resolved before the paid agent session starts. The guard covers the CI-fix, gate-fix and PR-feedback fix modes of the implementer session, and the implement step of a template that carries refuseWorkflowChanges (the ci-triage fix); a step may also set a floor of warn or block with its own testIntegrity config, and a block floor cannot be lowered by the setting. The change is committed with hooks off, the analyser reads the diff between the starting commit and that committed sha, and that same sha is what is pushed, so what is analysed and what is pushed cannot differ. A diff that reads empty while the trees differ at a non-generated path is treated as unreadable, never as clean. The analyser works over diff text, ignoring comment-only lines: it looks for deleted or renamed test files, removed test cases, added skip, focus or expected-failure markers, commented-out or early-returning tests, dropped or trivialised assertions, test configuration that excludes tests or lowers a coverage threshold, test commands or CI steps changed so failures are ignored, and changes to .gitattributes. In warn mode a trip becomes a ci_fix.test_integrity_guard activity event, counted per repository in the outcome report. In block mode a high-severity finding fails the step non-retryably with TEST_INTEGRITY_GUARD before anything is pushed and the fixer is not told why; low-severity findings (a deleted fixture, a regenerated snapshot) are recorded but never block, and an unreadable or too-large-to-read-in-full diff fails closed as TEST_INTEGRITY_GUARD_UNAVAILABLE. A diff longer than the analysis cap records a degraded event and is read by its head and its file list only.
features.title: A fix session’s change is checked for deleted, skipped or weakened tests before it is pushed

features.body: Per-repository routing settings and a fail-closed rule decide which open pull requests need a person and in what order a reviewer meets them, and a report measures how long reviews take.
features.detail: Routing is read from five prEvaluation settings (a minimum risk class, a changed-line limit, always-human path globs, a quick-review size, and whether a bot approval with armed auto-merge skips a person), and a repository’s owning-team lead or a platform admin may add a per-repository override. An override can only tighten: at read time each key takes the stricter of the setting and the override (lower risk floor, lower non-zero size limit, union of paths, skip-on-bot-approval only if both allow it), so a looser stored value is inert, and the PUT answers 403 ROUTING_LOOSER_THAN_SETTINGS for a value that would loosen what is in force or for dropping stored strictness (only a platform admin may remove it). Path globs that can never match are refused when saved. The decision is pure and fail-closed: a pull request with no evaluation at its current head, a cut or unrecorded path list, a path too long to match, or a match that exhausted its work budget needs a person; a draft or non-open request needs nobody yet. A listed always-human path asks first, whatever approvals stand; otherwise enough trusted approvals with no standing change request clear it, then risk and size ask, then a bot approval may skip, otherwise it is below threshold. GET /pull-requests with order=attention covers open requests only and returns them as deep, standard, quick or none with needsHuman and the reasons. GET /pull-requests/review-time reports, per repository and team, time from ready to first human review and first view, first review to merge, review rounds and change-request rate as p50 and p90 with low-sample flags, from stored timestamps only.
features.title: Review routing orders the open pull-request queue and says why a person is needed

features.body: The channel assistant, reactive turns and the ambient digest can reply with a card the model describes as JSON and fixed code validates and renders, and several run notices are cards built entirely by fixed code.
features.detail: The model never writes Block Kit. A card is a flat list of header, text, fields, table, context, divider and buttons components checked against Slack’s caps (50 blocks, 3,000-character sections, 150-character headers, 75-character button labels, five buttons a block, up to ten fields, tables of up to six columns and thirty rows rendered as aligned monospace with cells cut at 40 characters). parseSlackCard lists every problem as a separate line, and the postCard tool returns that list to the model so it can correct the card in the same turn; an accepted card is recorded and posted after the turn, a later accepted call replacing an earlier one. All model text is escaped for ampersand and angle brackets, so a card cannot carry a channel broadcast, a mention or a disguised link; the only links are link buttons, http or https only, and when a host list is set the host must match exactly and carry no userinfo. Buttons carry no interactive action. An explicit SKIP in a reactive turn still wins over a card, and a card that was refused and never corrected leaves the prose to post as before. The run-complete, step-failure, PR-ready and task-result notices are built by fixed code through the same validator and fall back to the plain line when the card cannot be built; the PR button may point only at the dashboard or an approved repository host. The task result card escapes the result prose wholesale, so Slack link syntax in it shows as typed. Separately, plain text a model writes to Slack passes a linear-time scan that defuses channel, here, everyone and user-group mentions while leaving links and single-person mentions, and a source rule allows only the known writer files to name the post and update endpoints.
features.title: Slack replies and notices can be validated cards built from a closed component catalogue

features.body: An ADMIN can track a plugin marketplace repository, approve its entries as hash-pinned harness profiles, switch a plugin’s hooks on or off, and let teams enable approved plugins for their own agents.
features.detail: A marketplace source is a repository folder with a marketplace catalog, pinned to a commit. A nightly workflow (MARKETPLACE_SYNC_ENABLED, MARKETPLACE_SYNC_CRON) asks the host which commit the ref now names and marks the source or a profile UPDATE_AVAILABLE; it never moves a pin or approves anything, which an admin does by previewing, accepting the update or approving a catalog entry. A profile’s hooks switch is one boolean decided by a platform admin and applied only when the plugin is written into the run container: with it off, the hooks and monitors files, the LSP file, the matching keys of the plugin manifest and the hooks frontmatter of every skill and command are left out of the container copy while the stored snapshot and its hash stay unchanged, and a source that cannot be removed reliably refuses the plugin with PROFILE_HOOKS_UNREADABLE. An Agent version can list several plugins and a name collision is refused. Only a team-scoped agent version, which team admins can write, needs the team’s enablement of each plugin it binds; versions at global, organization, channel and template scope are admin-written and need none, and a team-scoped binding without enablement fails closed. Disabling a plugin for a team answers with the agents it stranded. A run pin records each plugin’s version, the hook switch as read and the team and agent versions whose binding passed the enablement check, so removing an enablement is not bypassed through a version another agent pinned. A bundle carries plugin references (source, commit, expected content hash) that install re-reads and verifies without carrying plugin bytes. Skills a plugin contains are projected as managed, unverified skill rows that follow the plugin and go inactive while it is disabled.
features.title: Plugin lifecycle: tracked marketplaces, a hook switch, team enablement and update tracking

features.body: A read-only worker script splits each recorded implementer model request across its prompt segments and prints token and price-equivalent shares per runtime and model.
features.detail: Run as an operator with database and artifact-store access, it streams complete implementer transcripts for one run or a recent window and, for each recorded HTTP model call, divides the provider’s own reported input total across the tool schemas, system prompt, user and assistant messages, tool-call arguments per tool and tool results per tool in proportion to characters, with images given a fixed weight. Cached input is treated as a prefix of the prompt, so cache reads and writes land on the earliest segments and are weighted by the model’s cache rates, with a flag for a rate the price table lacks. It prints aggregates only, never transcript text. Shares are estimates of a real total, not tokenizer counts; harness session-file records cannot be attributed and are counted as unmeasurable; truncated transcripts are skipped because they lose the largest prompts; price-equivalent figures are meaningful only within one model and runtime. It does not write the transcript access log the gateway’s reads do.
features.title: An operator script reports where implementer input tokens go

features.body: Each gateway route declares a capability, a check its handler makes, a service scope, plain authentication or a stated public reason, and one resolver answers them from the caller’s platform, organization and team standing.
features.detail: Three stored role enums replace the single role: platform ADMIN or USER, team ADMIN, LEAD or MEMBER, and organization ADMIN or MEMBER. A migration maps the old values (a platform LEAD or ENGINEER becomes USER, a team ENGINEER becomes MEMBER, the ORG_ prefixes are dropped) and deletes every role-grantee settings grant and every user grant held by a former platform ENGINEER. One module reads stored role values and recognises only the current spellings; the retired ones (ENGINEER, ORG_ADMIN, ORG_MEMBER) are not accepted, and an unrecognised value resolves to no standing and confers nothing. The catalog states each capability’s scope (platform, organization or team), class (governance, operation, sensitive or read), the lowest team role and organization role that confer it, and whether platform ADMIN holds it. decide() is a pure function over a loaded standing: a service principal is refused every capability because it is judged by its token scopes; an organization ADMIN reaches a team-scoped capability only when it is governance or read (members, settings, repositories, budget), never one that launches work, answers an approval or holds a credential, whatever a catalog entry says; and a deactivated team confers nothing for a non-read capability, with platform ADMIN never stopped. For member changes an actor acts at the rank the resolver computes (platform ADMIN or the team’s organization ADMIN count as ADMIN), which also bounds the role they may grant. A route declares requireAuth({ capability }) and the hook answers 403 FORBIDDEN naming the missing capability, or 404 for a route that hides existence; a route whose resource comes from the body or a lookup declares handlerChecked and calls can() itself. A request-scoped cache holds each decision for that request only. Separation-of-duties constraints (not yourself, the launcher, not the author, the assignee) are composed with a capability and platform ADMIN does not satisfy them, with one documented exception for reviewing a generated template version the administrator authored. GET /me/permissions returns the caller’s own capabilities per team and organization, each tagged with its authority, and the dashboard’s useCan reads that answer instead of comparing roles; a narrowed query for a team the caller has no standing on answers 403 whether or not the team exists, and only a platform ADMIN is told 404. A settings key is writable by a platform ADMIN or, when it is grantable, by a grant that covers it, and a role grant covers the named team role and every higher role (MEMBER, then LEAD, then ADMIN), matched against the actor’s role in the grant’s own team. Audit rows written under a capability decision carry its authority in their context JSON. A source check fails code that decides authorization by comparing a role value outside the permissions module.
features.title: Capabilities, not role comparisons, decide who may act

features.body: Any signed-in person can browse the active teams and ask to join one, and, in an organization that turns it on, create a team of their own.
features.detail: The directory lists active teams of active organizations with name, description, organization, member count and the viewer’s relationship to each (member, requested or none), searchable by name, slug and description and paged by cursor; teams.directoryScope (platform by default) narrows it to the viewer’s organizations, and a team outside the scope answers like an unknown one. A request carries an optional message of up to 500 characters and is refused for a member, for a second open request to the same team (a partial unique index also decides a race), for a team that rejected the person within teams.joinRequestCooldownHours (72 by default, 0 disables) and beyond teams.maxOpenJoinRequests (5) open requests, counted under a per-person advisory lock. A request from someone already in the team’s organization is decided once, by anyone holding team.members.manage on the team (a team LEAD or ADMIN, or an organization ADMIN), who may name the role to grant but not above the rank they act at; a request from outside the organization moves to PENDING_ORG after the team step and needs an organization ADMIN, whose approval creates the organization MEMBER row and the team membership together, audited. Each decision is a conditional update on the expected status; an approval is also taken under the organization lock and then the team’s, re-reads the requester’s organization membership under it and re-checks that the team and the requester are still active, while a rejection needs only the status predicate; nobody decides their own request, and the requester can withdraw. Self-service creation is off by default (teams.selfServiceCreation, overridable per organization). Where on, a member of the organization can create a team there and becomes its ADMIN, up to teams.maxCreatedPerUser (3) active teams counted across organizations. The organization route asks org.teams.create first and the setting only of someone without it, and otherwise returns that capability’s own refusal, so a caller learns nothing about whether the organization exists or has the setting on; only an organization ADMIN may appoint another person as the first team admin. A team’s overview carries the number of open requests for those who decide them.
features.title: Team directory, join requests and self-service teams

features.body: A team’s membership stays inside its organization, organization admins create teams and invite people without a platform-wide role, and team leads invite new people into their own team.
features.detail: The organization route creates a team and its first ADMIN membership in one audited transaction under the organization’s row lock: the creator by default, or a named admin who must already belong to the organization. Adding a member to a team requires that the user is already in the team’s organization (ORG_MEMBERSHIP_REQUIRED); only a platform ADMIN adding someone creates the organization membership on the way. team.members.manage covers inviting, adding, changing and removing members and is held by a team LEAD or ADMIN and by an organization ADMIN, who acts at ADMIN rank; a granted role never exceeds the actor’s own rank (PRIVILEGE_ESCALATION), and nobody removes or demotes themselves. A team LEAD, or an organization ADMIN with the team capability too, can invite a new email straight into a team: one transaction creates the user, the organization membership and the optional team seat, and the magic link is sent after commit; an existing email answers USER_EXISTS. The invitee is active at once only when a platform ADMIN invites, or when the organization is active and has trusted invites on (recorded as an org_admin or team_lead approval source); otherwise the account waits for approval. Removing an organization membership removes that person’s memberships in the organization’s teams in the same transaction, taking the organization lock first and the teams’ in ascending id order; the organization’s own admins cannot remove or demote its last admin (the operator may), and the cascade may leave a team with no ADMIN only for an actor with organization or platform authority, which the team overview then flags to those who can appoint one. Repository management follows the same split: a team LEAD or ADMIN, and an organization ADMIN without membership, manage a team’s repositories, while launching work still needs membership or a share.
features.title: Organization admins create teams, bound membership and invite people into teams

features.body: An organization admin can install the instance’s GitHub App and tie the installation to the organization, so only that organization’s teams can import and onboard repositories through it.
features.detail: The connect route (org.github.manage, held by an organization ADMIN and a platform ADMIN) returns the App’s install URL with an HMAC-signed state bound to the user, organization, App and API host. It answers GITHUB_CONNECT_NOT_CONFIGURED unless the instance App id, private key and OAuth client are set, both URLs are https on one host family, and the App’s identity read through its own JWT matches the configured id. The claim route verifies the state’s signature, expiry and that it names the caller, asks the capability again, refuses an installation id that is already registered, and has GitHub confirm that the authorizing user can see the installation (the user token is not stored) before it creates a GitHubInstallation row for the instance host with the account login and the organization, audited. Only the instance’s own host can be claimed this way. An installation linked to an organization is listed for import only to a platform ADMIN or someone who manages an active team of that organization; an installation with no organization stays available as before. Creating or importing a repository, or changing its installation, is refused when the installation’s organization differs from the target team’s (the generic GITHUB_ACCESS_UNVERIFIED for a non-admin), and the same check applies to the instance’s default installation when none is named. An organization admin can list and retire the organization’s installations; a platform-registered installation answers INSTALLATION_EXISTS and its organization link stays a platform admin’s to manage.
features.title: Organization admins link a GitHub App installation to their organization

features.body: A team lead sees failures nobody owns and can assign them, nudge an overdue approval in Slack, and ask whoever sets the cap for a higher team budget.
features.detail: An unowned failure is the latest failed attempt, inside the 30-day desk window and visible to the caller, of a run attributed to the team as its owner (work on a repository merely shared to it is not the team’s to own) whose launcher is unknown, an automation or no longer an active member, and which has no assignment held by an active member. team.attention.read (team LEAD) lists them, up to 100, and the overview counts the same set; team.attention.manage assigns one to an active member, replacing an assignment that lapsed with its assignee’s membership. The assignment is its own row and never changes launchedById, the key a per-user credential is resolved by, and an assigned failure reaches the assignee’s desk only while they remain a team member. A team LEAD or ADMIN of a team that owns the run can post one fixed reminder as a reply in the Slack thread of an overdue, pending approval step: it needs the recorded announcement message, only the escaped step title and the date the step was requested vary, the slot is claimed before posting so a step is nudged at most once every 4 hours, and a missing bot token answers 502. team.budget-requests.create lets a LEAD file a reason of up to 500 characters, one pending request per team enforced by a partial unique index; whoever may set the team’s cap (the team ADMIN or an organization ADMIN) lists and dismisses requests, and saving the cap, changed or not, resolves them. The request carries no amount and no response gives the LEAD the cap or the spend.
features.title: Team leads get a needs-attention list, failure assignment, nudges and budget requests

features.body: Platform admins can see who signed in and how, what people did, which accounts are failing password sign-ins, and export the people table.
features.detail: The authentication hooks write sign_in, sign_in_failed and sign_out activity events carrying a closed set of methods and coarse browser and OS families, beside the Session audit row each sign-in already wrote. A failed attempt is stored only for the password endpoint and only when the attempted email belongs to an existing user, so the table never holds a guess at someone else’s address or the address itself; every failure, known or not, increments a metric. Failed rows are not collapsed (a per-account bucket of 30 a minute bounds them) while other sign-in events are collapsed for 60 seconds. Routes under /platform/analytics need platform.audit.read, are refused to the in-app assistant, and give an overview (daily, weekly and monthly active people, stickiness, sign-ins by method, browser and OS, failures, actions by entity type, peak hours), a people list and one person’s detail, which is itself recorded as a sensitive read. A person is active on a day with a sign-in, page-view, read or export event or any audit row they authored other than a Session row. The scan covers at most 30 UTC days, per day with limited concurrency, cached for 30 seconds. The alerts route lists accounts with at least analytics.failedSignInAlertThreshold failures (5, at least 2) inside analytics.failedSignInAlertWindowMinutes (15) as a sliding window, at most 50, with the methods used and whether a sign-in followed, and reports thresholdReachable false when the per-account rate limit makes the configured threshold impossible; a per-process tracker also counts each crossing in the auth.sign_in.threshold_exceeded metric. The people export is CSV with spreadsheet-formula neutralization, is recorded as an export event, and answers 413 EXPORT_TOO_LARGE instead of a partial file when more than 5,000 people match. An opt-in script copies historic sign-ins from Session audit rows into activity events, never at boot, with a dry run.
features.title: Admin user analytics: sign-ins, actions, failed-sign-in alerts and CSV export

features.body: A team lead starts a campaign from a dialog, watches each repository move from pending to a draft pull request or a reason, and cancels while it runs.
features.detail: The Campaigns page lists campaigns newest first, filterable by state and team and paged thirty at a time, and refreshes every ten seconds. The Start button and the dialog appear only for someone who holds team.launch.multi-repo on some team, and the dialog offers as owning team and as target repositories only active git repositories whose owning team the person may launch on, within the owning team’s organization; it takes a name, a brief (the agent’s instructions and the pull request text, with a note that nobody can answer the agent’s questions), an optional recipe (an npm dependency or a Go module, each with a package name and an exact version), an optional budget tier and parallelism, and at most two hundred repositories. The dialog keeps one Idempotency-Key for as long as the request is unchanged, so a retry after a lost response returns the campaign the first call started, and a changed request gets a new key. The gateway still decides every launch. A campaign page shows the brief, a progress bar of finished repositories out of the total, and one row per repository with its state, path (recipe, agent, recipe then agent, or no change), verification result, failure reason, the live phase of a running child, a link to the child run when the viewer can read it and a link to the draft pull request’s review page when the campaign’s ticket id finds it; the page polls every ten seconds until the campaign reaches a final state. Visibility follows the gateway: a campaign is listed to its owning team’s members and to anyone who can reach at least one target repository, and the detail names only the targets in repositories the viewer can reach while counting the rest as hidden. The Cancel button is offered to the creator and to someone who holds team.launch.multi-repo on the owning team, behind a confirmation that says repositories not yet started will not start, runs in flight are asked to stop and opened draft pull requests stay open; the gateway repeats the check and a campaign already cancelling can be sent the signal again.
features.title: The campaigns page starts, follows and cancels a campaign

features.body: A person launches an orchestration from the Start page, follows its conversation and agents live, and, only as the launcher, steers it and answers its requests.
features.detail: The Orchestrations list shows each conversation’s status, team, repository (or none), agent counts, spend and last update, for the launcher and the members of its team (a platform ADMIN sees all). The launch form is the Start page’s orchestrate mode: a task of bounded length, a team or repository, the agent allowlist (defaulting to the platform default for that team, with the write-capable agents of that default marked), the team’s MCP connections, a budget tier and a delivery default, followed by a review step; the form keeps one idempotency key for an unchanged request. The detail page has a conversation column and an agents column (tabs on a narrow screen) and keeps a live connection to the events stream, which resumes from the last event id, treats a stream silent for forty-five seconds as dead, backs off with jitter, and falls back to polling every three seconds when the server refuses, throttles or cannot stream; the gateway allows four concurrent streams per person. The page asks the gateway whether the viewer is the launcher: only then does it show the composer, the per-agent message box and Cancel buttons, the cancel and end controls, and the attach, decline, approve and deny cards; everyone else sees a read-only note and the same cards marked as waiting for the launcher. The agents column links each child to its run (or its request before it starts) and shows undelivered steering messages, since an agent takes messages between steps.
features.title: The orchestrations pages launch, watch live and decide

features.body: Two write tools start an orchestration and send a message to it or to one of its agents; every decision stays with the person in the dashboard or CLI.
features.detail: orchestrations_launch takes a task, a repository or a team the person belongs to, an optional agent allowlist (up to twenty keys; omitted means the platform default, and the result names the allowlist applied and which agents can change files), an optional delivery default and a required idempotency key. orchestrations_message sends text, as the signed-in user, to the orchestrator or, with a child id, to one running agent, and is refused for anyone but the launcher and for an orchestration that has ended. Both only call the orchestration REST routes as the user, so the route’s own guards run: the writes-enabled switch, the per-user burst limit, the STANDARD budget tier (a launch cannot ask for another), the idempotency key, the in-flight run cap and the delivery default: a launch’s default must be one of the modes the platform allows through MCP at that moment, and a message steers only an orchestration whose default is no broader than the broadest allowed mode. An orchestration started through MCP carries no MCP connections, so its agents cannot widen their reach, and a bridged message cannot restart a finished orchestration because that would skip the concurrency check. The server registers exactly these two orchestration write tools: attaching or declining a repository, approving or denying a child’s MCP write, and cancelling or ending an orchestration have no tool, and the CLI and dashboard are where those happen. The read tools for orchestrations belong to the read-domain registry.
features.title: MCP clients can start and message an orchestration, and nothing more

features.body: The channel assistant can offer a single-use Generate plan button; clicking it starts a plan as the clicker, and approval happens only in the dashboard.
features.detail: The assistant’s proposeRun tool records only a mode and an agent key; fixed code after the turn decides the rest. It takes the goal from the person’s own message (over-length text is refused), requires a linked, active user, resolves the repository from the channel’s own binding (a model-supplied repository hint is honoured only when the person’s message names it), checks that person’s reach to it, and posts a message whose button value is a token signed with the Slack signing secret. The token binds the person’s Slack id, the channel and thread, the goal verbatim with its hash, the repository, mode and agent, a random id and a fifteen-minute expiry; it is signed, not encrypted, and Slack caps the value at two thousand characters. The click handler verifies signature and expiry, requires that the clicker is the person named and that the message is in the channel and thread the token names, refuses an unlinked or deactivated Slack account with a private note, and starts generation through the same function POST /run-plans uses, as the platform user the clicker links to, so repository reach, quotas, the kill switch and launchable agents are the route’s own and the channel’s identity is not used. The generation is started under an idempotency key derived from the token id, so a second click is told the button was already used, while a click refused before the job starts consumes nothing. It then posts a Review plan link into the thread. It never approves a plan or starts a run: the plan is reviewed and approved in the dashboard.
features.title: A Slack button starts plan generation as the person who asked

limits.body: Setup-secret injection is scoped to setup commands, not a separate trust boundary inside the workspace.
limits.detail: The platform does not add these values to the agent's normal environment, but repository-controlled setup commands run as the workspace user and can persist credentials or start processes. Setup output redaction and write-only management responses are not proof that later code cannot recover a value. Secret values are not part of the dependency-cache identity, so rotating one does not itself invalidate that cache; setup steps still execute on a hit. Queued setup-file status is a Temporal execution state, not a worker-health or progress signal.
limits.title: Setup credentials inherit repository-command trust

limits.body: A dashboard filter can narrow only the data its view has loaded; an empty view is not proof of an idle or healthy platform.
limits.detail: The trace stream distinguishes older events not loaded by the server from matching events held back by its rendering limit. Search sees the loaded payload representation, which may be trimmed. Assistant-failure search and common-cause summaries are page-local. Full-payload mode disables run-detail polling, not worker execution. Draft-discard prompts protect participating forms and ordinary same-origin link clicks or unloads; they are not a universal router interception or an authorization boundary. Role-conditioned controls and confirmations still rely on gateway permissions. The live run page also keeps bounded data: a watched run holds at most its newest 5,000 traces and becomes a sliding window past that, the live activity tail keeps the newest 500 rows, and a step’s inputs and outputs are serialized only while opened and cut at 100,000 characters with a note of how much was dropped.
limits.title: Loaded views and UI safeguards have local boundaries

limits.body: Workspace expiry is not a live-ownership query or a global fan-out to every worker host.
limits.detail: The scheduled workflow runs one activity on the engineering task queue, and that activity inspects only the chosen worker's Docker daemon or Kubernetes namespace. Workers using separate daemons or namespaces are not all visited by one sweep. Selection trusts platform marker labels, creation times, configured deadlines and grace periods, not a lookup of each owning Temporal activity. Missing labels, disabled schedules, failed listing/removal, or a backlog larger than the cap leave resources behind. Docker counts sidecars and services separately against its removal cap. This is best-effort cleanup, not immediate resource reclamation, authorization against malicious labels, or a guarantee that all substrate hosts are covered.
limits.title: Workspace sweeps inspect one substrate at a time

limits.body: A working probe is not proof of an executable workflow, and no tracker marker is not proof that every tracker write landed.
limits.detail: Connection tests sample particular requests, not a clone, push, private-package install or full workflow. A registry 404 or redirect counts as reached without confirming its credential; a public success response does not establish private-package access. A GitHub host App identity can pass even when its installation listing is unavailable, and a repository token that reports no permission flags is described as visible rather than proven push-capable. Each request in a check has a ceiling of about ten seconds (eight for the GitHub token test), and an App check makes up to three (identity, token mint, listing), so a check can pass while a later step, such as a push blocked by branch protection, fails. The GitHub token test against the saved API URL uses a plain fetch, because a self-hosted host is often private, so a connection failure there reports the client’s own error message (never a remote response body); a typed, unsaved URL goes through the guarded fetch. Tracker write-back recording covers eligible terminal notifications, not every PR link, CI comment, transition or webhook. Jira treats a matching current status name or category as already there when no named transition exists; if the status read fails, it records no missing-transition claim. Linear can silently leave an unmapped or already-current state unchanged. Finalization side effects run after the terminal transaction and are not replayed by an activity retry that finds the run already ended. Writing the notice is itself best-effort. The record holds one failure class per run, for the first write of the closing event that the tracker refused; a 404 reads as not_found whether the issue is missing or the token cannot see it, a failure of the sync itself is recorded as unknown, and a GitHub start event writes nothing. The marker is neither an external delivery receipt nor a durable retry outbox.
limits.title: Diagnostic success has a narrow scope

limits.body: Indexed KB search and filesystem reference copies do not expose exactly the same files.
limits.detail: The index accepts selected text extensions under per-file, file-count and total-byte caps, records skipped files separately from injection-flagged files, and refuses a truncated repository tree. Checkout instead fetches the configured subtree at the pinned SHA, deletes symlinks, Git metadata and files listed as flagged, and applies a separate total-byte cap. It does not delete every file skipped by the index, so an unsupported extension or an indexing cap is not a filesystem exclusion. The checkout sets file permissions to 444 and directory permissions to 555; this is a permission-restricted copy, not a read-only bind mount. Prompt summaries and search excerpts are untrusted reference data, not approval of every file available in that copy. Ready snapshot IDs can remain searchable even when that reference's file checkout fails.
limits.title: An indexing skip is not a checkout exclusion

limits.body: PR-label and push automations turn event text into work; their recorded branch and commit are not automatically a review target or checkout pin.
limits.detail: The PR-label source creates a synthetic ticket from the label occurrence and describes the pull request's title, body and refs. Its default ticket-to-merge template is not the PR-feedback push path. The push source similarly describes the pushed commits and supplies no extra event-derived template fields. Both use the shared payload builder, which combines template defaults, saved automation options and the source's explicit fields; it does not automatically turn an event head into baseBranch or reviewOf. The chosen template and configured options determine the work. A label or push therefore does not promise a review of that exact head or a fix on the existing PR branch. Push path filtering sees only the bounded webhook file list; a truncated list with no matching file is a non-match, not permission to assume omitted paths matched.
limits.title: An event reference is not an exact-head execution contract

limits.body: The tenant query guard detects missing filters; it does not establish a caller's authority or provide database row-level security.
limits.detail: The ORM extension checks an allowlist of tenant-scoped models and multi-row operations for a structurally narrowing predicate. It does not inject the caller's tenant or check that a supplied team id belongs to them. Single-row findUnique/findFirst operations are outside the guard, raw SQL bypasses it, and intentional runUnscoped regions exempt named models. Warning mode logs and permits a violation. Route-specific role, membership and ownership checks remain necessary. Review-preset management illustrates the distinction: with no team the check names no resource, which only a platform ADMIN satisfies; for a selected team it asks team.codereview.manage (team LEAD or ADMIN on that team), and no platform role is involved. Assistant confirm policy is another layer, not a replacement for those checks.
limits.title: A tenant-shaped query is not an authorization decision

limits.body: Automatic review intents have bounded recovery; a recorded start or queued retry is not proof that a worker consumed it.
limits.detail: Successful non-review finalization inserts attached-preset intents in the terminal transaction; an insertion failure rolls that bookkeeping back. Dispatch happens afterward, so dispatch failure does not undo committed source completion. A stale-intent sweep retries unexpected failures within an attempt budget, but classified launch errors become skipped and are not automatically revived when configuration changes. Dispatch records RunInput and ActiveWorkflow before starting Temporal; WorkflowRun may not exist until setup runs. Manual launch therefore opens the existing request panel rather than a nonexistent reserved run page. Fix retries persist a queued marker after Temporal acceptance and update the decision when the worker processes the attempt. Stable review/attempt identities coalesce duplicates; these markers do not promise worker availability or immediate execution.
limits.title: Review acceptance and execution are separate states

limits.body: Inline review findings are optional, advisory comments, not approval requests or verified fixes.
limits.detail: prEvaluation.postReviewFindings controls posting. Selection takes warning/critical findings on changed files, excludes reviewer-crash placeholders, and suppresses lint/style/type categories when CI already failed. Only lines anchorable on the new side of the diff become inline comments; unanchorable selected findings can still appear in the bounded brief. Posting checks existing finding markers and rereads the head immediately before creating a comment-only review. A moved head, host refusal or read/post error returns a reason without failing evaluation, so inline delivery is not guaranteed. Suggested fixes are escaped prose, not click-to-apply suggestion blocks, and /auto-swe is neutralized. The human-thread feedback gatherer ignores marked platform finding comments; the explicit review_findings trigger reads review-run data instead.
limits.title: Inline findings are best-effort advice, not an approval gate

limits.body: Checked model output and approval do not make document comments or ticket-plan creation atomic.
limits.detail: The document-review pack checks bounded JSON shapes, not the truth or completeness of the review and plan. A quoted passage is anchored when found; an unsupported anchor falls back to a footer comment with the quote. Comments are sent sequentially, and a transient error can leave earlier comments behind. Ticket-plan creation likewise creates an epic, tickets and subtasks sequentially without rollback; a failure reports the items created so far. These writes use the outcome ledger rather than blindly retrying an uncertain partial effect. A valid plan still needs a person's structure approval even if the autonomy policy allows the later tracker write automatically.
limits.title: Document-review writes can leave partial effects

limits.body: A review is bounded evidence about one change, not proof of correctness or a promise that a fix starts.
limits.detail: Network chunks see the full file list but only their part of the diff, so cross-chunk interactions may be missed. Changes above the hard size cap are refused. Stored verification rejects unsupported or unsafe patch forms; failures remain explicitly unverified and skip the optional test gate. Even verified stored reviews have no PR and never feed PR evaluation. Tests are opt-in, not an implied successful gate. PR fixes need an enabled repository automation opted into review_findings, the matching open platform PR and unchanged head, push eligibility, budget and remaining rounds; a skipped decision is surfaced rather than treated as a successful fix. Stored fixes remain unpublished agent runs. Retry eligibility is limited to recorded transient decisions and rechecks guards. Publication waits up to five minutes for review completion before reevaluation, which rereads the PR's current head. Branch-only reviews have no fix hook. The opt-in test result is input to the review, not a separate hard approval gate. A retry's queued marker is durable publication-step JSON written after Temporal accepts the request; it is not a live worker-health or progress check.
limits.title: Review evidence and fix attempts have explicit limits

limits.body: References are capped, indexing and checkout are best-effort, and revocation cannot recall content already handed to an agent.
limits.detail: Indexing limits file count, individual and total bytes; checkout has a separate byte cap. Mandatory references still face the run cap and operational failures. New runs and later resolutions recheck attachability, but existing workspaces and tools bound to copied snapshot IDs are not actively scrubbed or cancelled. Reindex requests coalesce on the KB workflow ID, and a READY snapshot for the same KB/SHA/path is reused rather than rebuilt. A changed scanner or embedding configuration alone therefore does not force that snapshot to be rescanned or re-embedded. The text-only planner requests no checkout credentials, but reference resolution and indexing may still authenticate to the host. Its context is best-effort: no ready pins means no block, and an error while assembling or retrieving context omits the block rather than failing the plan. Sanitized, quoted summaries and untrusted-data instructions do not prove immunity to prompt injection. Snapshots have no dedicated retention sweep. Live authenticated GitHub, embedding-provider and vector-search integration and the KB dashboard browser UI are not end-to-end verified by the mock/component tests.
limits.title: KB snapshots are bounded reference context, not revocable instructions

limits.body: HubSpot and generic HTTP API handlers are deliberately narrow.
limits.detail: Every pair in GENERIC_STEP_CONNECTION_TYPES (shared/lib/connectionTypes.ts) has a concrete handler, and any other pair (every step over git_repo, readSource over slack_workspace, a type the build does not know) fails non-retryably with CONNECTOR_NOT_IMPLEMENTED before a claim; none returns a stub success. The http_api connector is https-only with no private-network opt-in, caps responses at 256 KiB, omits non-text bodies, and its base path is a request-construction boundary rather than an authorization one; readSource on it is an ungoverned credentialed GET. HubSpot covers CRM v3 objects through a private-app token only, with no OAuth flow, associations or batch calls. An MCP tool-level error fails the generic steps and is not retried.
limits.title: HubSpot and generic HTTP API connectors are narrow

limits.body: A failed post-diff security gate can leave code on a remote branch.
limits.detail: executeImplementation commits/pushes first, then scans the diff and may throw SECURITY_GATE_FAILURE, or SECURITY_GATE_UNAVAILABLE when the gate cannot complete; both are non-retryable, so the pushed commit stays and is not scanned again. Exhausted TDD iterations can also return failing tests, as can a loop stopped after a test command that could not run (exit 126/127, npm’s missing test script or missing package.json): the change is committed and pushed either way, with that cause in the implementation notes. Do not interpret activity failure as “nothing was published.” Agent Run delivery uses a different trusted-container path.
limits.title: Engineering push happens before the critical diff gate

limits.body: The approval guard lives in lib/externalWrite.ts and covers the three generic connector-writing steps (writeOutcome, a mutating runTool and a non-read-only mcp node), conditional on a recorded publish decision.
limits.detail: A run with no recorded decision that required approval is not gated by assertApprovalSatisfied, so a template that writes without a publishOutcome step writes ungated, and the requirement is run-wide rather than tied to the write it was recorded for. The risk class is a declaration the author writes, not derived from the effect. Built-in steps that write elsewhere — pull-request creation and update (createOrUpdatePullRequest), CI triage comments (reportCiTriage), CI-fix pushes (pushCiFixToPullRequest), tracker item creation (createTrackerItems), ticket comments (postTicketComment, one best-effort attempt on the run’s own ticket through the instance’s tracker configuration; no built-in template uses it), the tracker sync (status transitions, pull-request links and CI and failure comments on the run’s ticket, from the implementation, pull-request and run-end steps and the merge and CI webhooks) and run callbacks — are covered neither by assertApprovalSatisfied nor by the outcome ledger, nor are pull-request evaluation’s commit status, brief and finding comments, approver-App approval and auto-merge arming, which are governed by ADMIN switches and the repository’s evaluation mode rather than by a publish decision. On the GitHub Issues tracker the ticket comment, the sync and tracker item creation write only to a repository the run targets (see the GitHub tracker scope card); that bounds where they write, not whether anyone approved it, while Jira and Linear writes (the comment, the sync’s status transitions and comments) are bounded only by the optional tracker.allowedProjectKeys list, which likewise limits which tickets they touch, not whether anyone approved it. An agent’s own MCP tool calls, and arbitrary shell or container egress, are outside that helper too. Validation warns WRITE_WITHOUT_POLICY on a writeOutcome step or mcp node that no publishOutcome step reaches (the shipped Notion draft records an internal_write decision first, which the default policy publishes without approval), but the warning never blocks a save, promotion or activation, it checks reachability, so a write that a path skipping the decision also reaches passes, and it ignores runTool, whose tool is usually bound at run time. Template design and tool permissions remain important. Several of those writes (git pushes, pull-request creation, the tracker syncs, PRD ticket creation, knowledge-base page writes and non-read-only MCP calls) are additionally recorded afterwards as RunEffect rows; the record gates nothing (see the effects ledger cards).
limits.title: Outcome policy covers the writing steps, not every outbound path

limits.body: An effect is claimed before the provider is called, so a retry after any failure that left the claim refuses rather than retries.
limits.detail: The approval guard and the connection checks (authorization, active, supported type, token) run before the claim, and the writeOutcome and runTool handlers release it on their own payload and tool-name refusals, so those stay retryable. A transient provider error, a timeout, or a refusal raised elsewhere after the claim — a connection config that fails to parse, a connector’s own pre-request check, an mcp call that fails before reaching the server — leaves the claim, and the next attempt — a Temporal activity retry, or a node-level {retry} re-dispatch, which keeps the same dispatch key — fails non-retryably with OUTCOME_AMBIGUOUS, stopping the run; there is no way for a person to resolve a claim. Exactly-once is not claimed either: a new run for the same work is a new workflow id with an empty ledger.
limits.title: The write ledger refuses an uncertain retry instead of repeating it

limits.body: The run-start pin applies to GLOBAL lineage, not every scope.
limits.detail: fetchActiveAgent looks up active template/channel/team/org versions before applying the GLOBAL version clause. An explicit key@version is threaded through the same map, so it does not force a matching version at a more-specific scope. The runtime is the exception: the run pins it at start even when a scoped row supplied it.
limits.title: Scoped agent versions remain live

limits.body: Workspace setup executes repository-controlled shell commands and restores dependency artifacts, not a separately sandboxed or approved build recipe.
limits.detail: Saved definitions require platform ADMIN or owning-team admin membership; checked-in definitions follow repository write access instead. Setup selection is not a frozen content snapshot: the file comes from the recorded base/pin, while callers pass the repository's saved field when creating the workspace. Commands execute after the egress lock with the workspace user's permissions; normal steps run even after a cache restore. A definition error is non-retryable, whereas a failed shell step is retryable, so commands must tolerate activity retries. Cache keys segregate teams, repositories, definitions, key files, images and architectures, but a cache hit is not dependency verification. Caching requires non-PostgreSQL artifact storage and a positive size limit; it is optional, restores tar data into the workspace and falls back to executing the steps when cache operations fail. Unused entries are swept after the retention window. The file-proposal action only adds a missing setup file and never updates an existing one.
limits.title: Setup commands and caches inherit workspace trust

limits.body: Restricted and blocked repository workspaces have network locks; restricted ephemeral steps are locked to wired proxies before author code starts.
limits.detail: An explicitly open ephemeral step uses the private-range/metadata baseline, DNS filtering and host pins; direct public-IP traffic can bypass its cooperative proxy. Restricted is the default: baseline union team hosts are enforced through a verified IPv4/IPv6 default-deny holder lock before author startup, allowing only wired egress and registry proxy endpoints. Detached sidecars share that lock, with worker-gateway ingress and established replies for their published port. Blocked, or restricted with an empty effective baseline/team list, forces network none; sidecars are refused instead. Repository workspace locks also admit git and model proxies, unlike step locks. Allowlists are live, not frozen per run. Failed locks remove the workspace or step and holder. Policies govern container traffic, not worker-originated connector or MCP calls. The Docker policy broker constrains container options and ownership, but Docker still shares the host kernel and per-object limits are not aggregate host quotas.
limits.title: Workspace locks and step egress have different boundaries

limits.body: Kubernetes workspace locks depend on enforcing, correctly scoped NetworkPolicies; container-step sandboxes are not available and several Docker workspace controls do not apply.
limits.detail: Restricted/blocked locks add a pod-owned IP allow policy and switch the pod away from the namespace's broad egress policy. NetworkPolicies are additive: another matching broad policy can defeat narrowing. Each lock requires a public destination reachable before locking and two consecutive closed probes afterwards; no suitable baseline or probe tool fails closed. This is a sampled reachability check, not proof of every forbidden destination. DNS remains reachable through cluster DNS, leaving a low-bandwidth exfiltration channel. The separate boot probe covers metadata and the cluster API only and can be disabled; that does not disable per-workspace lock verification. Creating a per-pod policy requires NetworkPolicy create permission, which the boot RBAC check does not test. WORKSPACE_DNS, the Docker workspace network setting and metadata-block sidecar do not apply. Pods share the node kernel unless a runtime class such as gVisor or Kata is configured, and have no per-pod PID limit beyond the node's. Shell/container steps, sidecars and helpers fail non-retryably with WORKSPACE_BACKEND_UNSUPPORTED. Pod deletion is forced and not retried: a failed delete is logged, the hard lifetime is the fallback, and the orphan sweep later deletes a pod that has terminated or is still running ten minutes past its deadline (at most 25 per sweep). The worker's RBAC also controls pods, exec and Secrets; the boot check refuses a model, registry or egress proxy URL whose host is a loopback, unspecified or Docker-alias name, but does not test that its Service is reachable.
limits.title: The Kubernetes backend relies on the cluster’s NetworkPolicy and runs no container steps

limits.body: Secret delivery keeps values off the worker’s docker and kubectl command lines, not out of the workspace: git still receives the header on its own command line, a creation-time secret sits in the container’s environment, and the guard recognises only the names and value shapes it knows.
limits.detail: The shell inside the container expands ASW_GIT_AUTH into git’s own argument list, so a process there could read it from /proc; the agent workspace’s authenticated git calls first kill every stray process, but anything that records process arguments on the Docker host or Kubernetes node sees the header on each call. On Docker a creation-time secret such as the registry token is visible to docker inspect; on Kubernetes the per-pod Secret holds it base64-encoded, readable by anyone allowed to get secrets in the workspace namespace; on both it is in the container’s process environment by design. A Kubernetes worker refuses to start unless it may create and delete secrets in that namespace and list and watch pods, so upgrading one needs the matching role. The stdin preamble cannot carry an empty value or one with a line break. The pinned Claude Code settings file sits in the harness home, owned by the same user the agent’s commands run as. The guard refuses by name and by known value shapes only: a secret under an innocuous name or in an unrecognised form passes, and a value written into a script or argv rather than an env pair is not inspected; its name rule is a copy of the source-invariant rule, kept in step by hand.
limits.title: Secret delivery protects command lines, not the workspace itself

limits.body: Soft scores do not automatically stop a run, and aggregate score is not the authoritative gate result.
limits.detail: decideGate blocks hard floors. judgeAdvisory:false can enable a judge threshold. The workflow still chooses which eval nodes to include and how to branch on their outputs.
limits.title: Judge scores are advisory by default

limits.body: Each case’s flake-screen state is stored and counted, but no flake rate or judge/human kappa is computed against the configured ceilings.
limits.detail: The suite-health endpoint counts each dataset’s quarantined, screened, never-screened and failed-screen cases and returns the configured thresholds beside them; its stale rate has no history. A screen judges a case by its reference only, and cases whose screen kept being killed show as could-not-be-checked rather than flaky. A trend filtered to a template keeps results of runs of that template, so offline harness rows, which have no run, drop out.
limits.title: Suite health reports screen counts, not a flake rate

limits.body: A staging or monitoring signal reports work done elsewhere.
limits.detail: The graph waits and branches on flags, returning FAILED or TIMED_OUT when necessary. A rollback-required termination is not an actual rollback command.
limits.title: Release-gate templates do not perform deployments

limits.body: A Mastra Agent Run and a Mastra implementer turn debit per step and every harness turn (Claude Code or Pi) per model call; ordinary multi-step generate loops debit at completion.
limits.detail: A model call can overshoot a checked budget before returning, and a Mastra implementer turn runs its model loop ahead of the step hook that debits it, so a stop lands about one step late, and up to the turn’s remaining step budget when the debit is slow; steps that finish after the stop are still charged, without a check. A turn that throws after spending is still charged what it owed and leaves one trace row carrying its error. A harness turn re-checks the budget only after each call, so an exhausted budget stops it one call late. Through the worker’s model proxy every call, side calls included, is debited as its response ends, and a call cut off mid-stream is charged the input and output the provider had reported. Without the proxy a call is debited only once the next begins, calls the harness makes without streaming a message are charged when the turn ends and never trigger the check, and a turn stopped by its deadline, or whose process dies, is metered from its streamed messages, which miss those calls; a turn that ends at its turn cap is metered from the harness’s own totals. A harness turn that fails while its activity is cancelled reports the cancellation, and what that turn spent is not accrued. Workflows with no run have no ActiveWorkflow ledger; a per-execution token cap summed from their trace rows and this worker’s unpersisted calls bounds them instead. It cannot see calls still in flight on another worker, and a failed budget read lets the call through.
limits.title: Budget precision differs by execution path

limits.body: Launches and each later model call are refused once cached spend has reached the cap, so spend can still land after it is crossed, and some spend is outside it.
limits.detail: The guard runs before each budgeted model call and refuses only when the cached organization spend has already reached the cap.
