Up to one cache window of new calls from every run of the organization at once, plus the full cost of every call or harness turn already admitted, can land after the cap is crossed: an admitted call completes and bills in full, its cost accrues to the ledger only after it returns, and a Claude Code harness call accrues only once it ends. Concurrent launches see the same total. A spend or cap read that fails lets the call through. Spend with no derivable organization is outside the cap (a connection-free run of a global template launched by a person or through its webhook among it), and a repo-less channel task bills its channel, so the organization cap never refuses it. An epic’s planning is attributed to the first repository it names even when the epic spans organizations; each child is billed to its own repository’s. An unpriced model is refused when the run’s billed organization (the same billedOrgId rule as the cap, so a PRD run or a code-route channel task counts through its connection) has a cap, or when a runless workflow’s spend owner does, and under a channel cap; a repo-less channel task bills its channel, so it is not refused on the organization’s account. A team’s own cap is a separate check with the same shape (see the team cap boundary).
limits.title: The organization USD cap is checked before each call, so spend can overshoot it

limits.body: A run whose workflow ended without finalizing still counts as in flight until a sweep reaches it, and only while the sweep is enabled.
limits.detail: A run is looked up only after a ten-minute grace, and a sweep asks about a bounded batch, never-checked runs first, so a crowd of live runs cannot hold the batch. A failed Temporal lookup leaves the run alone, because a live run must never be billed. The schedule is set from the environment when the gateway starts and is paused when disabled, after which stranded runs count against the cap indefinitely. A run that closed long ago is ended silently, with no Slack notice, channel report or tracker update, so a first sweep over history does not post for old orphans. Reaped spend is billed to the month of finalization, so a run reaped late lands in the month it is reaped. A dashboard cancel of a run whose execution is gone leaves the run for the reaper to bill rather than ending it unbilled.
limits.title: The run reaper bounds unfinalized spend; it does not remove the window

limits.body: Team and organization breakdowns read the owner stamped on each trace row.
limits.detail: Rows older than the owner columns, spend with no derivable owner and rows written while the run lookup failed land under no team. The usage report has no per-repository breakdown (the delivery report’s repository slice sums run spend, not trace rows), and the platform-wide report is ADMIN-only. Spend is attributed to a person only when the trace came from the execution that wrote the run row (its Temporal run id matches), so a later execution of the same workflow id, and traces older than that id, count as unattributed. Rollup rows have no relations, so a day already rolled up keeps the spend of a team, run or user deleted afterwards.
limits.title: Usage is attributed when a trace is written

limits.body: Live report reads are capped at 10,000 rows per source, built days older than the rollup horizon come from daily rollups, the budget projection is a straight line, and the client CSV flattens nested values badly.
limits.detail: Each report’s row reads fetch one row past 10,000 and return a per-source flag beside an overall truncated flag, with two exceptions: quality’s step grouping has no row cap, and each organization’s budget top runs fetch six and keep five, flagging the sixth. Quality’s step counts are therefore an exact grouping, but only over the at most 10,000 newest cohort runs. Delivery’s live run read (which carries each run’s ledger rows nested, so they are bounded with it), its pull requests and its finished CI-fix steps, and quality’s live runs, pull requests, CI-fix steps and reviewer traces, are each cut at 10,000, so slices past it are partial; days read from the rollup table are not row-capped. The pending-approval count is of the at most 10,000 oldest pending steps. Budget top runs rank by each run’s own accrued cost without the ledger fallback and pass the caller’s report scope, so an organization ADMIN whose organization has org-wide reporting off sees only the runs in their own teams, repositories and launches, a partial top five beside the whole-organization spend. The projection assumes the rest of the month spends at the month-to-date daily rate. Delivery slices by template, repository and team. For each built day older than the rollup horizon, delivery and quality read the workflow_run_daily_rollups table (model WorkflowRunDailyRollup), so those days carry the figures the nightly sweep built, not a fresh read of the run table. Approvers are still grouped by resolving user id: each carries counts of interactive (web, Slack) and automated (API token, MCP, assistant) resolutions and the report counts every resolution by how it arrived, but nothing marks a user id as a person or a machine identity. The quality merge comparison counts runs with a pull request (merged if any of its pull requests merged), not the merged-over-resolved rate of pull-request outcomes. The Reports page’s CSV writes a nested value, such as CI-fix round statistics, severity counts, top categories or an automation outcome breakdown, as one JSON cell, not as separate columns. The report routes and the usage and analytics exports are not tagged for activity events, so unlike the pull-request outcomes export they write no export row.
limits.title: Reports are bounded reads over rollups and live rows

limits.body: A run’s workflow span appears only when its workflow code ends, an externally terminated run never exports one, and a signal is a link rather than a parent.
limits.detail: Each run has a workflow span, exported from a Temporal sink when its workflow code ends, so a long run (an approval wait included) has no span in a trace backend until it finishes and its activities sit under a parent the backend does not yet have. A run terminated or timed out from outside never runs workflow code, so no span is exported and its activities stay under a missing parent. A plain error thrown from workflow code fails the workflow task, which is retried, so it exports nothing until the run ends; RunnableWorkflow turns its own graph failures into a failed run, so those export a failed span. A final workflow task that Temporal rejects or retries exports the span again, with the same span id. A run cancelled while awaiting an activity is recorded as cancelled, not as an error. The span covers the run, not the idle time between activities. A signal or update context reaches only activities scheduled after it, and only the newest one is linked; work already running and earlier signals are not. The worker’s own signals are not stamped. Worker and gateway structured logs export over OTLP, and audit lines do only inside an activity; other plain console output stays on stdout. A tool call that fails input validation or names no tool never executes, so it is recorded from the step results with zero duration, and only when generation returned: if it throws, those calls are lost. HTTP instrumentation requires the --import preload, and the start scripts and Dockerfile commands silence one Node deprecation code only (DEP0205, the module register hook the OpenTelemetry loader still uses).
limits.title: Tracing and log export have deliberate gaps

limits.body: With the claude-code runtime and no model proxy, the harness receives the model key inside the container the agent controls; through the proxy it holds a token good only for its own turn’s model calls.
limits.detail: The key, or the proxy’s turn token, stays off command lines and every tool call passes the worker-side policy, but what the agent runs in that container can read it. The token spends only on the Messages API, against the run’s budget, at the credential’s own host, until the turn ends. The proxy’s upstream calls to that host are resolved, checked and pinned like other model calls; only the no-proxy path, where the container reaches the host directly, is outside that check (under an environment proxy the upstream call is checked but not pinned). The shipped compose files run the proxy (HARNESS_MODEL_PROXY_PORT); a deployment that sets no port hands the harness the key, except on the Kubernetes backend, where the worker refuses to start without the proxy and a URL pods can resolve. This applies to implementer-family sessions and to agent runs whose agent selects the Claude Code harness (Pi’s model calls and key stay in the worker); an agent run’s diff is still judged and published from a fresh container. The repository’s own CLAUDE.md, .claude settings and hooks load, but managed settings make the harness ignore the repository’s permission allow rules, so a tool call the policy does not approve is refused, and writes to .claude/, CLAUDE.md, CLAUDE.local.md and .mcp.json are refused. Only anthropic/<model> specs are supported; any other fails non-retryably with HARNESS_UNSUPPORTED_MODEL. A credential base URL can route through a gateway; used without the proxy, one with a path, query, fragment or userinfo is delivered as a secret and the pinned settings layer is staged as a file in the harness home instead of passed inline, so the URL stays off command lines.
limits.title: Without the model proxy, the Claude Code runtime puts a model key in the workspace

limits.body: An Idempotency-Key binds permanently to its first ticket, repository, description and budget tier.
limits.detail: Ledger rows are written before the Temporal start, so a same-key request during the start gets 409 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_IN_PROGRESS. A failed stamp after a successful start, or failed compensation after a failed start, leaves the key in progress until an operator repairs the rows. Keys are never swept. POST /work-requests replays a reused key. POST /agent-runs builds its workflow id from the repository, the caller and the key, so the same key from another caller or on another repository is a separate launch. Through the MCP server, a retry by the same user with the same key and inputs is answered with the original work request and one with other inputs is refused with 422 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_MISMATCH, and a bridged launch the per-user MCP run cap refuses gets the MCP run-cap refusal; a key the same caller reuses on the same repository outside MCP gets 409 RUN_CONFLICT.
limits.title: Work-request idempotency keys never expire

limits.body: This explorer is a source snapshot, not an operational test or security audit.
limits.detail: Routes, schemas, seed specs and tests establish implemented surfaces. No infrastructure, external credentials, LLM calls or full platform test suite were exercised for this analysis. Test presence is not a passing test result.
limits.title: Implementation is not live deployment proof

limits.body: Discovery lists ids from the keys the platform holds; it supplies no prices and judges retirement by what one key can see.
limits.detail: Discovery stores no price; price hints from a listing or the community price list only prefill a form or a bulk add the admin confirms, and can be stale or wrong (long-context and batch rates are not shown, a model the list keys under another provider name gets no hint, and each gateway replica caches its own copy). Only GLOBAL credentials are asked, so a model reachable through a team or organization key is not found. Listings follow a bounded number of pages and drop non-text models by a name filter; a listing past the cap, empty, or with a continuation it cannot follow is incomplete: it still records new suggestions but deletes nothing and flags no retirement candidates. A retirement flag is a hint measured against one key’s view, and an apiBase on a private address is refused as blocked address unless its host is listed in models.privateNetworkHosts. The list is matched against the apiBase host text. The fetch still resolves the name and connects only to an address it checked, but nothing verifies that a listed name points at the intended server, so a listed name may reach any private-range address it resolves to; loopback, link-local and metadata answers stay refused. A built-in provider behind an apiBase never yields retirement candidates, because its listing is the proxy’s, not the vendor’s. The list applies to every provider credential, and to run-time model and embedding calls too, not to one credential. The schedule’s cron and enabled flag take effect only after a gateway restart.
limits.title: Model discovery finds ids, not prices

limits.body: Connected means the first connection was made, not that Temporal is reachable now, and while it is pending workflow operations are refused.
limits.detail: The health body reports connecting until the first connection succeeds and connected afterwards; after that the SDK’s channel reconnects on its own and the gateway does not probe, so connected does not mean reachable at this moment. While the state is connecting no workflow start, signal, cancel or schedule operation can run, and nothing queues them: the caller gets a retryable refusal (usually 503). Per-channel and per-work-request schedules are not re-synchronized when the connection comes up, so a schedule that diverged while Temporal was down is corrected only by the next write to its row; the environment-driven system schedules are corrected at the next gateway start. Only the scheduled-work list reports an unknown state (exists: null, unavailable: true) instead of a missing schedule; other reads that need Temporal, including the status of the system schedule settings, answer 503. The shipped app Compose file still starts the gateway only after Temporal reports healthy, so the background connection protects other deployments and later outages, not a Compose start.
limits.title: Temporal health is the first connection, not live reachability

limits.body: The refresh agent reads untrusted pricing pages; the guards confine where it can write, not whether it can be wrong.
limits.detail: The workspace has network access and a shell. The path guard and checkScope keep the diff to the catalog file, the prompt treats fetched text as data, and a failed provider listing reaches the agent only as fixed words, but a hostile or misread page can still put a wrong price inside that file. The price-list rule is checked in code, but it proves only that a row differing from the community list carries a comment, it sees only rows it can parse, and it passes without checking when the list is off or unreadable. The runTests gate runs in warn mode, so a failing test is recorded and the run continues to a draft PR; CI on the draft is the hard check. A run that stops because the previous refresh is still open ends SUCCESS, so a stuck schedule looks green, and the guard trusts the git binary in the container.
limits.title: The catalog refresh contains untrusted input, not prevents it

limits.body: The pull request exists, ready for review, before any person has signed off; in consensus-review it also precedes every reviewer agent (four-eyes runs its agent review loop first).
limits.detail: four-eyes and consensus-review open a non-draft pull request and run CI before their gate, so opening it can notify Slack, sync trackers and request CODEOWNERS reviewers early, and a run that ends FAILED or TIMED_OUT leaves it open. Draft-producing library graphs include model-catalog-refresh, ci-triage-and-fix, docs-refresh and vulnerability-remediation; there is no step that marks a draft ready. A step that promised a draft fails non-retryably (EXISTING_PR_NOT_DRAFT) instead of updating a pull request that has since been marked ready; the branch push that precedes it has already happened, so the new commits can still show on that pull request. It also fails non-retryably on a repository that cannot hold drafts (DRAFT_PR_UNSUPPORTED). four-eyes, consensus-review and ci-triage-and-fix guard a no-op CI fix with retryIfUnchanged; the other repush templates can still wait out a CI signal that never comes. docs-refresh has no CI-fix loop.
limits.title: Gated templates open a ready PR before the gate

limits.body: The four-eyes graph requests two sequential approvals but does not enforce different users across those two steps.
limits.detail: The second sign-off asks for an independent reviewer in its description. Both nodes are separate single-approver steps: the resolver authorizes and records a response per step without comparing the previous gate's actor. Distinct approver counting applies within a multi-approver step, not automatically across sequential gates. Two parallel consensus branches likewise call the same review-network implementation; separate calls do not establish different model or reviewer identities.
limits.title: Two review gates do not prove independent reviewers

limits.body: A host has at most one PAT and at most one App, and a repository on a host with neither is reachable only with a user’s own token.
limits.detail: A repository on another host with no recorded credentials fails with REPO_CREDENTIAL_HOST_MISMATCH unless its launcher saved their own token; two Apps or per-organization PATs on one host are not expressible. A login records the account it was read from, and the takeover check verifies against that account. Only a login with no recorded source (written before it was recorded) held by a user with several linked GitHub accounts is unverifiable, so no takeover is detected for it until a sign-in records one; a non-github.com host with no credential gets none either (a github.com account with no applicable credential is asked unauthenticated, so the check is rate-limited). Installations are registered only by an admin: GitHub’s events can retire, reactivate or rename a registered one, never add one.
limits.title: Host credentials are one set per host

limits.body: Skill pinning covers runs that have a WorkflowRun row, and it is not a freeze of every skill input.
limits.detail: The channel assistant’s own conversational runs pin GLOBAL agent versions and skill revisions on the row they create, for the turn’s team and organization (taken from its Slack channel when the turn does not name them), and the run-pinned settings at the scope the turn reads them with: its template, its channel and that tenant. An epic’s children are runs of their own and pin at their own start. A skill with no entry in the map, such as one created after the run began, resolves its current revision. isActive is read live, within the config cache window. A missing pinned revision row falls back to the live text, with a warning in the log and, inside an activity, a skill.pinned_revision_missing trace event, which is the swap pinning exists to prevent. A repo-less channel task finds its tenant by Slack channel id, which is unique only per workspace.
limits.title: Skill revision pins have gaps

limits.body: Grouping attempts by request reads every matching execution identity before status filtering and paging.
limits.detail: The cost therefore grows with history. A request appears once its first execution row is recorded. A retry amends only the attempt description (and the payload description when one exists), so a custom workflow that reads another input field does not see the added instructions.
limits.title: The request list groups before it paginates

limits.body: Pinning to a commit fixes what is read; it does not vouch for the author, the files kept beside the text, or the host.
limits.detail: Reference files are stored unscanned, so whatever first reads them to an agent or a person must scan them first. The host check reads address text and literal addresses, and a fetch resolves and pins the host it connects to, so a listed name is trusted to mean the intended server only as far as that resolution allows. Commit signatures are not checked. The scheduled check asks about the ref, not the history of the source’s path, so any commit on the ref flags the source, and in a monorepo an unrelated commit reads as an update whose diff shows nothing. A diff and an accept each read the whole new commit through the bounded fetch, so reviewing then accepting costs two budgeted fetches beside the check’s one request. An accept updates only skills already installed: a skill added upstream is listed, and can be installed only once an accept has moved the pin (an install reads the pinned commit), one removed upstream is flagged and stays, and an upstream rename is shown and not applied. Reference files from an accept are stored unscanned, like an import’s. There is no way to decline a change, so a skill left behind keeps the source flagged. An install into a source reads only the pinned commit and an accept moves the pin only when nothing changed upstream is left behind, so a hand-edited or unparseable skill that is never accepted keeps the source flagged and keeps skills added upstream uninstallable. Hand-edit detection compares content with the last revision an import or accept cut, so a revert to the same content reads as unedited. The review is an ADMIN flow in the dashboard, the API and the CLI. Each full-text read the dashboard makes costs one more budgeted fetch of the whole source. Only imports (a first import or an install into an existing source) take the name-allocation lock, so the skill API can still create a name an import has just checked.
limits.title: Skill import is pinned and bounded, not verified

limits.body: The guard checks URL text early and resolves and pins at connection time, but its opt-in is per connector rather than per address.
limits.detail: The text check alone does not resolve a name, so the dispatcher resolves it at connection time, refuses the request if any answer is internal and connects only to a checked address; a name that cannot be resolved is refused. The opt-in applies to the connector as a whole, so with it on every other private address is reachable from that connector, not just the one service the admin meant. The save-time check covers the stored configuration only; environment-variable fallbacks are checked when a guarded connector runs or Jira field detection is called, so a refused one surfaces at that point. A base URL that points at loopback is refused with or without the opt-in. GitHub Issues follows a redirect to another origin only if that origin passes the strict guard, so a private-network server that redirects to a different private origin is refused. The hop cap and the header allowlist are fixed in code. An MCP connection’s opt-in is per connection and applies only to that connection’s own origin: with it on, its URL may name or resolve to a private-range address, while redirects to other origins stay strict. Where the pin itself stops is in the resolve-and-pin coverage card.
limits.title: The connector SSRF guard resolves and pins, and the opt-in is coarse

limits.body: The pin covers the call sites that use the guarded fetch; a proxy, a Claude Code harness run without the model proxy, and the GitHub API clients sit outside it.
limits.detail: With a process-wide environment proxy (NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY, or --use-env-proxy on the command line or in NODE_OPTIONS) the host is resolved and checked locally first, but the proxy resolves it again, so the connection is not pinned to the checked answer; a network that resolves names only through its proxy fails closed. The worker’s chat and embedding clients and the Claude Code model proxy’s upstream calls take the same guard (modelCallFetch), so a public apiBase name that resolves to a private address is refused on an agent’s model call as well as on the credential test. A Claude Code harness run without the model proxy calls the credential’s host from inside the workspace container, outside the worker and outside that guard. Octokit and GitHub Enterprise API calls, the GitHub connection test against the saved API URL (a GitHub Enterprise host is often private), the sign-in organization-membership check that auto-approves a GitHub sign-up (it sends the platform credential to the instance’s API URL and follows no redirect), and the sign-in library’s Okta discovery fetch use a plain fetch; fixed public hosts such as Slack, Linear, Notion and Figma are not pinned either. For a repository on a GitHub Enterprise host every hop of the CI-log download may reach a private address, so a redirect from that host can aim the worker at another internal service (without the token). 198.18.0.0/15 is treated as private, so behind a fake-IP proxy tool every connector needs its opt-in, and provider probes, model discovery, the catalog refresh and the model and embedding calls need the host listed in models.privateNetworkHosts, and bundle URLs, which have no opt-in, are refused. The bare-fetch invariant is a text tripwire over a fixed module list and does not see an aliased fetch or another HTTP client.
limits.title: Resolve-and-pin covers listed call sites, not every outbound request

limits.body: A team marked inactive keeps its members’ repository access and its shares, even though its role-based authority stops.
limits.detail: Team membership predicates read membership rows only and ignore Team.isActive, so members of a deactivated team still reach its repositories and a shared team keeps its shares; removing a share is what ends a shared team’s access. What the team loses is authority: for a non-read capability neither its team roles nor its organization’s roles confer anything while it is inactive (platform ADMIN is not stopped), and the refusal says the team is deactivated only to someone with standing in the team or its organization. A join request to it is refused as inactive, and the directory lists active teams only.
limits.title: Deactivating a team does not remove repository access

limits.body: A pull-request webhook updates a row; of those events only a merge reaches the workflow, and only a delivered webhook updates anything.
limits.detail: Only pull requests that a workflow’s pull-request step or an Agent Run’s draft delivery opens get a row. CLOSED and MERGED come only from signed pull_request webhooks, so without delivery (polling-only CI, a lost delivery) the row stays OPEN, and the list and the PR_CLOSED_BY_REVIEWER refusal both depend on delivery. An Agent Run’s own execution has ended by the time its pull request merges, so a merge is recorded without a signal, and its generated ticket id is never synced to the tracker. If an older row still holds the pull request’s number in that repository, the new row is not written. A run waiting on its merge keeps waiting after its pull request is closed unmerged, until a merge arrives or the wait ends; the refusal appears only when a later push step reaches the pull-request activity. A webhook for a pull request the platform did not open finds no row and changes nothing. Reopening restores only CLOSED to OPEN, and event times come from the host’s payload when it parses, else the time of receipt. The ticket list shows the tracker’s title, status and link as captured when a request was submitted, from the newest visible request that holds an answer; they are not refreshed. RunInput.ticketIsSynthetic marks an id the platform generated: the template launch and template webhook fallbacks, PRD runs (PRD-… ids), scheduled work requests (…-SCHED-… ids), event-automation runs (ci-<run>-<attempt> for a failed Actions run, issue-<number>-<hash> for a labelled issue, prlabel-<number>-<hash> for a labelled pull request, push-<first 8 hex characters of the sha> for a push, evt-<digest> for an inbound event) and PRD stories the tracker gave no id; it defaults to false, so a user- or tracker-supplied id is never flagged. Agent runs and channel tasks are flagged and also recognised by template origin, template name or channel id; the channel assistant files no request of its own. An adopted pull request is re-linked only when the executing workflow has a ledger row of its own; without one it stays linked to its earlier execution, whose workflow receives the CI signal, and the close check does not cover it. Adoption matches by request and repository only and no head branch is stored, so after a branch prefix change or a missed close webhook the adopted pull request can have a different head branch than the one pushed. A retry is refused while a live ledger row of its request exists, a scheduled fire’s or a template-launched run’s included, and a fire is skipped while a live non-fire row does; each row is confirmed with Temporal before it blocks (the allocator’s own conflict row included), and each check reads the ledger and then acts, so a retry and a fire that both read before either writes its row can still push the same branch, and the later one to reach the pull-request step adopts and re-links the other’s pull request, so the other waits for a CI signal that now goes to the adopter until its wait ends.
limits.title: Pull-request tracking records the host’s state; it does not steer the run

limits.body: A modal has no private reply channel, so some Slack confirmations are public in the thread.
limits.detail: An approve or reject button always opens the modal, so every approval is answered by a modal submission, which carries no response_url. The note that a multi-approver step still needs approvals is therefore always posted publicly in the announcement’s thread, the thread known only from the click that opened the modal, where a one-click answer would have got a private reply. A failed post is dropped silently and not retried; the decision itself is already recorded. The message edit that shows the decision applies only to the message the worker recorded.
limits.title: Slack modal approvals confirm in the thread, not privately

limits.body: Agents a run’s start snapshot lacks are pinned at first use, so an edit made before then reaches the run.
limits.detail: An agent created after the run started, and an agent run’s agent (resolved in a narrower scope than the run’s), are pinned where first resolved; an agent whose inheritsModelFrom chain was broken at start is left out of the snapshot and fails where it is used. The save-time model check follows the platform-wide inheritsModelFrom chain only; a scoped override of the parent, or a parent edited later, fails with HARNESS_UNSUPPORTED_MODEL when a run resolves it. A new override starts on the platform-wide row’s runtime, but a later change to that row’s runtime does not reach existing overrides.
limits.title: Some runtimes pin at first use, not at run start

limits.body: Scheduled regression runs pass no runtime override, and a runtime breakdown sees only offline harness rows.
limits.detail: The scheduled eval prepares its run from a dataset slug and two refs only, so the nightly gate uses each agent’s resolved runtime. Online result rows carry no runtime, the runtime column holds the candidate’s runtime only, and a template-filtered trend excludes harness rows, so a runtime split there has no runtime values.
limits.title: Runtime comparisons cover manual eval runs and harness rows only

limits.body: The binary is hashed by sha256sum inside the workspace, which the agent can modify.
limits.detail: The check catches a replaced or damaged copy between turns, but it relies on the container’s sha256sum, which the agent can write. It runs before each turn, not during one, and needs sha256sum in the image. Pi installs no binary in the container, so it has none to check.
limits.title: The harness binary check trusts the container’s sha256sum

limits.body: A harness is admitted only if the worker answers each of its tool calls before the call runs.
limits.detail: A harness must ask the worker before every tool call over a channel the worker owns, wait for the answer, not run a refused call, and offer no repository or container file that can grant a call without that answer. The registry refuses any harness that does not declare this, with HARNESS_POLICY_UNENFORCEABLE. Pi meets it by running its loop in the worker, not as a CLI in the container, where a repository setting could prefix every approved shell command. A harness supplies only provisioning (none for Pi), a mapping of its tools onto the canonical vocabulary, usage normalisation and the turn protocol; binary verification, process cleanup, cancellation, the decision deadline and trace bounding are shared. Harness profiles are consumed only by the Claude Code runtime.
limits.title: Claude Code and Pi are the only harnesses the worker admits

limits.body: Memory gate refusals and recall drops are security events, but a drop is reported at most hourly per row and per process, and the gate matches patterns, not intent.
limits.detail: Lesson, consolidation and channel writes refused for a match are MEMORY_WRITE_REFUSED events and dropped recalled items MEMORY_RECALL_DROPPED, carrying ids and pattern names, never the text. A drop is reported once per memory id per hour per worker process, written in the background so recall does not wait; a drop of another team’s channel row records only a count. An event raised outside an activity, or whose trace write fails, is only logged, and a write refused because an INJECTION pattern overran or is quarantined is traced as an outage (memory.write_scan_unavailable), not a refusal. A consolidation whose scan failed, did not complete or could not load is traced the same way (memory.consolidation_scan_unavailable). These outage events are ordinary activity events in the run’s trace; the security-events view lists and counts only matches and recall drops, so a pattern outage that is stopping memory writes appears in no security count. A write whose pattern set could not load is thrown (commitToMemory) or logged, not traced. On such a load failure recall returns nothing. The fence labels memory as reference data; it does not stop a reworded instruction that no INJECTION pattern matches.
limits.title: Memory refusals are pattern-based, drop reports are throttled, and a scan outage is not a security event

limits.body: The saver passes a launch decision when an enabled automation is saved or enabled; when it fires, nothing re-checks the saver.
limits.detail: A fire checks the repository, the kill switch, the organization’s monthly budget, the limits and the connections its options declare (with the owning team’s reach), not the saver’s continued access or role. The run carries no launchedById and uses the platform credential. Person-triggered sources check the event actor rather than the saver: for an issue label or a pull-request label the person who added it, for a push the person who pushed, and for pull-request feedback the reviewer or commenter behind a changes-requested review or a fix command, must be an active platform user whose linked GitHub account matches, a member of the repository, and pass the launch decision at that moment; that user is recorded as requestedById and the run still acts as the platform. Qodo-triggered feedback and PR review-findings fixes have no human trigger actor, so they do not perform that requester check. A review-findings fix instead binds to the successful blocking review's database output and unchanged PR head. For labels the check matters because an issue form adds labels on behalf of whoever opens the issue, so the label alone says nothing about who asked.
limits.title: An automation runs as the platform, not as the person who saved it

limits.body: Nothing polls GitHub for a failure, a label, a push or a review the platform was not told about; only Jira filter automations poll their host.
limits.detail: The engine retries a start three times (after one and two seconds) and then answers 503, so a host that redelivers recovers; one that does not leaves a FAILED_TO_START decision for a manager to retry. A Jira poll whose start fails leaves the issue unseen, so the next poll decides it again. Turning a kill switch off stops later decisions; it does not stop runs already started.
limits.title: GitHub automation decisions rest on the webhook; a missed delivery is not recovered

limits.body: A poll sees what the JQL returns at that moment, through the platform’s one Jira credential; the project allowlist, not the automation’s owner, bounds which issues may start runs.
limits.detail: An occurrence waits for the next poll, and a status a ticket enters and leaves between two polls is never seen. Only Jira is polled, with one JQL and one repository per automation. Anyone who can write in an allowed Jira project writes the text a run starts from: it is marked as data in the run description, not filtered. The self-trigger guard is a rule over three status names, not a view of who moved the ticket: a person’s move into In Progress, In Review or Done on a ticket that has any run is suppressed too, and a Jira workflow whose statuses are named differently is not recognised. AutomationSeenIssue rows are never pruned (one per issue, or per issue and status) and go only with their automation. A filter matching more than 1,000 issues does not poll at all. A poll abandoned at its deadline keeps running and holds its lease until it ends or the lease expires. Turning the kill switch off stops later polls, not runs already started.
limits.title: Jira polling is periodic, Jira-only and platform-credentialed

limits.body: The template has no human node and no review network; the fix is reviewed only as part of the pull request it lands on.
limits.detail: Before the push a fix must pass the implementer’s path guard (workflow and action files, symlinks and submodules refused), the implementer’s security gate, the push step’s own checks and its own workflow-path check on the pushed range. Lint, typecheck and tests run too, but their failures are warnings and do not stop delivery. Verification labels the fix but does not gate it. The push step re-checks workflow paths only, not symlinks; that refusal lives in the implementer’s guard. Draft fixes are revised up to maxCiFixAttempts, while a pushed fix gets at most one follow-up.
limits.title: A pushed CI fix has no approval step

limits.body: A log that evades the INJECTION patterns reaches the implementer fenced as data, with the path guard behind it.
limits.detail: Redaction covers common token shapes only. The screen uses INJECTION patterns only, and the template-injection pattern is excluded because ordinary build output matches it. With more than ten failed jobs, the implementer’s per-job excerpt (4,000 characters) is longer than the share of the screened tail each job got, so part of it was never screened. A scan that cannot complete counts as not clean, so such a log is diagnosed but never fixed from.
limits.title: CI log screening is pattern-based

limits.body: Only the whole run: of a failed step without Actions expressions is run, and nothing is installed first.
limits.detail: Setup-dependent failures read as unverified or still failing; a command that passes before the fix reads as not reproduced. The workflow file is read from the failing branch’s tip in the workspace, not from the failing commit.
limits.title: Verification runs only a whole failed step’s command

limits.body: A changed built-in input schema reaches an existing deployment only if its stored schema equals one recorded in the previous-schemas map.
limits.detail: Sync moves a built-in template’s input schema only while the template is active on its latest built-in version, runs no A/B experiment, and stores a schema an earlier release shipped; anything else is treated as an admin edit and kept. A built-in schema change not added to that map reaches fresh databases only. ci-triage-and-fix has no entry in the map.
limits.title: Built-in input schemas move forward only from a schema a release shipped

limits.body: A denial with no identified person is a metric, and a read off the allowlist is not recorded at all.
limits.detail: The activity table cannot say who attempted a request that failed authentication or that a service token was refused, only how often and on which route template. Sensitive reads are recorded only for routes tagged for activity, so a new read or export stays unrecorded until its route is tagged, and repeated reads collapse to one row per window, so the table shows that a read happened, not how often. The queue, dedupe memory, per-person rate budget and drop counter live in each gateway process, so events still queued when a process is killed are lost, the budgets and bounds apply per replica, and the dashboard shows the drop count of whichever replica answered. Page views are opt-in, invisible for a browser that sends Do Not Track or Global Privacy Control, batched on a timer so the last few seconds before a tab closes are lost, and a browser told they are off stays quiet until it reloads or another person signs in.
limits.title: User-activity events are bounded and partly opt-in

limits.body: A failed transcript write or access-log write never stops the activity or the read, so a transcript or an access record can be missing.
limits.detail: A write failure when a transcript is created, a part is stored or the transcript closes is logged, counted by stage and left as a transcript.persist_failed trace event, and the activity carries on. Close waits a bounded time for responses still streaming and for its own write, then returns with the write continuing in the background, so records that arrive later are lost to that transcript. A failed access-log insert or outcome update is logged and counted by action while the read or export goes ahead, a row left started is marked aborted by the sweep after an hour, and a refusal by an unidentified caller writes no row. The bundled observability container receives alert rules on those two failure counters but no contact point, so an alert shows only inside Grafana until an operator adds one, and a deployment that does not run that container gets no rules. Redaction removes secret values the redactor recognises; everything else is kept in full, and PII is scrubbed only when a reader asks for it.
limits.title: Transcripts and their access log fail open

limits.body: STARTED rows and rows naming something the platform produced are kept for good.
limits.detail: Event-automation rows that started a run grow at most by each automation’s daily cap; every schedule fire or template webhook call that started a run adds one permanent row, with no cap. The sweep deletes the rest in batches of 2,000, up to 50 batches a run, and continues the next day; it covers every source, so old schedule and webhook refusals go with the event suppressions.
limits.title: Started decisions are never pruned

limits.body: The coverage model never decrypts a key or calls a provider, and the dashboard’s delete sends force.
limits.detail: A revoked or wrong key reads as covered. The worker’s boot gate resolves each GLOBAL agent for real and checks the embedding model’s rows only, so the two implementations of one rule can disagree on an edge (the coverage check also requires an apiBase on any non-built-in provider’s credential, agent or embedding, which the boot gate does not check). A channel or workflow-template agent counts any credential for its provider. The delete guard protects API callers: the dashboard’s delete confirmation lists what the delete would strand and then sends force=true, and a forced delete by a team admin audits only the dependents that admin may see. The per-provider flag on the readiness route is derived from the same rows, so it inherits that blindness and also follows the embedding rule above: an embedding fault that is not a missing credential or an unpinned apiBase never marks a provider, so an agent on that provider shows no badge for it.
limits.title: Coverage checks rows, not keys, and the dashboard always forces

limits.body: A model or embedding call to a host that resolves to a private address fails unless the host is listed, and so does a provider that answers with a redirect.
limits.detail: A host that resolved publicly when a credential was saved and privately later is caught now, but an admin must list a legitimate internal host. A listed name is trusted to mean the server intended: any private-range address it resolves to is reachable, and only loopback, link-local and metadata addresses stay refused. The list is global to every credential, and under an environment proxy the check is not pinned.
limits.title: Guarded model calls fail closed for in-cluster and redirecting providers

limits.body: Custom providers get the response schema as prompt text, which a model can ignore.
limits.detail: Compatible embedding endpoints without truncation support only work at a native 1536 width. Pricing keys off the canonical provider/model spec text, so a model reached through a proxy is priced by the spec, not by what the proxy actually serves.
limits.title: Provider differences are bridged, not erased

limits.body: When the poll on the pushed commit times out or loses access, the run ends SUCCESS “Fix pushed” with no CI verdict.
limits.detail: The watch step continues on error, so a poll deadline or a failed fetch takes the same path as a pass: the work branch is removed and the run ends as pushed. The commit’s later failure is still recognised as the platform’s own output and not acted on again, so nobody is told it failed unless someone reads the pull request’s checks.
limits.title: A pushed fix’s CI watch that cannot finish still ends the run as pushed

limits.body: The model guard is passed as fetch to each client the worker builds; a client built another way would not have it.
limits.detail: The worker re-exports the raw provider constructors, and the bare-fetch invariant is a text tripwire that does not see an SDK constructor called without a fetch option. A new client added outside the two model-building modules would call its host unchecked until someone passes the guard to it.
limits.title: Nothing enforces the guard on a new provider client

limits.body: Glossary definitions, node help and inline help are static prose; tests check that their doc links resolve and that examples parse, not that the sentences are true.
limits.detail: The glossary says its definitions are written to agree with the concepts doc, and the link table says a test checks each entry against the docs files and headings. Neither derives a definition from the code, so a behaviour change can leave a tip stale while every link still resolves. Node help, the tour steps and the run verdict sentences are hand-written constants too; tests parse each node example with the real schema, check that every output path in a node’s Output line appears in its section of the node reference, hold the starter specs to zero validation warnings, assert a few of the node gotchas and check that every tour anchor exists in the sidebar, but most sentences are not checked against behaviour. The reader and its search show the docs shipped with the web app, so a running deployment can show docs older than its gateway, and both cover only the top-level docs, so a link to or a search for anything else would not resolve. The standing warnings on the admin pages are likewise fixed text that nothing keeps in step with the behaviour it describes. Tips, the checklist, the tour, node help and the verdict are shown in the dashboard only; the CLI and API have no equivalent. The page tours the Help panel offers on the run page and in the workflow editor are hand-written too; a test checks that each anchor appears in the owning page’s source, not that a sentence is true. One verified drift: the product tour’s first step says the sidebar is grouped into Work, Teams, Build, Connect, Knowledge and Admin, while the sidebar’s own labels are Home, All teams, Teams and insights, Build, Connect, Knowledge and Admin.
limits.title: Help text is hand-written and only its links and examples are checked

limits.body: The dashboard asks before a risky save and before leaving unsaved edits; a call to the API or the CLI does not pass through those prompts.
limits.detail: Saving Auto for an external or mass communication risk class, creating a broad configuration grant (a pattern covering every setting, or a whole role at global scope) and leaving a form with unsaved edits each open a confirmation in the browser, and so do other destructive or trust-widening actions on admin pages. They are page behaviour: the policy and grant routes take the same request without any confirmation field, and what the gateway enforces is its role, scope and visibility checks. Unsaved-change protection covers only the forms that use the guard, and depends on the browser’s own leave-page dialog for a reload, a closed tab or a typed address, on a confirmation when an in-app link is clicked and on one before the command palette navigates; the browser Back button leaves without asking.
limits.title: Dashboard confirmations are prompts, not server-side controls

limits.body: A command written into a gate step, a runQualityGates gate or an eval gate scorer runs in the agent workspace with network access; the role and the audit row are its only controls.
limits.detail: Unlike container code it takes no image allowlist and no network policy. Coverage at sign-off is matched by node, image and command, and rows of active and draft templates are never pruned (only old rows of archived templates are, by an admin’s request), so a version needs the role again only when no row covers its code, such as an older built-in version the built-in sync did not record; the table grows with the versions that carry code. A gate command is checked when it is saved or moved, not when a run starts, so a stored command stays in use after the admin who set it loses the role. A repository’s gate commands reach every run on it that sets no command of its own.
limits.title: Authored gate and eval commands are gated, not sandboxed

limits.body: A detected stack picks gate and test commands for one target directory and, where the deployer configured one, that stack’s workspace image; a layout that does not resolve to one place, or a stack with no image set, falls back.
limits.detail: A repository’s workspace image is its executor image (only a platform ADMIN may set one), else the deployer’s WORKSPACE_IMAGE_PYTHON, WORKSPACE_IMAGE_JVM or WORKSPACE_IMAGE_GO for its target’s stack, else WORKSPACE_IMAGE (node:24-alpine unless set). Detection records a suggested Dockerfile but builds no image, so a Python, JVM or Go repository on a deployment with no image for its stack gets its stack’s commands with no toolchain to run them: its gates fail, and the TDD loop stops at the first test run that cannot find the runner. A run does not pin its detection: each activity reads the repository’s stored detection when it runs, so a scheduled scan that lands mid-run can move later steps to another image or directory. The target is the root whenever it has a stack signal, so a polyglot root is served as its Node side only; otherwise one directory is chosen only when it is the only signalled one in a complete listing, so a repository whose real build is a root file detection does not read (a Makefile, say) beside one nested package.json is targeted at that directory. Several signalled directories and no root signal leave every stack-default gate unconfigured and the workspace on the default image, and a truncated listing (the provider’s tree, or more than 50 signalled directories) with no root signal keeps the built-in yarn commands. A Node component’s manager comes from its lockfile names alone. A Python target has no default lint, typecheck or build, Yarn Classic no default vulnerability scan, and the package-registry proxy serves npm only, so another ecosystem’s private registry is not fronted. Eval cases pick their own pinned image from the stack they name.
limits.title: Multi-stack support resolves one target and only deployer-configured images

limits.body: The pin authorizes what the payload declares, so every launch path must decide those connections itself; a literal mcp reference is in no pin.
limits.detail: A launch path that forgot to decide a declared connection would widen the pin rather than fail. A run created before the pin existed, or a channel-assistant run (its row is written without one), is let through with a logged warning. An Agent’s bound MCP connection (Agent.mcpConnectionId) is not in the pin: each use checks that the run’s team owns it (a run with no team, that its template’s own team does), and otherwise the agent runs without it, its token never read, with a warning and an mcp.binding_refused trace event; the connection’s URL and token are read live, not pinned. A literal mcp connection is judged against the run template’s current team, so reassigning a template mid-run moves that authority. A scheduled work request declares no payload connections; its repository is re-decided on every fire.
limits.title: The connection pin is derived from the payload

limits.body: Unreviewed learnings are readable locally before anyone reviews them, and human-curated items are not scanned when written.
limits.detail: A learning is scanned on write and every item on workflow recall, with INJECTION patterns only; passing is not proof the text is benign, and recalled knowledge is labelled untrusted rather than filtered further. Publication stops at the owning organization. The knowledge tools are bound only to the Mastra implementer by explicit toolKeys, and the retrieveKnowledge and captureLearning steps are used by no built-in template.
limits.title: Knowledge review governs publication, not content

limits.body: The ticket reaches agents as a bounded, framed block, not a scanned one, and only Jira adds comments and a parent.
limits.detail: Ticket text is written by people other than the operator. The block is cut to fixed lengths, carries no raw provider payload, sits inside a delimiter its own text cannot close and is framed as requirements, but the injection scanners do not cover it. Only the ticket’s own fields, its parent issue and its newest comments reach the agents: linked knowledge-base pages and attachments do not, and other trackers ignore the comment and parent options. The ticket is stored at submission or on first fetch, and the gather step re-reads it once to add comments and the parent; an edit after that is not seen by the run. With the fallback setting off, a template without the gather step gets no ticket in its prompts; an empty gather normally leaves no ticket. A narrow exception lets validation re-read after an explicitly empty gather block for a thin unstructured request: unauthorized or forbidden credentials then stop validation without a model call, while a readable ticket feeds that validation. This does not rewrite the gatherer's original output; a later not-actionable result can still display its earlier unavailable reason. On the GitHub Issues tracker a ticket in another repository than the ones the run targets is never fetched, so it gives the agents nothing.
limits.title: The tracker ticket is framed and bounded, not scanned

limits.body: A service principal’s repository grant is decided when it is added; a callback signature proves the platform sent it, not who launched the run.
limits.detail: Adding a repository to a principal’s allowlist is a launch decision by the lead who adds it; later launches re-check only that the principal’s team still reaches it. A principal’s runs use the platform credential. Any member of a team may name its callback endpoints, so someone in two teams can make one team’s run report to the other’s endpoint, and receivers should check launchedBy and treat context as theirs only if they issued it. Callbacks are at least once, so receivers deduplicate by delivery id, and under an environment proxy their connection is not pinned. Inbound event text is the sender’s, and the guards count decisions per endpoint.
limits.title: Machine callers are bounded by grants and signatures, not identities

limits.body: An unsigned call is accepted unless the template or policy requires signing, and the URL token still names the template.
limits.detail: There is no IP allowlist. A sender that retries must resend the same timestamp and body to land on the same run. An optional signature on a template with no secret is ignored.
limits.title: Template webhook signing is opt-in

limits.body: Docs answers come from the docs the worker image shipped, clipped per section; the inventory covers built-in templates only.
limits.detail: A team’s own templates are not in workflowInventory. A section longer than the clip is cut, keeping matching table rows only when tables make up most of it. The confirmation path exists in the gateway but no assistant tool proposes a write. A reply that failed before its turn wrote any trace row, or before replies were tagged, has no tagged rows, and the failures view falls back to rows matched by time.
limits.title: The in-app assistant answers from shipped docs and built-in content

limits.body: Pi’s extensions, skills, prompt templates and settings are not loaded, files are read as text, and the context budget is a character estimate.
limits.detail: Compaction never makes a model call; it estimates three characters per token and can only drop whole exchanges to fit a reasoning-heavy history, and the newest exchange is sent whole if nothing else fits. grep honours .gitignore only when the image has ripgrep, and find honours no ignore file. The reasoning gate copies logic from the provider adapters, so an adapter upgrade could disagree with it.
limits.title: Pi loads none of its own extension systems, and compaction is an estimate

limits.body: Private-channel access follows the last Slack sync, and the sync only ever tightens a channel’s privacy.
limits.detail: Someone removed from a private channel keeps its dashboard content until the next sync replaces the member list, or until the list ages past the staleness window when the sync keeps failing; someone added waits for the next sync. Access follows the linked User.slackId, so an account linked to the wrong Slack user sees that user’s private channels. Without the sync a channel converted to private in Slack keeps its old flag until an admin changes it, and with it a channel made public in Slack stays private here, because the sync never turns the flag off. A channel with more than 10,000 members is never synced, so its content stays admin-only.
limits.title: Private-channel access lags Slack by a sync, and privacy is only tightened

limits.body: Qodo's text is screened and fenced, not verified, and a Qodo-triggered round trusts no person.
limits.detail: A finding is derived from the diff Qodo read, so anyone who can push to the pull request's branch can influence it. The INJECTION screen is a pattern tripwire applied string by string, so a phrase split across two fields is not matched, and fencing marks the text as data without making it safe. The containment that remains is the unchanged push gate: a default or protected branch, a non-fast-forward push, and changes to workflow files are refused. A Qodo-triggered round has no requester, so the engine makes no per-actor access decision and no human-author gate applies to its findings; the organization budget is still checked. The run's trace records the screened result the agent receives, so a string the screen withheld is not stored. A review that Qodo has not finished by the end of the wait spends that head's one decision, and so does a run that opened the pull request and is still waiting on CI after the 15-minute cap on the round's wait for it. Reading a review needs Qodo's pull request bot installed on the repository, and the platform cannot ask Qodo to start one. The read list uses the names of Qodo's CLI catalog; a server that advertises them differently binds nothing, which the connection test reports.
limits.title: Qodo findings are screened and fenced, not verified, and the Qodo path trusts no person

limits.body: Delegation follows a run by polling, reports a coarse outcome, and leaves every human step and merge to a person.
limits.detail: wait_for_run samples status every three seconds, so a transition between two polls is not seen, and each poll makes up to three inner gateway reads; given a work request id it follows that request’s newest run. The outcome get_run returns is what the run recorded: a branch or diff stat that is not in the run’s result is null, the failure type is UNKNOWN for any prefix outside the fixed list, and step errors, inputs and traces are left to the dashboard link. With deliver none there is no branch to fetch. No MCP tool approves, rejects or answers a human step or merges: wait_for_run only hands back the step and an approvals-page link. The MCP run cap’s lock is taken only by bridged launches, so a dashboard or CLI launch at the same instant can take the user past the cap, and the burst limit is counted per gateway process. The delivery-mode check runs before the replay, so a retry of a launch whose mode an admin has since removed is refused rather than replayed; and a key the same caller reuses on the same repository outside MCP gets 409 RUN_CONFLICT, not a replay. The MCP bridge refuses a personal access token, so a client needs an interactive OAuth sign-in. The Claude Code and Codex packaging is configuration only: its root test checks the tool names it mentions, not that a given client can reach or authenticate against a deployment.
limits.title: Delegated runs are followed by polling and stop at human steps

limits.body: A repository without a preview recipe skips the check successfully, and what is not configured is not exercised: the built-in smoke pass covers paths, one optional selector, console/page errors and 5xx responses, not interactions or assertions, which is what the e2e command is for.
limits.detail: Workspace agent nodes can bind browser tools on Mastra, Claude Code or Pi when their Agent grants browser; a node without a workspace has no checkout browser toolset. Evidence over uiValidation.maxScreenshotBytes or maxVideoBytes, or past maxEvidencePerRun, is dropped and reported in the step's notes instead of failing the gate, and kept for uiValidation.evidenceRetentionDays. Inline PR screenshots need an S3-compatible public bucket even when artifacts live on the filesystem store, and the browser image is not one of the published executor images. The step runs in the repository's configured executor image, so an image without Playwright and Chromium fails the check rather than skipping it. Injection screening of what the agent browser returns covers its text (the page snapshot and tool output); nothing in this code inspects the pixels of a screenshot image sent to the model.
limits.title: Browser verification is opt-in and bounded

limits.body: The class reads paths, sizes and patches the host returned, a bad merge is recognised only from a revert’s default wording, and the withdrawal sweeps stop at a cap.
limits.detail: Rules are path-glob and text matching: a test skip is a pattern over added lines, a patch that is missing or too large to scan is an exclusion rather than a pass, and nothing reads what the code means. A review result counts only for the head it names, so a push after the review leaves the new head HIGH until that head has been reviewed. Approvals are counted from the host’s review list by login (the exclusion of anyone who launched or requested the work also matches by account id); one person with two logins is not detected, a launcher or requester who cannot be matched to a linked GitHub account refuses arming and bot approval instead of being guessed, and only the first twenty distinct approvers are checked for write access. The engagement counts show whether reviewers acted on the brief, not whether it was right, and are approximate: a delivery GitHub sends twice counts twice, a review that arrives before its head’s evaluation row exists is not counted, and the pull request’s author, bots, dismissed reviews, edited comments and text the platform wrote never count. The withdrawal sweeps are bounded (200 pull requests for one repository, 500 for a deployment-wide change), and a repository’s sweep is skipped for 60 seconds after one that found pull requests, a memory held per gateway process; past the cap the rest are withdrawn only when they next change, and until then an auto-merge already armed on GitHub stands. A merged LOW change is marked a bad merge only when a later merged revert says so in GitHub’s default wording within 14 days, so a revert written in other words is not seen and the evidence gate cannot count it; the evidence is literal to the deployment, so every organization and team on the instance shares one history. A person who dismisses the evaluator’s approval suppresses it on that pull request.
limits.title: Pull-request evaluation is a rule-based screen, not a review

limits.body: A scoped token keeps every permission the App was granted on its repository, and a personal access token cannot be narrowed at all.
limits.detail: The mint narrows the repository set only; the token’s permissions are the App’s. A repository with no stored name, and every path that spans an installation (listing its repositories, a probe of the installation itself, the sign-in identity and organization checks, skill-source imports), mints a full-scope token. For a renamed repository whose stored name is stale, the minting process mints a full-scope token for the lookup, which stays in the process token cache under the unscoped key until it expires, before minting by id. A personal access token is not an installation token and is never narrowed. The platform does not update a stale stored repository name; it logs a warning and keeps minting by id.
limits.title: Installation tokens are narrowed by repository, not by permission

limits.body: Only calls that go through the worker’s fetch, plus the egress proxy’s own rows, are recorded; bodies are redacted by pattern and cut, and writing is best effort.
limits.detail: A harness process, git and package managers in a workspace that do not pass the egress proxy (which must be configured, and which the repository’s own git host bypasses), any client that opens its own sockets, and anything outside an activity (the workflow isolate has no network) are not captured. The proxy’s rows carry host, port, status and byte counts, never a body, and they are written whatever the capture switch says. Body redaction is pattern-based over JSON values, strings and credential shapes: it does not guarantee that no secret appears in a stored body, and the path keeps everything except query parameters named like credentials. Model bodies are not in this table; they live in the agent transcript, which has its own retention. A row is buffered after the call ends and written in batches of up to 100, mostly when the activity ends; that close can hold the activity for up to ten seconds, after which it stops waiting, so a crash, a slow database or a body that outlasts the close timeout can lose some. A call is marked blocked only when the outbound guard or the egress proxy refuses it. Capture, body size and retention are GLOBAL settings only, with no team or template override.
limits.title: The action log records fetch calls, not everything a run sends

limits.body: Proxy variables are a request to the client: unless a restricted lock closes every other route out of the workspace or step, code in it can clear them or open a socket directly, and the repository’s git host is exempt.
limits.detail: The allowlist and the audit reach only HTTP and HTTPS clients that honour the proxy variables. Under the restricted policy a workspace is locked to the egress proxy (when the effective baseline plus team list is non-empty), the repository’s git host, the model and registry proxies and any LFS storage hosts setup needs; every other outward destination is closed, so HTTP(S) to anything else must go through the proxy. A restricted ephemeral step or sidecar is locked to its wired proxies before author code starts. Only an open workspace or an explicitly open step is unlocked, so a process there can unset the variables or reach a public address directly, and UDP and other TCP traffic are not seen. The git host bypasses the proxy by design. Under the open policy an empty team allowlist allows every host; under restricted an empty effective list proxies nothing, the workspace is locked down as for blocked and an egress-enabled step is held to no network. A wildcard entry does not match its bare domain. A CONNECT tunnel is logged without content, so a tunnelled request’s path and payload are not in the log, and a row is written when the exchange ends, so a worker that dies mid-exchange leaves none.
limits.title: The egress proxy covers clients that use it, not every connection

limits.body: An orphaned Docker workspace can live for hours before the sweep may remove it, and only marked containers and pods are candidates.
limits.detail: Age is the only proof an object is unused, so an orphaned Docker container lives for about seven hours (the six-hour agent-run activity ceiling plus an hour of slack) before it is eligible, and one without a readable creation stamp is never swept. A backlog larger than the 25-removal cap drains over several sweeps. Volumes and every other Docker object are left alone. The sweep reaps the backend of the worker that picks it up, so a deployment that mixes Docker and Kubernetes workers is swept only for whichever backend runs it. Kubernetes cleanup relies on the list and delete permissions on pods that the worker’s boot check already requires. A sweep that cannot list or remove reports it in the worker log and the counts of its activity result, and raises nothing else.
limits.title: The workspace sweep is age-bounded and does not remove volumes

limits.body: A rollup day is as current as its last rebuild, and a digest is withheld for a week with any unbuilt day.
limits.detail: A day older than the window is read from its rollup, so a change to a source the dirty-day scans do not watch (the ledger rows that supply a run’s spend when its accrued cost is zero, for one) is not seen once the day ages out, and with the default backfill of zero a day that was never built before the sweep first covered it stays on the live read. Dirty-day rebuilds are capped at sixty a sweep, so a mass edit of old rows takes several sweeps to show. A digest is not sent for a week with any unbuilt day, so a failed or disabled rollup sweep delays or withholds digests within the workflow’s retries and the subscription records the error; a week skipped as too soon or out of order is not sent later. A target that has failed three times for a week is not retried for that week and the subscription keeps showing the error. Delivery is best effort: a missing SMTP or Resend transport fails the email target, a Slack post needs a bot token for the channel, and neither confirms the message was read. The worst-gate figure is omitted past 50,000 gate rows, and the digest’s other figures come from the same rollups as the Reports page, so they share its bounds.
limits.title: Rollups and digests are only as complete as the sweep that built them

limits.body: Launches and later model calls are refused once the team’s spend has reached its cap, so concurrent work can overshoot it.
limits.detail: The launch decision reads month-to-date spend without a lock, so concurrent launches see the same total. The mid-run guard reads through a cache of one config window and refuses only after the cached spend has reached the cap; a call already admitted completes and bills in full. A spend or cap read that fails lets the call through. The pre-call check a Claude Code or Pi turn makes fails open the same way for anything but a genuine spend refusal, and calls already in flight when a cap is crossed still finish and bill. A run is counted against the team its spend is attributed to, the repository’s OWNER; a team whose members launch on a repository shared with it neither spends nor is limited by its own cap there. A run with no attributed team is outside every team’s cap, and so is the in-app assistant of a person who belongs to several teams or organizations. The Slack notice is a side effect of the guard’s cache refresh, so a team that makes no model call is told nothing; the notice goes to the team’s notify channel only, a permanently failing post (channel gone, archived or not joined, token revoked) keeps its claim and is not retried that month, and a team with no channel or no bot token is sent and claims nothing. The team cap does not change token tiers, and both USD caps are checked independently, so the lower one binds first.
limits.title: A team’s USD cap is best-effort, and the owner pays on shared repositories

limits.body: Members see a state and a percentage of a cap; that is a summary and not a secrecy boundary.
limits.detail: The organization’s dollar cap and spend are returned only to an organization ADMIN, and a team’s only to its team ADMIN, an organization ADMIN or a platform ADMIN. The team overview withholds month cost in dollars from a viewer whose binding cap is the organization’s unless they are an organization ADMIN. Anyone who can read a spend figure for the same scope elsewhere (a team LEAD’s usage report of their team, for example) can divide it by the percentage and recover the cap. The refusal text also tells a refused launcher that the budget is spent. Report digests choose dollars or percentage once per message for all recipients; a team digest always carries a percentage.
limits.title: A budget percentage hides the amount only until a second number is known

limits.body: A team’s lists include work on repositories shared with it, while reported totals count only the owning team.
limits.detail: List scopes (the team space, ?team=, the desk) include work on repositories the team owns or that are shared to it and runs of its templates; metrics scopes attribute a run to exactly one team, the owner, so a shared repository is not counted by both and a sharee’s totals do not include it. The team filter is checked for membership and narrows only: it grants nothing, and visibility and repository-access gates still apply. The personal desk is bounded to the caller’s own active teams even for a platform ADMIN, lists at most 25 items, and looks at attempts from the last 30 days plus any still running. Preference slugs are format-checked but not checked against membership, so a stale or foreign slug resolves to nothing. Deactivating a team does not remove repository access (see that boundary).
limits.title: A team space and a team filter narrow lists; reports count owners only

limits.body: Only the Claude Code runtime offers the question tool; Mastra and Pi never pause, and a resumed run is a new container, not the old session.
limits.detail: pausable() grants allowPause only when the resolved runtime is claude-code. The resumed agent sees the questions, the answers and a truncated, credential-masked digest, not its earlier conversation, and only the working tree (including its own local commits, folded into the patch) survives; processes, installed packages outside the tree and anything outside the checkout are gone. Nothing answers on a person’s behalf: a timeout fails the step non-retryably. A tree over 20 MiB, state over the size cap, an answer that stays unusable after three re-asks, and a rebase conflict each fail non-retryably instead of continuing. The human step is an ordinary INPUT step, so who may answer follows the human-step rules, not the agent’s credentials.
limits.title: Ask-and-resume is Claude Code only and keeps a patch, not a live session

limits.body: A RunEffect row is written after the change and gates nothing; a failed or timed-out write loses the row, and several outbound writes never call it.
limits.detail: It does not replace the outcome ledger that makes writeOutcome and runTool retries refuse, and it takes no part in approvals. The call sites are the git pushes in the implementer, the decomposition push and agent-run finalization, pull-request creation, the tracker syncs from the run steps, the PRD ticket and page creation, the pull-request link written to a knowledge-base page and MCP tools. A CI-fix push, a ticket comment, a run callback, a Slack post, the generic connector writes and shell or container egress are not recorded. The digest cannot recover the input, and MCP tool classification trusts the remote server’s annotation. The ledger is read through one route that cuts at a fixed page size, with a truncated flag.
limits.title: The effects ledger is a record, not a control or a complete list

limits.body: Approval pins what an administrator read, not what it does: plugin scripts and hooks execute inside the run container, and profiles reach only the Claude Code runtime.
limits.detail: The scanners and structure checks produce warnings an admin acknowledges; they do not block, and a script can behave differently from how it reads. Instructions and skills are appended as data to the agent’s prompt, and anything a plugin does inside the container is subject to the same confinement as the harness itself, not a stronger one. A profile is global, so every team’s agent bound to it gets the same version unless the run pinned another. A pin keeps a disabled profile working for runs that already have it. On the Claude Code runtime with a workspace, a profile’s tools list can name only Skill and Agent, and the runtime adds whichever it names to the agent’s granted list whatever the agent’s toolKeys say, so the list can widen the grant only by those two built-ins; its plugins’ hooks still run commands in the container outside the tool grant. Mastra and Pi ignore a bound profile and record agent.profile_not_applicable. The workspace tools come from toolKeys alone: readFile and listDirectory grant Read, Glob and Grep, writeFile grants Write and Edit, bash grants Bash. For an implementer step a null, empty or non-matching list grants all six; for an agent run or agent node a null list grants only Read, Glob and Grep and an empty or non-matching one grants none. MCP tools of the agent’s own connection bind only from that connection and toolKeys (an explicit mcp key, or a null or empty list). A plugin server an ADMIN mapped is relayed to the agents bound to its plugin, only for the profiles the run was given, under the mapped connection’s own allowlist, screening and access rule, and only where the agent’s toolKeys enable MCP. Browser tools bind only from an explicit browser key, and a profile cannot grant them. The Skill tool runs only skills and commands the profile’s own plugins declare, an Agent call must run in the foreground on the session’s model, and a sub-agent’s own tool calls are decided against the same granted list, so a sub-agent cannot use a workspace tool the agent’s toolKeys leave out.
limits.title: An approved profile is trusted content that runs in the workspace

limits.body: The sidebar only reads the server’s permission answer; the gateway and the route layouts are the controls.
limits.detail: An unknown state (the answer not loaded, a key the server did not list) counts as not held, so an entry can be absent while loading or after a failed read without the person having lost access. The Setup button renders nothing when the readiness read fails or when every item is ticked, so its absence says neither.
